units.la: CUm anno 1570. & aliquot sequentibus, maxima esset apud nos fames & rerum omnium penu-ria, ita ut ex longinquis etiam regionibus petendum esset frumentum: LVDOVICVS LAVATERVS Ecclesiae nostrae minister, cum explicaret libros Paralip. tres Conciones de fame & caritate annonae habuit, quae cum omnibus gratae fuissent, & plurimum consolationis attulissent; (cui enim non gratum fuisset, in tanta angustia, in tanta miseria, audire tam graves adhortationes, tam suaves consolationes, in primis ab illo viro, qui nec avaritiae, nec prodigali-tatis suspectus erat.) Has rogatu amicorum, ut aliis quoque communica-ret, in lucem edidit: Lectae & relectae sunt in his miserijs tam à diuitibus, quam ab egenis, singulari cum volu-ptate, voluptatē animi dico, propter consolatione & institutionem, quam inde omnes pariter perceperunt.
units.tr: When in the year 1570 and several years following there was great famine and a complete scarcity of all goods among us, so that grain had to be sought even from distant regions, Ludwig Lavater, minister of our Church, expounded the three books of Chronicles and delivered three sermons on famine and the price of grain. They were welcomed by everyone and brought great comfort. (For who would not have been glad, in such distress and such misery, to hear such grave exhortations and such gentle consolations, especially from a man who was suspected neither of greed nor of prodigality?) At the request of friends, and so that others might share them too, he has now published them. In these hardships they have been read and re-read, by the rich and the poor alike, with singular delight (I mean delight of mind), because of the consolation and instruction that all equally received from them.

units.la: Quid Magistratus interim? Is au-tem officio suo fideliter functus est. Latæ & obseruatæ sunt sumptuariæ leges: Institutæ sunt publicæ preces publico decreto, maxima frequentia & deuotione habitæ. In morū emen-datione, pietatis exercitio, commune fere omnium ordinum fuit studium. Hic etiam dici non potest quanta fue-rit magistratus nostri, in distribuen-do & vendendo frumento, nō nostris tantum, sed & vicinis & confœdera-tis, æquitas, quanta in erogandis e-leemosynis (turmatim etiam exte-ris confluentibus) munificentia, quanta denique ciuium erga omnes egenos promiscuē liberalitas? Pluri-ma publica & priuata extruebantur ædificia. Est enim in tanta penuria, maxima fere misericordiæ. species, artificum & operariorum opera vti. Quid speciem dico:Est summum ge-nus misericordiæ. Egestatis namq;ma[?] ter imò nouerca est luxus & otium. At his malis mederi potest, si magi-stratus, vt Paulus monet, ἀτάκτως[?] cohibet, otiosos non fert, laborare & aliquid operis facere volentes condu-cit, inuitos autem adigit ad labores, his inquam artibus efficitur, vt in a-bundantia rerum, nec luxu, nec otio torpescant: nec in penuria, labori-bus & frugalitate assuefacti, egeant. Hæ fuere superioribus annis, Amplissimi nostri magistratus constitu-tiones, hæc vitæ & morum emenda-tio, hæc erga egenos liberalitas, erga ignauos legum seueritas.
units.tr: What, meanwhile, did the magistrates do? They performed their office faithfully. Sumptuary laws were enacted and observed. Public prayers were ordered by public decree and held with the greatest attendance and devotion. In the amendment of morals and the practice of piety, nearly all orders of society shared a common zeal. Here too it cannot be said how great was the fairness of our magistrates in distributing and selling grain, not only to our own people but also to neighbours and allies; how great the generosity in dispensing alms (even foreigners flocking to them in crowds); and, finally, how impartial the kindness of our citizens towards all the needy. Many public and private buildings were being erected. For in such a scarcity, employing craftsmen and labourers is almost the greatest form of mercy. I say "almost": it is the highest kind of mercy. For luxury and idleness are the stepmother of poverty. These evils, however, can be remedied if the magistrate, as Paul advises, restrains those who live disorderly [ἀτάκτως], does not tolerate the idle, and hires those willing to labour and do some work, while compelling the unwilling to toil. By these methods it is brought about that, in plenty, people are not made sluggish by luxury or idleness, and that in scarcity, being accustomed to labour and thrift, they do not lack. These were, in recent years, the ordinances of our most distinguished magistrates: this the amendment of life and manners, this the generosity towards the needy, and towards the idle the severity of the laws.

units.la: Misericors ergo Deus, pro singula-ri sua erga genus humanum, in pri-mis erga Remp. Tigurinam veræ Ecclesiæ nutricem, misericordía & benignitate, consumpto omni frumento,
units.tr: Therefore God, merciful, out of his singular goodwill towards the human race, and above all towards the Commonwealth of Zurich, the nurse of the true Church, in his mercy and kindness, when all the grain had been used up,

units.la: praeter omniu spem fertilem annum, frumenti copiam, frugu vbertatem, vini abundantiam dedit. Medimnus[?] frumenti qui sex ante florenis Germanicis emebatur, duobus post messem emitur, facta haec sunt Anno 1575. Sed vt fit, rerum copia, proteruiores reddit homines, non obseruata est legum sæueritas, morum probitas. Multi namq; ad ingenium redierre. Deus ergo iusto iudicio reuocauit famem & rerum caritat[?], an rursum his medijs ad pristinam pietatem, constantiam, probitatem nos reuocare possit. Præmisit duros monitores (pios monitores multi amplius audi-re noluerunt) pruinam, frigus, diutur-nas pluuias, hæ vites perdiderut (qua in re peccamus, in eadem punimur.) Annus in primis 1584. inauspicatus fuit, in ipsis Calendis Ianuarij, ful-gura & tonitrua audita sunt. In car-nispriuio terra tremuit, homines, iu-menta, pagos integros obruit, &c. in ipso Ascensionis festo, horrenda, longe lateque vastans grando, segetes, & viueta prostrauit, arbores dissiecit. Subsequuntur eodem & sequenti anno frequentes, maximae & insolitae aquarum inundationes, quæ & ipsa frugibus maximum damnum intule-runt. Has calamitates sequitur maior quam vnquam antea rerum omnium penuria, caritas & dira fames, quę nō nostram tantum regionem sed vniuersum fere orbem terrarum perua-fere. In his calamitatibus, multos viros graues, doctos & pios amisit Ecclesia & Resp. nostra, quorum consi-lio, auxilio & consolatione sumopere indigemus. Sed age cum viuos audire non possumus, mortuos audiamus. Et cum vniuersalis sit hæc poena, ideo visum est Latino sermone tres has Conciones in lucem dare, vt exterae nationes, ex earum lectione consolationem & consilium in his angustijs capiant. Inseruit quidem, easdem, author ex versione cuiufdam studiosi Concionibus quas in Ezechiel ad cap. 14. Geneuæ edidit, ordine tamen multum immutato, multis etiã, ex industria, omissis. Quas cum non omnes habeant, nec facile comparare possint: Curauimus nos, ne quid defit, & vt omnia Germanico exemplari respondeant, ac sumptibus consuleremus ementium, prioren versionẽ aliqua ex parte nouam fieri. Eam nunc tibi Candide Lector, in officina Frofchouiana renatam communicamus. Tu pro tuo candore, his fruere. Vale. Tiguri, Anno vltimi temporis 1587. 25. Ianuarij.
units.tr: beyond all hope gave us a fertile year, an abundance of grain, a richness of crops and plenty of wine. The medimnus of grain, which had been bought for six German florins before, was bought after the harvest for two. This happened in the year 1575. But, as usually happens, the abundance of goods made men more wanton; the strictness of the laws and the integrity of morals were not observed. For many relapsed into their former nature. God therefore, by a just judgement, withdrew the famine and the dearth of goods, to see whether by these means he could again recall us to our former piety, steadfastness and uprightness. He sent harsh warnings beforehand (many would not listen to the godly warnings any longer): hoarfrost, cold, and long rains, which destroyed the vines. (In what we sin, in the same we are punished.) The year 1584 began unpropitiously: on the very Calends of January lightning and thunder were heard. In Shrovetide the earth trembled, and it overwhelmed men, beasts and whole villages, and so on. On the very feast of the Ascension a terrible hail, devastating far and wide, beat down the crops and the vines and tore apart the trees. In the same year and the following one there followed frequent, very great and unusual floods of water, which also inflicted the greatest damage on the crops. These calamities were followed by a scarcity of all goods and a dire famine, greater than ever before, which spread not only through our region but over nearly the whole world. In these calamities the Church and our Commonwealth have lost many grave, learned and godly men, whose counsel, help and consolation we need greatly. But come, since we cannot hear the living, let us hear the dead. And since this affliction is universal, it has seemed fitting to publish these three sermons in Latin, so that foreign nations, from reading them, may gain consolation and counsel in these straits. The author indeed has included the same sermons which he published at Geneva, on Ezekiel chapter 14, in a translation by a certain scholar, though with the order much changed and many things deliberately omitted. Since not everyone has them, nor can easily obtain them, we have taken care, so that nothing may be lacking and that they may correspond to the German exemplar, and to spare the expense of buyers, to make the earlier translation partly new. We now present it to you, kind reader, reborn in the workshop of Frosch. Enjoy it, in your candour. Farewell. Zurich, in the year of the last time 1587, 25 January.

units.la: HAC DOCETUR ANNONAE CARITATEM & famem, divinitus imitti. Item quam dira & horribilis sit pœna fames.
units.tr: HERE IT IS TAUGHT THAT THE CHARITY OF THE GRAIN SUPPLY AND FAMINE ARE SENT FROM GOD. Also how dreadful and horrible a punishment famine is.

units.tr: 31. So that they may fear you and walk in your ways all the days that they live upon the face of the land that you gave to our fathers.

units.la: Salomon sapientiæ & pietatis nomine clarissimus rex, extructo & perfecto templo Ierosolymitano, illud piis & artendibus [?] precibus ad Deum,
units.tr: Solomon, most famous as a king for his wisdom and piety, after the temple at Jerusalem was built and finished, consecrated it to God with pious and ardent prayers

units.la: præsenti omni populo consecrauit. In his pre‑cibus primo omnipotentiam, veritatem & misericordiam eius commendat & prædicat. Deinde petit vt promissionum Dauidi patri factarum memorem esse, easq; præstare, item præsentiæ suæ signum, in tàm sacro, augusto, ipsiusq; cultui dicato templo exhibere velit, exaudiendo nimirum hoc in loco denuotas piorum ad se clamantium preces. Enumerat autem sex septemuè calamitatis species, ex quibus populum in hoc templo ad se clamantem, liberare dignetur. Ex his tertia species est siccitas, Iudeæ in primis infesta, petit vt in hac necessitate petentibus pluuias det. Quarta est fames, annonæ caritas, pestis, varij & inauditi morbi vitium, segetum, vrbium obsessio, aut aliæ huius generis calamitates, & in his malis iugiter clamantes exaudiat, & pœnam hanc auertat. Sed omissis singulis, quæ in hac oratione obseruanda veniunt, de caritate & fame, in præsentia auxilio diuino pluribus agemus: hac enim pœna multis iam annis non malos tantum, sed & viros bonos exercuit; om‑ nibus ergo ex æquo grauis & molesta est.
units.tr: in the presence of all the people. In these prayers he first commends and proclaims God's omnipotence, truth and mercy. Then he asks that God remember the promises made to his father David and fulfil them, and likewise that he be willing to show a sign of his presence in this so sacred, august temple dedicated to his worship, namely by hearing the prayers of the pious who cry out to him in this place. He lists six or seven kinds of calamity, from which he deigns to free the people who cry out to him in this temple. Of these, the third kind is drought, which is especially hostile to Judea; he asks that he give rain to those who petition him in this need. The fourth is famine, dearth of grain, pestilence, the affliction of various and unheard-of diseases, the blight of crops, the siege of cities, or other calamities of this kind; he asks that he hear those who cry out continually amid these evils and turn away this punishment. But, leaving aside the individual matters which are to be observed in this prayer, we shall speak, with God's help, at more length about dearth and famine, since this punishment has for many years now afflicted not only the wicked but also good men; it is therefore equally heavy and troublesome for all.

units.la: Verendum quoque ne annonæ præcium in hac rerum omnium penuria in tam corrupto & auaritiæ luxuique dedito seculo augeatur, ni seria pœnitentia iram Dei anteuertamus. Pater cœlestis non secundum nostra merita sed secundum immensam suam miseri-cordiam nos tractare dignetur.
units.tr: We must also fear that the price of grain, in this general scarcity of all things, will rise in such a corrupt age, given over to avarice and luxury, unless we forestall the wrath of God by earnest repentance. May the heavenly Father deign to deal with us not according to our merits but according to his immense mercy.

units.la: Vt autem omnia melius ac plenius intel-ligantur hoc ordine procedendum statui.
units.tr: So that all these things may be understood better and more fully, I have decided to proceed in this order.

units.la: 1. Docebo, unde sit annonæ caritas & fa-mes nimirum à Deo.
units.tr: 1. I shall teach whence dearth of grain and famine come, namely from God.

units.la: 2. Deinde quàm dira & grauis pœna sit demonstrabo.
units.tr: 2. Then I shall show how dire and grave a punishment it is.

units.la: 3. Tertio loco, cur Deus hoc flagello mu-dum castigare soleat.
units.tr: 3. Thirdly, why God is accustomed to chastise the world with this scourge.

units.la: 4. Quartò loco quomodo diuites & pauperes tempore famis tam publicè quàm priuatim sese gerere debeant.
units.tr: 4. Fourthly, how rich and poor ought to conduct themselves in time of famine, both publicly and privately.

units.la: Postremò promissiones aliquas audiemus, quibus Deus pollicetur, se electos suos tempore famis non solum seruare, sed & plagam auertere velle.
units.tr: Finally, we shall hear some promises by which God pledges that he wishes not only to preserve his elect in time of famine but also to avert the plague.

units.la: Quod ad vocabula caritatis & famis attinet, est aliqua sed per exigua differen-tia. Caritas est, quando omnia illa, quæ ad hominis victum pertinent, puta cibus, potus, vestes, hospitia, aliæq; res magno pretio emuntur. Fames vero est, quando hæc quæ dixi, vænalia non sunt, etiamsi pecuniæ non desint. Apud diuites hæc differentia quidem valet, pauperes autem & egeni, nullam inter caritatem & famem differentiam norunt: nam etiam in copia rerum, quia pecunia destituuntur, esurire tamen, & fame cõtabescere coguntur.
units.tr: As far as the terms dearth and famine are concerned, there is some difference, though a slight one. There is dearth when all those things that pertain to man's sustenance, such as food, drink, clothing, lodging and other goods, are bought at a high price. Famine, however, is when those things I have mentioned are not for sale, even though money is not lacking. Among the rich this difference indeed holds, but the poor and needy know no difference between dearth and famine: for even in an abundance of goods, since they lack money, they are compelled to go hungry and waste away with hunger.

units.la: Est autem fames vel caritas alia vni-uersalis, alia particularis. Uniuersalem voco, quando in omnibus fere regionibus frugum est penuria, qualis hæc est, quam hodie experimur. Particularis quando ratum[?] pagus aliquis vrbs, regio, hisce rebus destituitur.
units.tr: Moreover, famine or dearth is of two kinds, one universal and the other particular. I call it universal when there is a shortage of crops in almost all regions, such as the one we are experiencing today. It is particular when some village, town or region is deprived of these things.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem omnes aliæ cala-mitates diuinitus immittuntur, idem etiam de caritate annonæ & fame statuendum est. Deus enim in lege expressè populo sao[?] famē minatur si verbo ipsius non obtemperet, Letuit. 26. ad hunc modum loquitur: Si non audientis me, nec feceritis mandata mea, sed spreueritis leges meas &c. frustra feretis sementem quæ ab hostibus devorabitur. Si autem nec sic obedieritis mihi, dabo uobis cælum desuper sicut ferrum, & terram æneam. Consumetur incassum labor uester, non proferet terra germen, nec arbores poma præbebunt, quod si nec sic uolueritis recipere disciplinam, frangam baculum panis uestri, ita ut decem mulieres in uno clibano coquant panes, & reddant eos ad pondus & commendetis, nec saturabimini. Deut.28.pluribus hæc repetit dicens. Quod si audire nolueris uocem Dei tui, ut custodias & facias omnia mandata eius, & ceremonias quas ego præcipio tibi hodie. Venient super te omnes maledictiones ista, & apprehendent te. Maledictus eris in ciuitate, in agro. Maledictum horreum tuum, & maledictæ reliquiæ tuæ, maledictus fructus uentris tui, & fructus terræ tuæ, armenta boum tuorum, & greges ouium tuorum, &c. Dominus mittet super te famem, & esuriem, & increpationem, in omnia opera tua, quæ tu facies. Et mox. Sit cœlum quod supra te est æneum, & terra quam calcas ferrea. Det Dominus imbrem terræ tuæ, pulverem, de cœlo descendat super te cinis, donec conteraris &c. Paulo post. Fructum terræ tuæ & vniuersum laborem commedet populus quem tu non noui sti. Mox. Sementem multam facies interram, & medicum congregabis, quia locustæ devorabunt omnia. Vineam plantabis & fodies & vinum non bibes nec colliges ex ea quippiam quoniam vastabitur vermibus. Oliuas habebis, in omnibus terminis tuis, & non vngeris oleo quia & effluent & deperibunt, etc. Omnes arbores tuas & fruges terræ tuæ rubigo consumet, etc. Seruies inimico tuo quem immittet tibi Dominus in fame & nuditate & omni penuria, & ponet iugum ferreum super ceruicem tuam donec te conterat. Adducet Dominus super te gentem de longinquo, & de extremis terræ finibus in similitudinem aquilæ volantis cum impetu, cuius linguam intelligere non possis, gentem procacissimam, quæ non deferat senem, nec miserēatur parvuli & devoret fructum iumentorum tuorum, ac fruges terræ tuæ do nec intereas, & non relinquet tibi triticum, vinum & oleum, armenta boum, & greges ovium donec te dispergat.
units.tr: Just as all other calamities are sent by God, so too must the same be determined concerning dearth of grain and famine. For God expressly threatens famine to his people in the law if they do not obey his word, and speaks in this way in Leviticus 26: "If you do not hear me, nor do my commandments, but despise my laws, etc., you will sow in vain, for your seed will be devoured by your enemies. But if you will not even so obey me, I will make the heavens above you like iron and the earth like brass. Your labour will be spent in vain; the earth will not bring forth its increase, nor will the trees give their fruit. And if you will not even so receive discipline, I will break the staff of your bread, so that ten women shall bake bread in one oven and shall give it back by weight, and you shall eat and not be satisfied." Deuteronomy 28 repeats these things at greater length, saying: "But if you will not hear the voice of the Lord your God, to keep and do all his commandments and ceremonies which I command you today, all these curses shall come upon you and overtake you. You shall be cursed in the city and cursed in the field. Your barn shall be cursed and your remnants cursed; the fruit of your womb shall be cursed, and the fruit of your land, the herds of your oxen and the flocks of your sheep, etc. The Lord will send upon you famine and hunger and rebuke in all the works that you do. And soon after: "Let the heaven that is above you be brass, and the earth that you tread be iron. May the Lord give to your land dust for rain, and let ashes come down upon you from heaven until you are crushed, etc." A little later: "A people whom you have not known shall eat the fruit of your land and all your labour. Soon: You shall sow much seed in the land and gather little, because the locusts shall devour everything. You shall plant a vineyard and dig it, but you shall not drink wine nor gather anything from it, for it shall be wasted by worms. You shall have olive trees in all your borders, but you shall not be anointed with oil, because they will drop off and perish, etc. Rust shall consume all your trees and the fruits of your land, etc. You shall serve your enemy whom the Lord will send against you in hunger and nakedness and all want, and he will put an iron yoke upon your neck until he has crushed you. The Lord will bring against you a nation from afar, from the ends of the earth, like an eagle flying swiftly, a nation whose language you cannot understand, a very insolent nation, which will not spare the old nor pity the young, and will devour the fruit of your cattle and the produce of your land until you perish, and it will leave you no wheat, wine or oil, nor herds of oxen or flocks of sheep, until it destroys you."

units.la: Scripta prophetarum legenti, plurima testimonia occurrunt (ex his quædam suo loco citabimus) quibus Deus populo suo minatur ni pœnitentiam agant se sublaturum frume-tum, vinum, oleum, fructus arborum, pisces, carnes, & alia quæ ad victum hominus pertinent. Apud proph: Amos. 4. cap. dicit Dominus. Ego dedi vobis stupore dentium (seu ut alii vertunt munditiem dentium i.penu-riam carnium) in cunctis urbibus vestris, & indigentiam panum in omnibus locis vestris, & non reversi estis ad me, dicit Dominus. Ego quoque prohibui a vobis imbrem, cum adhuc tres menses superessent usque ad messem, & plui super unam civitatem, et super alteram civitatem non plui: pars una cōpluta est, & pars super quam non pluvi, aruit, & venerunt duæ, & tres civitates ad unam civitatem, ut biberent aquam, & non sunt satiatæ, & non redijstis ad me dicit Dominus. Percussi vos in vento vrente, & in aurigine, multitudinem hortorum vestrorum & vinearum vestrarum, oliueta vestra, & ficeta vestra commedit verruca & non redijstis ad me dicit Dominus.
units.tr: When one reads the writings of the prophets, many testimonies occur (some of which I shall cite in their place), by which God threatens his people that unless they repent he will take away from them grain, wine, oil, the fruit of trees, fish, meat and other things that pertain to man's sustenance. In the prophet Amos, chapter 4, the Lord says: "I gave you blight of teeth (or, as others translate, cleanness of teeth, that is, lack of meat) in all your cities, and want of bread in all your places, and you have not returned to me, says the Lord. I also withheld the rain from you when there were still three months until the harvest, and I rained on one city and did not rain on another city; one part was rained on, and the part on which it did not rain dried up; and two or three cities came to one city to drink water, and were not satisfied; and you have not returned to me, says the Lord. I struck you with scorching wind and with mildew; your many gardens and your vineyards, your olive groves and your fig trees, the caterpillar has devoured, and you have not returned to me, says the Lord."

units.la: Ex his verbis manifeste intelligitur pennuriam rerum, quæ ad vitam conseruandam faciunt, à Deo proficisci, ipsum dare pluuias et rursum prohibere.
units.tr: From these words it is clearly understood that the lack of the things which sustain life comes from God, and that he himself gives the rains and again withholds them.

units.la: Si fames à Deo nō mitteretur serui ipsius Prophetæ nō potuissent ex ipsius instinctu tempus exacte prædicere, quando nimirum vetura esset, quam diu duratura, quando iterum auferenda, & alia huius generis minutiora, quæ humana prudentia percipi non possunt.
units.tr: If famine were not sent by God, his servants the prophets could not, by his prompting, foretell the time exactly: when it would come, how long it would last, when it would be removed again, and other such minor matters which human prudence cannot grasp.

units.la: Legimus autem in veteri & nouo Testamento sanctos Dei Prophetas hæc omnia exacte prædixisse Iosephus exponens somnium Pharaonis de septem pinguibus, & macilentis hoc bus, item de septem plenis, & tenuibus spicis ostendit Deum hisce significare septem ferti les, & totidem sterilesannos Gen.41. Helisæus pariter septem annorum famem prædixit. In
units.tr: We read in the Old and New Testaments that the holy prophets of God foretold all these things exactly. Joseph, interpreting Pharaoh's dream of the seven fat and lean cattle, and likewise of the seven full and thin ears, showed that God signified by these seven fruitful years and as many barren ones (Gen. 41). Elisha likewise foretold a famine of seven years.

units.la: B nouo Testamento Act.ii. scribitur. Agabus prophetam afflatu spiritus sancti prædixisse horrendam famem per totum terrarum orbem grassaturam esse, quod postea sub Imperatore Claudio factum est, etc. Hæc Deus suis fide-libus reuelari voluit, ut mature sibi de victu prospicere possent, ne postea cum ignominia Christiani nominis cogerentur tempore famis victum ab infidelibus petere.
units.tr: In the New Testament it is written in Acts ii. that the prophet Agabus, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, foretold that a dreadful famine would rage through the whole orb of the earth, which afterwards came to pass under the Emperor Claudius, etc. God wished these things to be revealed to his faithful, so that they might provide for their food in good time, lest afterwards, to the disgrace of the Christian name, they should be forced in time of famine to beg food from unbelievers.

units.la: Legimus quidem Astrologos quosdam ferties & steriles annos quandoque prædixisse.
units.tr: We indeed read that certain astrologers have sometimes foretold fertile and barren years.

units.la: Thales, ut est apud Diogenem Laertium, ac cusabatur quod occupatus studijs philosophicis rem familiarem negligeret. Is ostendere volens philosophiæ quoq; ad comparadas opes aliquem vsum esse. Oliueta omnia illo anno conducebat, quod ex Physicis causis intelli-gebat non felicem fore olei proventum sequenti anno, postea oleum magno pretio vedebat [?]. Etsi vero periti Astrologi interdum ex Physicis causis vbertatem & sterilitatem prædicant, tamen eorum prædictiones non raro fallunt. Deus enim non esse alligatus causis secundis, sed libere præter communem naturæ cursum multa agit. Propterea inter Prophetarum & Astrologorum prædictiones magna est differentia.
units.tr: Thales, as Diogenes Laertius relates, was accused of neglecting his private affairs because he was occupied with philosophical studies. Wishing to show that philosophy also has some use for acquiring wealth, he hired all the olive presses in that year, since he understood from natural causes that the olive yield would not be happy the following year; afterwards he sold the oil at a high price. Although skilled astrologers sometimes predict fertility and barrenness from natural causes, their predictions often fail. For God is not bound to secondary causes, but freely does many things beyond the common course of nature. Therefore there is a great difference between the predictions of the prophets and those of the astrologers.

units.la: Prognostici illi libelli seu prædictiones Astrologorum de singulorum annorum bellis, morbis, terræ fructibus, calore, frigore, siccitate & humiditate nulla certa ratione nituntur, sed ab Astrologis confictæ sunt, ut imperitis imponant.
units.tr: Those prognostic booklets, or the predictions of astrologers about each year's wars, diseases, the fruits of the earth, heat, cold, drought and moisture, rest on no sure reasoning, but are invented by the astrologers to deceive the unskilled.

units.la: Sed impostūram facile deprehendes si legis hunc vel illum diem pluviosum fore, tu serenum fere notato. Si ventosum tu tranquillum fore repone, & non minus te verum dixisse deprehendes quam calculatores illos.
units.tr: But you will easily detect the deceit if you read that this or that day will be rainy, and you note it as fair; if you set down that it will be windy, and it turns out calm; you will find that you have spoken the truth no less than those calculators.

units.la: Miraris certe non immerito, viros alioqui doctos, & iudicio præditos huiusmodi posse nugis fidem adhibere. Habent aliâs Ephemerides suum quoq; usum, ex illis enim motum lunæ, festa & alia huius generis petenda, reliqua suis authoribus relinquenda sunt.
units.tr: You certainly wonder, and not undeservedly, that men otherwise learned and endowed with judgment can give credence to such trifles. Almanacs have their own use, for from them the motion of the moon, the festivals and other things of this kind are to be sought, and the rest is to be left to their authors.

units.la: Habent & Rustici sua prognostica, tempestatum & ventorum per totum annum, quæ etsi vera esse interdum deprehendamus tamen ut plurimum etiam falsa sunt. Licet etiam suas Physicas rationes habeant: Tamen (vt ante dixi) Deus Dominus est totius naturæ, & ijs rebus non est adstrictus, sed cuncta gubernat suo arbitratu.
units.tr: Country folk also have their prognostics of weather and winds for the whole year, which, although we sometimes find them true, are for the most part also false. Although they have their natural reasons too, nevertheless (as I said before) God is the Lord of all nature, and is not bound by those things, but governs all things at his own will.

units.la: Ex his etiam colligitur, famem à Deo immitti, licet (vt postea dicemus) causis secun-dis interdum vtatur. Huc Salomon in precatione hac sua respexit, qua petit, vt si populus in templo Dei collectus, tempore famis Deum precaretur hanc pœnam ab eis auferre, commodam tempestatem & fertilitatem eis conferre, pruinas, grandines, pe-stesque telluris varias arcere & depellere velit. Ni enim hæc diuinitus immitteren-tur, sed casu fierent quid precibus opus ef-set?
units.tr: From these things too it is gathered that famine is sent by God, although (as we shall say later) he sometimes makes use of secondary causes. To this Solomon looked in his prayer, in which he asks that if the people, gathered in God's temple in time of famine, should pray that God remove this punishment from them, he would grant them suitable weather and fertility, and would ward off and drive away frosts, hailstorms, and the various plagues of the earth. For if these were not sent from God but happened by chance, what need would there be of prayer?

units.la: Præterea legimus Leuit.23. Deum mandasse populo Israelitico, vt postridie Paschæ gomer (est decima pars Ephæ) nouarum spicarum (vel vt alij exponunt manipulum nouarum frugum immolarent Deo, & tum demum nouis frugibus vescerentur. Postea festo Pentecostes, quod alio nomine festum nouarum frugum appellatur) iubebantur panes ex nouis frugibus coctos Deo offerre. Hinc Pontificiorum carnes, & liba confec-randi consuetudo orta uidetur. In Autum-no collectis frugibus, festum Tabernaculo-rum celebrabatur. His festis ac ceremonijs testabantur, se terræ fruges Deo uero tem-pestatum patrono, accepta ferre, non suis la-boribus, sudoribus & industriæ id tribuere. Huic uni & soli pro messe & uindemia om-nibusq; beneficijs præstitis gratias esse agen-das: Ipsumque precandum, ut frugibus, quas in horrea conuexissent, benediceret, illasque quæ adhuc in agris fuissent, defenderet, ipsis-que gratiam suam conferret, ut cum timore ipsius ueraque pace, eius donis suerentur. Huc illud D. Pauli facit qui Timoth.4.te-statur omnes cibos in hoc creatos à Deo, ut cum laude & gratiarum actione illis utamur, nec reijciendos esse si cum gratiarum a-ctione illis uescamur, cibos sanctificari per uerbum Dei & preces. Non ergo te pudeat cænam cum precibus, & gratiarum actione auspicari, & finire. Quæ enim dementia es-set huius te pudere, cum te non pudeat bis Dei donis plena mensa tanta cum ingrati-tudine & intemperantia abuti, quin & alios non exemplo tantum sed & verbis factoque ad pocula provocare.
units.tr: Moreover, we read in Leviticus 23 that God commanded the people of Israel that on the day after the Passover they should offer to God a gomer (which is the tenth part of an ephah) of new ears of grain (or, as others explain, a sheaf of the new fruits), and only then eat of the new fruits. Afterwards, at the feast of Pentecost, which by another name is called the feast of new fruits, they were commanded to offer to God loaves baked from the new grain (ref. 'panes' and so on). Hence the custom of the Papists of consecrating meats and cakes seems to have arisen. When the crops were gathered in during autumn, the feast of Tabernacles was celebrated. By these feasts and ceremonies they testified that they received the fruits of the earth from God, the true patron of the weather, and did not attribute them to their own labours, sweat and industry. To him alone thanks were to be given for the harvest and vintage and all the benefits bestowed, and he was to be prayed to, that he would bless the crops which they had stored in their barns, defend those which were still in the fields, and grant them his grace, so that with fear of him and true peace they might enjoy his gifts. To this the saying of St. Paul in 1 Timothy 4 applies, who testifies that all foods were created by God to be used with praise and thanksgiving, and that they are not to be rejected if we eat them with thanksgiving, since foods are sanctified by the word of God and prayer. Therefore let it not shame you to begin and to end your meal with prayer and thanksgiving. For what madness would it be to be ashamed of this, when you are not ashamed to abuse so full a table of God's gifts with such ingratitude and intemperance, and not only by example but by word and deed to provoke others to the cups as well. ...

units.la: Porro si Deus mundum fame & penuria punire vult, id ei non difficile factu est. Nam vt nos seruum aut ancillam uocare solemus, atque illis quod expediant mandare. Ita 2. Reg. 8. Psalm. 105. & alibi passim scribitur Deum famem, & penuriam vocare. Si veni re caritatem & famem iubet, etiamsi sit rerum omnium abundantia, praesto est. Sin recedere iubet etiamsi non sit copia frumenti, recedit & dictis paret: Nam & ipsa rerum omnium copia, ac abundantia, ancilla Dei est, illo vocante, insperato suo aduentu, ad illius obsequium adest, iussa exequitur. Hinc est quod Paul. ait Ro. 4. vocat illa quae non-dum sunt, vt sint, & praesto sunt. Tanta est Dei potentia.
units.tr: Furthermore, if God wishes to punish the world with famine and want, this is not difficult for him to do. For just as we are accustomed to call a servant or maidservant and to order them what is expedient, so 2 Kings 8, Psalm 105, and elsewhere throughout Scripture, famine and want are said to be called by God. If he bids dearth and famine come, even where there is abundance of all things, it is at hand. But if he bids it withdraw, even where there is no lack of grain, it withdraws and obeys his word. For the very abundance of all things is God's handmaid: at his call, it arrives unexpectedly and stands ready for his service, carrying out what is commanded. Hence Paul says in Romans 4 that he calls the things that are not yet, that they may be, and they are present. So great is the power of God.

units.la: Vsu compertum est, aliquando aestatem & autumnum, votis nostris respondisse. Frumenti, faeni, non solum copiam prouenisse, verum etiam commodè collecta esse, vuas pampinos numero æquasse, ac maximā omnes spē concepisse, fore, vt in tanta rerum omnium abundantia, (sic enim putabatur) vili ac bono precio omnia veneant. At contra omniū spem ex improuiso precium auctum est. Quis hic non manum ferientis Dei sentire, & certo certius cognoscere potuit? Deo maledicente peccata nostra, nihil prodesse copiam rerū. Vere ergo vernaculo sermone dicitur. Si Deus caritate & fame castigare vult, idenim facile factu est, etsi tantum farinæ copiam homines haberent, vt montes magnitudine & multitudine superarent. Est e-tiā pœna ac maledictio Dei, quod non frumen tum tantū, sed & omnia reliqua, quæ ad vitæ sustentationem necessaria sunt carè e-muntur, salis, butyri ac vini precium quoti-die augetur. Vide quid maledictio diuina possit? Factum est patrum nostrorum me-moria, Anno 1525, 1530, 1531, quando post copiosam messem maior rerum omnium ca-ritas, quam ante fuerit. Et quid non præte-ritis annis factum est? Rursum Deo beni-gno annuente, & fames, & inopia, & caritas ex improuiso recessit, & rursus recessuram speramus.
units.tr: By experience it has been found that sometimes the summer and autumn have answered our prayers: not only has an abundance of grain and hay come forth, but it was also gathered in conveniently, the grapes equalled the vine-shoots in number, and everyone conceived the greatest hope that in such abundance of all things (for so it was thought) everything would sell at a low and good price. But on the contrary, against everyone's hope, the price suddenly rose. Who here could not feel the hand of the striking God, and know it more certainly than anything? With God cursing our sins, the abundance of goods profits nothing. Truly, therefore, the saying in the vernacular goes: If God wishes to chastise with dearth and famine, it is easy for him to do, even if men had such an abundance of flour that it surpassed the mountains in size and number. There is also the punishment and curse of God, that not only grain but all the other things necessary for sustaining life become dear: the price of salt, butter and wine rises daily. See what the divine curse can do! It happened in the memory of our fathers, in 1525, 1530 and 1531, that after a plentiful harvest there was greater dearth of all things than before. And what has not happened in the past years? Again, with God graciously consenting, famine and want and dearth withdrew unexpectedly, and we hope they will withdraw again.

units.la: Habet autem Deus multas & varias rationes, plurima instrumenta, per quæ aut vitium aufert, aut precium auget. Terra inculta per se fructum non profert, & quod si diligenter colitur, tamen benedictio Dei, qui fructificandi vim & commodam dat tempestatem, expectanda est. 1. Cor. 3. D. Paulus ait: Nam qui plantat, rigat, nihil esse, sed Deum qui dat incrementum: Terra Israelitica antiquis temporibus, fertilissima fuit regio: Nostro seculo, qui ex illa redeunt, aiunt esse sterilem & incultam ferè. Ezech. 36. promittit Dominus suo populo, quod terram illam vastam & desertam, iterum fœcundam reddere velit.
units.tr: God has many and various reasons and very many instruments by which he either takes away the crop or raises the price. Uncultivated land does not of itself bring forth fruit, and even if it is diligently tilled, still we must await the blessing of God, who gives the power to bear fruit and a suitable season. 1 Cor. 3. St. Paul says: "For he who plants and he who waters is nothing, but God, who gives the increase." The land of Israel in ancient times was a very fertile region; in our age, those who return from it say that it is almost barren and uncultivated. Ezek. 36. The Lord promises his people that he will make that vast and desolate land fruitful again.

units.la: In multis fertilibus regionibus, interdum pauci agri coluntur propter metum vicinarum gentium. Sæpe fit permissu Dei, vt agri & vineta omnino non colantur. In diuturnis nanque bellis, agricultura intermittitur, agricolæ miserè trucidantur, captiui abducuntur. Nostra ætate agricolæ in obsidionibus bus urbium ad aggeres faciendos coguntur, quantus illorum numerus, & quam misere pereunt & trucidantur, principes id parum curant. At Deus in cuius conspectu præciosa est mors piorum, eorum curam gerit. Psal. 115. In bellis, vites, sepes arbores fructiferæ exuruntur, armenta & greges mactantur, & abiguntur, aut inopia pabuli pereunt, quæ causa est ut terra commode coli non posset.
units.tr: In many fertile regions, few fields are sometimes tilled for fear of neighbouring peoples. Often, by God's permission, fields and vineyards are not tilled at all. In long wars agriculture is interrupted, farmers are cruelly slaughtered, and captives are led away. In our own age farmers are forced to build earthworks during sieges of cities. How great their numbers are, and how wretchedly they perish and are slaughtered, the princes care little. But God, in whose sight the death of the pious is precious, takes care of them. Psal. 115. In wars vines, hedges and fruit trees are burned, herds and flocks are slaughtered and driven off, or perish for lack of fodder, and this is why the land cannot be properly tilled.

units.la: Etiam pace facta, magnam & diuturnam caritatem, inopiam jumentorum, olei, lactis, butyri, caseï, carnis, lanæ aliarumq; rerum consequi necesse est.
units.tr: Even when peace has been made, a great and lasting dearth is bound to follow: a shortage of draught animals, oil, milk, butter, cheese, meat, wool and other goods.

units.la: Peste grassante, homines & jumenta pereunt: agri, quia non purgantur, fordescunt vineæ incultæ relinquuntur. Ita fames, caritas pestem comitantur, hæc enim duo ferè cohærent. Ideo Græcus una tantum litera λιμὸς fames & λοιμὸς pestis, differunt.
units.tr: When plague is raging, men and beasts perish. Fields, not being tended, become foul, and vineyards are left untended. Thus famine and dearth accompany plague, for these two generally go together. That is why the Greeks differ by only one letter: [λιμὸς] famine and [λοιμὸς] pestilence.

units.la: Etsi vero agricolæ nullis laboribus parcant in colendis agris & vinetis, tamen sæpe culturæ & laboribus non respondent. Rara enim est messis & vindemia. Præterea hyems longa & aspera sementem, vites, arbores[?] perdit, gelu rigescunt omnia. Quod si maximè hyemis inclementiam euaserint, varijs tamen tempestatibus expositæ sunt, iam frigus, mox calor, iam humiditas, mox siccitas immodica illis molesta est. Nostra memoria saepius media æstate præ frigore calidis hypocaustis vsi sumus. Rursum ad Calend. Ianuarij (quasi re bene gesta) publica conuiuia sub dio celebrauimus. Deus est qui solus (at nostro magno malo) tempora & vicissitudines temporū mutare potest. Non hominum est.
units.tr: Although farmers spare no effort in tilling their fields and vineyards, the crops often do not answer their labour. The harvest and the vintage are meagre. Moreover, a long and harsh winter destroys the seed, the vines and the trees, and everything stiffens with frost. And if they escape the severity of winter, they are still exposed to changing weather: now cold, soon heat; now damp, soon excessive dryness troubles them. In our own memory we have more than once in midsummer used warm hypocausts because of the cold. Again, at the Kalends of January, as if things had gone well, we have held public feasts out of doors. God alone (to our great harm) can change the times and the seasons; it is not for men to do so.

units.la: In Iudæa, quia calida regio est; fructus facile præ siccitate pereunt. Helvetia autem nostra quo calidior & siccior est æstas, eò vniuersa regio est fertilior. Est enim montosa, perpetuas in alpibus nives habet, perennibus fluuijs irrigatur, has ob causas æstus minus nocere potest, sed regionem temperatissimam reddunt. Hinc vulgari apud nos Proverbio dicitur, Infantes calore solis non aduri. Interim tamen maleferiati rustici importunèsæpè pluuias flagitant.
units.tr: In Judea, because it is a hot region, fruits easily perish from drought. But in our Helvetia, the hotter and drier the summer, the more fertile the whole region is. For it is mountainous, has perpetual snows in the Alps, and is watered by perennial rivers. For these reasons the heat can do little harm, and instead makes the region very temperate. Hence a common proverb among us says that infants are not scorched by the heat of the sun. Meanwhile, ill-tempered peasants often demand rain importunately.

units.la: Sunt & infinitæ aliæ pestes frumenti, & arborum vitia, mures silvestres, sorices, locustæ, bruchi, lumbrici, melolanthæ & alia huiusmodi animalcula plurimum nocent. Pruina gemmas vitium & arborum adurit, ideò cineri ignito Psalmo 147. comparatur, diuturna pluuia flores plane perdit. Auster & rursum Boreas, nec non densæ nebulæ, (in nostris regionibus verno tempore maiorum futuræ calamitatis, malum præsagium) suffocant & auferunt flores cum immaturis fructibus arborum. Sunt & aliæ pestes quæ primò vere folia tenera arborum depascunt, & aridis scopis, vt nostro more loquar, nudiores reddunt. Si fructus arborum malignè proueniunt, maior est panis penuria. Nam in nostris regionibus fruges arborum optimum auxilium & baculum panis æstimantur. Infantes aliàs panem flagitantes pomo vel piro placare solemus. At quæ spes in tanta fructuum calamitate reliqua? Cum non minoris emas quam panem? Scitè maiores nostri dixere: Si ligna, hoc est, arbores & vineta terræ frugibus auxilio fuerint, fertilem futurum annum: optimum nanque habet panis sub-sidium.
units.tr: There are also countless other plagues of grain and defects of trees: wild mice, shrews, locusts, bruchi, earthworms, melolanthae and other such small creatures do much harm. Hoarfrost scorches the buds of vines and trees, and therefore it is compared to ashes sprinkled (Psal. 147.). Long rain utterly destroys the flowers. The south wind, and again the north wind, as well as dense mists (in our regions in spring, a bad omen of greater calamity to come), suffocate and carry off the flowers together with the immature fruit of the trees. There are also other pests which in early spring devour the tender leaves of trees and leave them, to speak in our own idiom, bare as dry brooms. If the fruit of the trees turns out poorly, the shortage of bread is greater. For in our regions the fruit of the trees is reckoned the best help and staff of bread. We usually placate children who beg for bread with an apple or a pear. But what hope remains amid such a calamity of fruit? When you buy them at no lower price than bread? Our forefathers wisely said: if wood, that is, the trees and vines, helps the crops of the earth, the year will be fertile, for bread has its best support in them.

units.la: Hic de locustis quædam nobis dicenda sunt, de quibus passim in sacris & prophanis historijs legitur, eas tanta turba volasse, ut solis aspectum prohibuerint, & ubi se in terram demiserint, multa iugera occupasse & contexisse, flores, herbas, folia depauisse: hanc illarum depopulationem extremam inopiam & famem imo saepe etiam pestem consequutam esse. Legas quae habentur Exod. 10. cap. quantum damnū Ægypto dederint. Plinius author est[?] in Cyrenaica regione, publico decreto, bellum geri tum locustis eos primo ova cōterere, deinde fœtum, postremo locustas. D. Ioannes in Apocalypsi, eurmam[?] Monachorum locustis comparat, non solum propter ingentem illorum multitudinem, sed & quod in omnibus locis (hoc præcipuè Monachi mendicantes faciunt) victum importunè colligendo, omnia consumant & devorent. Apud Ioelem 1. cap. minatur Dominus: Residuum erucæ commedet locusta, & residuum locustæ comedet bruchus, & residuum bruchi commedet rubigo. Et 3. cap. vocat Dominus locustas magnu suum exercitum. Etsi enim locustae, & alia insecta paruula sint animalia, illis tamen nulla humana potentia resisti potest. Quin bestiis potentissimus facilius profligari potest quam huiusmodi bestiolae. Annales Helueliorum testantur, Anno 1364. mense Augusto locustas tanta multitudine in has regiones aduolasse, vt densitate sua caelum obscurum reddiderint. Tiguri & in multis aliis locis campanarum pulsu tanquam horrendam aliquam tempestatem profligare frustra conati sunt. Anno 1548. locustae pariter tanta copia in Belgium venere, & flores, herbas, segetes depopulatae sunt. Casimiro secundo apud Polonos regnante, Anno 1335. Poloniam tanta vis locustatum peruagata est, vt volantes Solis aspectum hominibus adimerent, huni vero stratae, equorum vngulas altitudine superarent, quae depastae maturescentes segetes, angustiorem annonam fecere: Scribit Ioannes Herburtus in Polonica historia lib. 10. cap. 1. Idem Anno 1542. Poloniam & Silesiam maiori quàm antehac numero vastarunt. Et illi pulsu campanarum, sonitu buccinarum, tinnitu peluium, conati sunt abigere, sed operam lusere.
units.tr: Here some things must be said about locusts, of which we read everywhere in sacred and profane histories: that they flew in such a swarm that they blocked out the sight of the sun, and where they came down to the earth they occupied and covered many acres, stripping flowers, herbs and leaves. This stripping was followed by extreme want and famine, and often even by pestilence. Read what is said in Exod. 10. about how much loss they caused Egypt. Pliny is the authority that in the Cyrenaic region, by public decree, war was waged on locusts: first they crushed the eggs, then the young, and last the locusts themselves. St John in the Apocalypse compares a troop of monks to locusts, not only on account of their enormous number, but because in every place (and mendicant monks especially do this) they consume and devour everything by importunately collecting their food. In Joel chapter 1 the Lord threatens: "What the caterpillar has left, the locust will eat; and what the locust has left, the bruchus will eat; and what the bruchus has left, the rust will eat." And in chapter 3 the Lord calls the locusts his great army. For although locusts and other tiny insects are small animals, no human power can resist them. Indeed, the most powerful beasts can be more easily routed than such little creatures. The Annals of the Helvetians testify that in August of the year 1364 locusts flew into these regions in such multitudes that by their density they darkened the sky. At Zurich and in many other places people tried in vain to drive off this dreadful plague by the pealing of bells. In 1548 locusts likewise came into Belgium in such abundance that they stripped flowers, herbs and crops. When Casimir the Second reigned among the Poles, in 1335, such a swarm of locusts spread through Poland that in flight they took the sight of the sun from men, and when they lay on the ground they rose higher than the hooves of horses. They grazed the ripening crops and made the grain supply scantier. John Herburt writes this in his Polish history, book 10, chapter 1. In 1542 the same locusts laid waste Poland and Silesia in greater numbers than before. And people tried to drive them away with the ringing of bells, the sound of trumpets and the clanging of basins, but they were wasting their effort.

units.la: Adhæc si in aristas insurgunt segetes, si poma, pira, vites maturescere incipiunt, ut maxima spes sit fertilissimi anni, Deus subito grandine fruges omnes cōtundere, & prosternere potest. Sæpè etiā magnitudine avorum gallinæ decidit, aves, bestias, homines deniq; interfecit, & fruges usq; adeo perdit, agros, arbores, & vineas ita inficit, ut etiam sequentibus annis fuerint steriles.
units.tr: Moreover, if the crops rise into ears, and apples, pears and vines begin to ripen, so that there is the greatest hope of a very fertile year, God can suddenly crush and flatten all the fruits with hail. Often, too, hailstones as large as hens' eggs fall, killing birds, beasts and finally men, and they destroy the crops so completely, and so infect the fields, trees and vineyards, that they remain barren even in the following years.

units.la: Nihil opus est exempla hic ex antiquis historijs repetere, adhuc in recenti, heu, memoria hæret, experimur vtique magno nostro malo quantum damni grandines in nostris regionibus dederint.
units.tr: There is no need to repeat examples here from ancient histories. Still, the recent memory lingers, alas, and we have experienced to our great harm how much damage hailstorms have done in our regions.

units.la: Nimbi, procellæ, turbines, frumentum, siliginem, hordeum magna cum vehementia frequenter prosternunt, ut vix possint maturescere & aristæ plæreque ieiunæ maneant. Torrentes ex montibus magno cum impetu ruentes, non tantum aquarum inundatione datione omnia vastant, verùm etiam agros, & prata arena, lapidibus & truncis arborum complent, obruunt & in solitudinem redigunt. Procellosi venti arbores funditus euertunt, hæ equidem non publicæ sed privatæ egestatis causæ sunt: iis tamen, quorum interest, maximum damnum dant.
units.tr: Storms, gales and whirlwinds often flatten wheat, rye and barley with great violence, so that they can scarcely ripen and most of the ears remain empty. Torrents rushing down from the mountains with great force lay waste everything, not only by the flooding of waters, but also by filling fields and meadows with sand, stones and tree trunks, overwhelming them and reducing them to wasteland. Violent winds uproot trees entirely; these, to be sure, cause not public but private want, yet they inflict the greatest loss on those whom it concerns.

units.la: Hic jam offertur tractanda quæstio, quæ à doctis pariter & indoctis multum agitata est. An Lamiæ, striges, siue quocunque nomine vocare voluerint (cum Veier[?] de verbis non contendo) grandinem & tempestates ciere possint: Hic distinctione opus. Ut non omnis, sed quædam illis nocendi facultas neganda est, ita etiam absoluta non est concedenda. Negamus itaq; illas per se absolutam & liberam nocendi habere potestatem: Nam & ipse Sathan, (cuius aliàs magna est potestas, cuius etiam impuræ istæ mulieres miseræ sunt mancipia) lædere homines & animalia non potest, tantum, quantum vel quoties vult. Porcos impuros nõ nisi impetrata à Christo potestate, in mare præcipitare potuit. Quid ergo sagas, execrãda illius seruitia in aerem & tepestatem potestatis habere putandū est? Concessa autem à Deo iusto iu-ditio, potestate, quid non potest? hic ima summus miscet, mirandas res illico efficit. Agilis est spiritus, & mille artifex, ideò si-ne omni mora, opinione citius concessa pote-state abutitur. Porcos (ut dixi) data uenia non abstante mora irruit, & in mare præci-pitat. Magi in Ægypto stupenda miracula ædidere: Mosen & Aaronem immitati sunt. Nota & memorabilis est Iobi historia, qua docemur, illum nec hominibus nec bestijs dā-num ullum posse inferre, at nocendi licentia impetrata, nihil intentatum relinquere. Notandum interim & hoc, illum præscriptos habere terminos, quos ne latum quidem unguē possit transgredi. Huc faciunt Origenis verba quæ ad illum Iobi locum notat & ab au-thore ibidem citantur. O bonitas tua rex: O virtus: atq; magnificentia tua, æterne. Quā magnam consolationem tribuis ijs, qui ad te confugerint: & constantiæ fiduciam à te spe-rauerint: ut neque hominum: neq; iumento-rum: neque animatorum: neque inanimato-rum rum potestatem habeat aduersarium: nisi ubi fuerit permissus. Non autem permittitur: nisi ubi nouerit Deus pro fidei manifestatione & constantiæ approbatione, atque gloriosæ remunerationis retributione. Hæc scilicet nos scientes sollicitè atq; deuotè ad Deum confugiamus, instantissimè, atque sincerissimè in orationibus Deum inuocemus, ut auertat à nobis maligni insidias, ut eripiat nos de crudelibus illius incursionibus, & nõ permittat nos tentari supra id quod possimus sufferre. Hæc ille. Iam ad rem. Facta strigum cum diabolo stipulatione, illorũ opera utitur. Ne gari [?] id non potest. Præscribit, subministrat, dictat philtra, pharmaca, venena, exorcismos quibus homines, infantes, bestias armenta laedunt, pascua inficiunt, præstigijs ludunt, mira efficiunt. Neq; id per se possunt, ni Diabolus malitiæ ipsarũ suam operã adiungat. Etsi enim maximè consenserint, tenendũ tamen firmiter illud Pauli: Si Deus pro nobis quis contra nos? Et hoc certum est, etsi nec facultas, nec voluntas eis defit, potestatem tamen deesse. Nam in pios qui sunt, sub protecsione[?] altissimi nihil potestatis habent. Tempestates autē, pruinas, grandines facere posse, id constanter pernegamus: sacrae literae nobis assentiuntur, quae tempestatis gubernatione soli & uni Deo tribuunt. Inquies, At fatentur, non tantū tormentis adactæ, sed & sponte & constanter quidem se turbasse aerem & tempestatem concitasse. Fateor quidem, sed meram (ut alia quoq; multa) Sathanicā esse impostu-ram vere ac liberè dico. Satan enim non tantū naturali ratione, & pro celeritate ingenij causas, loca & effectā tempestatū nouit, verum etiam iusta, irati Dei iudicia, volens nolensq; exequitur. Est enim ut ille ait, Dei carnifex. His rebus cognitis, hac pote-state cum mandatis accepta, illico complices accedit, stipulationis nefandæ admonet, ul-tionem iam diu optatam ipsis pollicetur, modum docet, nefandā sacrificia, quibus hæc cōficiuntur, monstrat. Invitas vi & verberibus cogit. Dirae & ultrices striges ultrò & coa-ctæ, tandem rem aggrediuntur. Voti compotes fiunt, lætantur, de tam tristi, abominan-dæ artis exitu. Iam quod voluit & plura e-tiam tiam veterator ille impetravit actioreq; vinculo, falsa hac persuasione, deliras annus sibi conciliavit. Damnum dedit hominibus, pessi ma suspicione infecit quam plurimos. Omnis egestatis, calamitatis, damni culpa Iagis[?] tribuitur. De his tollendis conclamatur. Interim nulla fit mentio pœnitentiæ. Nemo de tollendis vitiis serio cogitat, & laborat. Sic pestifera hac opinione, vera mali culpa in eas quas hoc ipso Sathan prodit, reijcitur. Quæ non in eam partem à me dicta accipi velim, quasi negem coburendas esse. Sed huc omnis mea spectat intentio, Illas nequaquam posse tempestates excitare. Veteres Romani, à vera religione alieni crediderunt, homines fruges alienas, veneficijs & incantationibus posse perdere. Nam lege duodecim tabularum his verbis prohibetur: Qui fruges excantas-set, pœnas dato. Ne alienâ segetem pellexe-ris incantando, hoc est, Nullo præstigiarū genere alienum agrum sterilem reddas. Si Dæmon Domino permittente tale quid faciat, illudit hominibus, ut putent, quasi verè ab illo factum sit.
units.tr: Here a question is raised that has been much debated by learned and unlearned alike: whether witches, hags, or whatever name people wish to give them (I do not quarrel with Weyer about words), can raise hail and storms. A distinction is needed here. Just as they must not be credited with every power to harm, so they must not be granted an absolute one. We deny, therefore, that they have by themselves an absolute and free power to harm. For Satan himself, whose power is otherwise great, and of whom these wretched women are the slaves, cannot injure men and animals as much as he wishes, or whenever he wishes. He could drown the impure swine in the sea only after receiving power from Christ. Why, then, should we think that witches, the accursed servants of that detestable service, have power over air and storm? But once power has been granted by the just judgment of God, what can he not do? He, the highest, mixes up the lowest things and at once brings about wonderful effects. The spirit is nimble and a thousand-fold craftsman, and so, without any delay, he abuses the granted power more swiftly than thought. As I said, when permission was given, he rushed upon the swine without delay and threw them into the sea. The magicians in Egypt performed amazing miracles and imitated Moses and Aaron. The history of Job is also well known and memorable, by which we are taught that he could inflict no harm on men or beasts, but once permission to harm was granted, he left nothing untried. Meanwhile we should note this too, that God has set fixed limits which the adversary cannot pass by even a hair's breadth. The words of Origen, which he notes on that place of Job and which are cited there by the author, favour this: "O your goodness, King; O your power and magnificence, eternal God! How great a consolation you give to those who flee to you and hope from you for the confidence of steadfastness, so that the adversary has no power over men, nor over beasts of burden, nor over living things, nor over inanimate things, unless he has been permitted. Yet he is not permitted, except where God knows it is for the manifestation of faith, the approval of steadfastness, and the repayment of glorious reward." Knowing this, let us therefore flee to God carefully and devotedly, and call upon God most earnestly and most sincerely in prayers, that he may turn away from us the snares of the evil one, rescue us from his cruel assaults, and not allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear. So far Origen. Now to the matter. Once a compact has been made between the witches and the devil, he makes use of their work. He prescribes, supplies, and dictates love potions, drugs, poisons, and incantations by which they harm men, infants, and beasts and herds, infect pastures, mock with illusions, and bring about marvels. Nor can they do this by themselves, unless the devil adds his own work to their malice. For even if they have fully consented, we must hold firmly to that saying of Paul: "If God is for us, who can be against us?" And this is certain: even if they lack neither the ability nor the will, they nevertheless lack the power. For over the pious, who are under the protection of the Most High, they have no power at all. But that they can make tempests, frosts, and hailstorms, this we steadfastly deny. The holy letters agree with us, which ascribe the governance of the tempest to God alone. You will object: "But they confess that they stirred up the air and raised the tempest, not only under torture but also willingly and constantly." I admit it, but I say truly and freely that this (as many other things) is a mere Satanic deception. For Satan knows by natural reason, and by the swiftness of his intellect, the causes, places, and effects of tempests, and he also carries out, whether willing or unwilling, the just judgments of an angry God. For he is, as he himself says, the executioner of God. Once these things are known, and this power and these commands have been received, he at once approaches his accomplices, reminds them of the accursed compact, promises them the vengeance they have long desired, teaches the method, and shows the unspeakable sacrifices by which these things are accomplished. He compels them, unwilling, by force and blows. The dreadful and vengeful hags, both willing and compelled, at last set to work. They attain their desire and rejoice at the outcome of that sad and abominable art. Now the old cheat has obtained what he wanted and more; by this false persuasion he has bound to himself a most active and deluded crowd. He has done harm to men and infected very many with the worst suspicion. All the blame for want, calamity, and loss is laid on them. A cry goes up to remove them. Meanwhile no mention is made of repentance. No one seriously thinks about or labours at removing vices. Thus, by this pestilent opinion, the true fault of evil is thrown onto those whom Satan himself betrays by this very means. I would not have what I say taken in this sense, as if I denied that they should be burned. My whole intention aims at this only: that they can in no way raise tempests. The ancient Romans, alien to the true religion, believed that men could destroy the crops of others by poisonings and incantations. For the Law of the Twelve Tables forbids this in these words: "Whoever has charmed away the crops shall pay the penalty." That is: "Do not by incantation entice another's crop; by no kind of sorcery render another's field barren." If the demon, with the Lord's permission, does such a thing, he deceives men into thinking it was really done by those women.

units.la: Sed demus[?] miseras illas anus posse grandine producere, at id non possunt, nisi permittente & puniente Deo peccata nostra: His, vera poenitentia, sublatis, sublata est causa, nec praeterea timendae sunt sagae.
units.tr: But grant that those wretched old women can produce hail; yet they cannot, unless God, permitting and punishing our sins, does so. When these are removed by true repentance, the cause is removed, and the witches need not be feared any further.

units.la: Fit etiā interdum, vt propter continuos imbres, & pluuias fruges magna ex parte pereant, nec satis commodè colligi possint. Quae etiam egestatis causa esse[?]. Fruges etiam ad falcem maturae conteri, aut ab hostibus demeti, vel exuri possunt. Sic Samson caudibus vulpinis, faces ardentes alligauit, & Philistinorum sata perdidit.
units.tr: It also sometimes happens, through continual showers and rains, that the crops for the most part perish and cannot be gathered in properly. These too can be a cause of want. Crops that are ripe for the sickle may also be wasted, or carried off by enemies, or burned. So Samson tied burning torches to the tails of foxes and destroyed the crops of the Philistines.

units.la: Etsi verò fruges repositae sint in horrea, & vina in cellas conuecta, fit tamen vt laboribus etiam maligne respondeant. In trituratione[?], in furno, in canistro maledictio Domini sentitur:hac de re audiuntur crebrae agricolarum querelae. Item horrea plena frumenti fulmine tacta, vel alio incendio, pereunt: Vina in dolio accessunt vapescūt, aut alia vitia contrahūt, saepe effluunt. Nihil dicam quod hostes omne frumentum consumunt, hortos & granaria igne vastant: cados vini confringunt, gunt, gunt, vinum aquæ instar effundunt: & hæc caritatem ac famem faciunt.
units.tr: Even if the grain has been stored in barns and the wine carried into cellars, it nevertheless happens that the fruits of labour turn out badly. In threshing, in the oven, and in the basket the curse of the Lord is felt; and so farmers make frequent complaints about this. Likewise barns full of grain are destroyed by lightning or another fire; wine in casks turns sour, spoils, or contracts other faults, and often leaks out. I say nothing of enemies who consume all the grain, lay waste gardens and granaries with fire, smash jars of wine, and pour out wine like water; and these things cause dearth and famine.

units.la: Accedit huc & aliud malum: Pacefacta & summa ubertate & copia rerum divinarum concessa, faeneratores, monopolæ, & propolæ rem suam agunt, & novam caritatem moliuntur, fruges enim omnis generis coë-munt & recondunt, postea cum agricolæ nō amplius habent quod vendant, ipsi aucto precio reconditas promunt, aliorū iactura quæstum magnum faciunt. Fit interdum etiam iusto Dei iudicio, ut fruges ab auaris hac ratione reconditæ, corrumpantur, & auolent, ut nec ipsis, nec aliis usui sint.
units.tr: Another evil is added to this: when peace has been made and the divine gifts have been granted in great abundance and plenty, usurers, monopolists, and forestallers carry on their trade and contrive a new dearth. For they buy up and store all kinds of grain; then, when the farmers no longer have anything to sell, they bring out the stored goods at a raised price and make great profit at the loss of others. Sometimes too, by God's just judgment, grain stored up in this way by the greedy is spoiled and blown away, so that it is of use neither to them nor to others.

units.la: Etsi annona abunde suppetat, tamen in obsidionibus, oppidani, obsessis itineribus, cōmeatu prohibentur, ut tandē cibi inopia, impuris cibis vesci & ne fame pereant, si nō soluitur obsidio, hosti se dedere cogatur. Rapsaces minatur obsessis ciuibus Hierosoly-mitanis eò rem deducendam, ut aquæ inopia, lotio sitim restinguri sint.
units.tr: Even when food is abundant, in sieges the townspeople are cut off from supplies, with the roads blocked, so that at last, through lack of food, they are compelled to eat impure food, and, unless the siege is lifted, to surrender to the enemy lest they perish of hunger. Rabshakeh threatened the besieged citizens of Jerusalem that the matter would be brought to such a point that they would be reduced to drinking their own urine to quench their thirst, for lack of water.

units.la: Bella etiam magnam rerum inopiam fa-ciunt, & diuturna post se relinquunt famem. Ferro, igne, omnia vastantur, omnia populantur. Fruges non amplius in oppida, sed in castra convehuntur, multoque plus belli quàm pacis tempore insumitur. Si rumor belli est, maiores urbes, & proprium frumentum servant, & aliunde magnam copiam coemunt, donec constet de pace & bello.
units.tr: Wars also cause great shortage of goods and leave famine behind them for a long time. Everything is laid waste with sword and fire, everything is plundered. Crops are no longer carried into the towns but into camps, and far more time is spent on war than on peace. If there is a rumour of war, the larger cities keep their own grain and buy a large supply from elsewhere, until it is certain whether there will be peace or war.

units.la: Principes quidam quorum officium esset subditis prospicere, tamen eorum nullam curam gerunt. Illi ipsi illos ad pauperiem etiam in fertilissimis regionibus redigunt, atq; in hac ætate retinent. Nimijs exactionibus populum onerant, magnis sumptibus aula alitur, plurimum in canes, equos, agasones, moriones, & huiusmodi monstra & res nihili insumitur, his inquam artibus subditorum opes exhauriuntur, quibus hæc omnia solvenda sunt. Ex quo & illud sequitur, ut populus his exactionibus ad desperationem quasi redactus, nō curat rem familiarem, edit, bibit, ludit, ne quid reliqui sit quod principes rapiant. Itaq, nunquā ex paupertate emergūt. Sed quid de illis dico, qui sub iniquis illis principibus vivunt? An non maxima & communis munis fere est hodie egestas apud illos popu-los quoq; qui summa libertate fruuntur, & ab his oneribus immunes sunt? Quæ causa est? luxus, crapula, fastus. Nemo sua sorte am-plius contentus est. Non divites tantū, sed & pauperes, non nobiles, sed & artifices, in vestibus, suppellectili, cibo, potu, modu ex-cedunt. Quantis sumptibus, quam exquisitis edulijs, & novis delicijs, aliunde comporta-tis vinis, parantur convivia? Maiorum no-strorum magna liberalitas erat in excipiendis peregrinis & amicis, at domi natis contenti erant, amicitiæ potius quam crapulæ causa convivabātur. Multos alea & lusus chartā-rum, vera rei domesticæ pernities, perdit. Alij quod dies noctesq; beluantur[?], non tantū multa pessundant, verum etiam res suas domi negligunt. Inter pocula emunt & vendunt, magno tamen cum damno: sponsiones, fidei iussiones, frugales alioqui, incautos tamē pa-eres familias, egenos reddunt.
units.tr: Some princes, whose office is to provide for their subjects, nevertheless take no care of them at all. These same princes reduce their people to poverty, even in the most fertile regions, and keep them there to this day. They burden the people with excessive exactions, and the court is kept up at great expense. Much is spent on dogs, horses, grooms, jesters and such monsters and worthless things. By these practices, I say, the resources of the subjects are drained, and from them all these costs must be met. It follows from this that the people, driven as it were to despair by these exactions, do not look after their household property. They eat, drink and gamble, so that nothing is left for the princes to seize. And so they never climb out of poverty. But why do I speak of those who live under unjust princes? Is not great and general want almost everywhere today, even among those peoples who enjoy the greatest liberty and are free from these burdens? What is the cause? Luxury, drunkenness and pride. No one is any longer content with his lot. Not only the rich but also the poor, not only the nobles but also the craftsmen, go beyond due measure in clothing, furnishings, food and drink and in style. What great sums are spent on banquets, and how exquisite are the dishes and novel delicacies, and wines brought in from far away? Our forefathers were very generous in entertaining strangers and friends, but at home they were content with what they had, and they held dinners for the sake of friendship rather than drunkenness. Dice and card games, the true ruin of domestic affairs, destroy many. Others, because they drink-bout day and night, not only squander much but also neglect their own affairs at home. They buy and sell among their cups, but always to their great loss. Sureties and guarantees, although frugal men otherwise, make careful heads of families needy.

units.la: Vix aliud flagitium, ita opes minuit, rem familiarem perdit, atq; scortatio. Nam ut author noster ad versum 10. cap. 5. Prouerb. annotat magnis sumptibus meretrices sunt alendae, iam hæc, iam illa amoris pignora insatiabiles expetunt, vestes, annulos, & idgenus alia ornamenta. Apud Plautum in Truculento recte dicitur.
units.tr: Scarcely any other disgrace diminishes resources and ruins household property as fornication does. For, as our author notes on Proverbs 5:10, meretricious women must be supported at great expense; now this one, now that one, insatiable, demands pledges of love: clothes, rings and other such ornaments. In Plautus's Truculentus it is rightly said:

units.la: Meretricem ego idem esse reor, Mare ut est, quod das, devorat, nunquam Des quantumvis, nusquam (abundat. Apparet, neq; datori, neq; acceptrici.
units.tr: I think a courtesan is the same as the sea: whatever you give her, she devours; never, however much you give, does she have enough. It is evident that this is no good to the giver or to the receiver.

units.la: Accedit ad hæc quod meretrices amant lu-xuriosa convivia: & quod spurii magnis sumptibus clam alendi sunt. Lenæ item & Le-nones suam partem decarpunt. Vicini etiam nisi dederis, silentium non promittunt. Est præterea hoc adulterorum ingenium, ut cum erga uxorem & liberos tenacissimi sint, in scorta tamen & libidinum minis-tros sint liberalissimi. Exemplum habes in Herode, qui dimidium regni filiæ Herodiad. saltati pollicetur. Hinc fit, ut libidinosi illi homines ad egesta-tem redacti, in alienis ædibus in scortis, suas o-pes non sine gemitu cogantur aspicere. Maledi-ctio quoq; Dei opes eorum atterit. Infra ca. verf.3. etiam dicit: Pascens scorta, per-dit dit opes. Hæc ibi. Hæc illius verba, cum sint grauissima huc transcribere volui. Est enim proch dolor, commune ferè malum, egestatis non ultima causa.
units.tr: Added to this is that courtesans love luxurious banquets, and that bastards must be secretly supported at great expense. Procuresses and pimps likewise pick their share clean. Neighbours too will not promise silence unless you give them something. Moreover, this is the nature of adulterers: though they are very tight-fisted toward their wives and children, they are most generous to prostitutes and to the ministers of their lusts. You have an example in Herod, who promised the daughter of Herodias half of his kingdom for dancing. Hence it happens that those lustful men, reduced to want, are forced, in the houses of others and among prostitutes, to look upon their own resources not without groaning. The curse of God also wears down their wealth. Further on, in chapter 5, verse 3, he also says: "He who feeds harlots squanders his substance." So far his words. I wished to transcribe these words here because they are most weighty. For it is, alas, a common evil and no small cause of want.

units.la: Uxores quæ vitæ sociæ debebant esse, si fuerint contentiosæ, stultæ, & rei familia-ris negligentes, plus perdunt, quam maritus acquirere possit: maritos frugales aliâs im-portunitate sua domo expellunt, multa in suppellectilia & ornamenta corporis insumunt, atque ita magnas opes breui temporis spacio perdunt, ut tandem mariti solū vertere cogantur. Appositè ergò Salomon tales stillicidio comparat. Pro.19. & 27.cap. Vulgari proverbio grandinem culinæ immissam vocamus.
units.tr: Wives, who ought to be partners in life, if they are quarrelsome, foolish and careless of household affairs, lose more than the husband can gain. By their importunity they drive out husbands who would otherwise be thrifty, and they spend much on furnishings and bodily adornment. So in a short time they squander great resources, until at last the husbands are forced to leave their land. Therefore Solomon aptly compares such women to a dripping roof (Prov. 19 and 27). In common saying we call it hail let into the kitchen.

units.la: Quid de immorigeris liberis dicemus? Illi insciis parentibus, noctu vinum, frumentum exportare, pecunias clam eripere, æs alienū conflare solent, quod postea parentibus solvendum est, atque hac furtiva (si ita loqui licet) prodigalitate se parentesque perditum eunt. Sed quis omnes publicæ & privatæ egestatis causas exactè enumerare posset? Si fertiles, Dei beneficio, sunt anni, multi egestatis & penuriae quam superioribus annis passi sunt, obliuiscuntur, omnes reliquos tales fore opinantur, nihil recondunt, nihil reliqui faciunt: sed omnes terrae fruges, quasi adhoc nati sint, consumunt. At spe tandem frustrantur, sequuntur anni steriles, cum nihil superfit, non habent, unde viuant, paruo frumentum vendiderunt, magno rursum emunt, vix denique habent, ut census annuos soluant, ideo terram vertere coguntur in exilium actu[?]: atque ita nemo alterius egestatem subleuare potest.
units.tr: What shall we say of disobedient children? Without their parents' knowledge they are wont at night to carry off wine and grain, to steal money secretly, and to contract debts, which must afterwards be paid by their parents; and by this stolen prodigality (if I may so speak) they ruin themselves and their parents. But who could list exactly all the causes of public and private want? If the years are fruitful by God's blessing, many forget the hunger and scarcity they suffered in earlier years; they suppose that all the years to come will be like this, they store nothing, they save nothing, but consume all the fruits of the earth as if they had been born for this alone. At last they are disappointed in their hope. Sterile years follow; when nothing is left they have nothing to live on. They sold grain cheaply and buy it back dearly, and at last they can scarcely pay their annual dues; so they are forced to leave their land and go into exile. And thus no one can relieve another's want.

units.la: Multitudo hominum, artificum omnis generis copia, impostura variae, fraudes, iniquae artes, tantam inopiam augent.
units.tr: The multitude of people, the abundance of craftsmen of every kind, the various impostures, frauds and wicked arts, increase such great want.

units.la: Iam si malis his, malignus frugum proventus, maledictio Dei accesserit, res pessimo sunt in loco.
units.tr: Now if, with these evils, a poor harvest and the curse of God should also come, things are in the worst state.

units.la: Deus in lege sua minatur, se panis baculum fracturum, hoc est, se subtracturum panis vim alendi famelicos. Nam ut senes & aegroti baculis innituntur, si eis subtraxeris, concidunt: Ita nisi Deus indat vim alendi, satusaturari vix possumus. Rursum si accesserit benedictio divina, parvo cibo, suos alere, & sustentare potest. Externis medijs, si vsus, necessitas, postulauerit opus non habet. Deus, 8.[?] scribitur: quae verba Christus Math. 4. in grauissima tentatione repetit. Homine non solo pane viuere, sed omni verbo quod egre-ditur ex ore Dei. Per verbum Dei, intelli-gunt aliqui, id quod Deus in cibum hominis destinauit. Alij exponunt, per Verbum, Nutum & bene placitū, & decretum Dei quod publicauit, quoad tuendum naturae ordinem, & fouendas creaturas. Sensus ergo erit du-plex, Deum qui nunc pane utitur in nostrum alimentem, aliter quoties visum fuerit, da-turum, ut viuamus.
