Item non panis virtu-ti acceptam ferre decet, sed arcanae gratiae, quam pani Deus ad nos pascendos inspirat.
units.tr: God threatens in his law that he will break the staff of bread, that is, that he will withdraw from bread the power to feed the hungry. For just as old men and the sick lean on staffs, and if you take them away they fall, so unless God gives the power to nourish, we can scarcely be satisfied. Conversely, if the divine blessing comes, he can feed and sustain his own with little food. If use and necessity demand it, he has no need of external means. It is written in Deuteronomy 8 (?), and Christ repeats these words in Matthew 4 in the most grievous temptation: man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. Some understand by "word of God" that which God has appointed as food for man. Others explain it as the will, good pleasure and decree of God, which he has made known, for preserving the order of nature and cherishing creatures. The sense will therefore be twofold: God, who now uses bread for our nourishment, will give it, whenever he sees fit, so that we may live otherwise. Likewise it is not fitting to ascribe the power to bread, but to the secret grace which God breathes into bread to feed us.

units.la: Tempore famis saepè obseruatum est quid sit baculum panis confringere, multum enim commedendo, vix etiam saturantur homines. Sunt qui id referant ad auaritiam, seu ut illi loquuntur nimiam hominum fru-galitatem. Solere eos (dicunt quorum interest, curiosius obseruare, & quodammodo nummerare quid & quantum quis edat, & expensarum diligentiorem habere rationem. Id verũ esse aliqua ex parte fateor: quid non auari faciunt? Sed si rem penitius consideraueris, facile est iudicare maledictionem esse Dei, qui vigorem pani subtrahit. Eadẽ potus est ratio, non semper vim restringendi sitim habet, vt fit in febribus aliisq; morbis, cum ne aquæ nec vini potu sitim restinguere possunt. Vestes etiam non diu durant, sed statim conteruntur. Est etiam benedictionis Dei loco habendum si vestes & calceamenta diu durant. Id quod Israelitarum exemplum docet, quorum vestes, & calcei singulari Dei beneficio non fuerunt in deserto attriti. Sunt qui pellibus bene & accuratè vestiti incedunt, noctu stragulis diligenter se tegunt, non tamen frigus arcere possunt. Hæc aliaque Deus per Haggeum impijs comminatus est. Atq; sic Deus in magno rerum copia famem potest immittere. Iamsi accedat malignus frugum proventus, & Deus baculum panis frangat eo res peius se habet. Hæc in genere dicta sint, nec enim necesse est minutius singula persequi.
units.tr: Often in time of famine it has been observed what it is to break the staff of bread: men, though they eat much, can scarcely be satisfied. There are those who refer this to avarice, or, as they put it, to excessive thrift among men. Those whose interest it is, they say, are wont to watch closely, and in a way to count, what and how much each person eats, and to keep a more careful account of expenses. I admit that this is true to some extent: what do not misers do? But if you consider the matter more deeply, it is easy to judge that it is the curse of God, who takes away the strength from bread. The same is the case with drink; it does not always have the power to quench thirst, as happens in fevers and other diseases, when neither water nor wine can quench thirst. Clothes too do not last long, but wear out at once. It is also to be counted as a blessing of God if clothes and shoes last long, as the example of the Israelites teaches, whose clothes and shoes were not worn out in the desert by God's singular kindness. There are those who go about well and carefully clad in furs, and cover themselves diligently with coverlets at night, yet cannot keep off the cold. God threatened these and other things to the impious through Haggai. And so God can send famine in great abundance of goods. Still, if a poor harvest comes too, and God breaks the staff of bread, things are worse. These things have been said in general; for it is not necessary to pursue each point in more detail.

units.la: Ex his quæ à me pluribus dicta sunt intelligitur, famem à Deo immitti, qui ad eam rem procurandam, varijs externis medijs, rebus naturalibus, malitia, & negligentia, hominum liberè utitur. Is cuncta gubernat: Ergo sine nutu & voluntate Dei externa nihil possunt. Nã vt hostes, nominē possunt bello infestare, & agros populari, ita nec insecta, pruinæ, grandines, procella, segetes lædere & perdere possunt ni Deo visum fuerit. Is tempestates regit & gubernat. In cuius rei confirmationem producam testimonia, quædam psalm.37. Qui præcipit niui, vt descendat in terram, & hyemis pluuijs, & imbri fortitudinis suæ psal.146. Qui operit cælum nubibus, & parat terræ pluuiam. Qui producit in montibus fœnum & herbam seruituti hominum. Qui dat iumentis escam, & pullis coruorum inuocantibus eum. Et mox, nimirum 147. Psalm. iuxta antiquam versionem, Qui adipe frumenti satiat te, qui mittit eloquium suum terræ, velociter currit sermo eius.
units.tr: From what I have said at greater length it is understood that famine is sent by God, who freely uses various external means for bringing it about: natural things, malice and the negligence of men. He governs all things. Therefore external things can do nothing without the nod and will of God. For just as enemies can harass with war and lay waste the fields, so insects, frosts, hailstorms and storms cannot harm and destroy the crops unless it seems good to God. He rules and governs the weather. To confirm this I will produce some testimonies. Psalm 37 (as printed): "He who commands the snow to fall on the earth, and the rain and showers of his strength." Psalm 146: "He who covers the heaven with clouds, and prepares rain for the earth; who makes grass grow on the mountains for the service of men; who gives food to the beasts and to the young ravens that call upon him." And soon after, namely in Psalm 147 according to the old version: "He who fills you with the fat of wheat; who sends his word to the earth; his word runs swiftly."

units.la: Qui dat nivem sicut lanam, & nebulam sicut cinerem spargit. Mittit cristallum suum sicut buccellas ante faciem frigoris eius, quis sustinebit? Emittit verbum suum ut liquefaciat ea, flabit spiritus eius, & fluēt aquæ. Sequenti Psalm. 148. Ignis, grando, nix, glacies, spiritus procellarum, quæ faciunt verbum eius. Montes & omnes colles, ligna fructifera, & omnes Cedri. Bestiæ, universa pecora, serpentes & volucres pennatæ. Ierem. 14. Num quid sunt in sculptilibus gentium qui pluant, aut cæli possunt dare imbres? Nonne tu es Domine Deus noster quem expectauimus? Tu enim fecisti omnia hæc. Magnus est profanorum numerus qui contingenter famem & caritatem evenire existiment. Dicunt: Semper, quantum memoria possint repetere, fuisse rerum vicissitudines, bellum sequutum pacem, abundantiam rerum caritatem, etc. eam rerum mutationē & vicissitudinem ad finē usq; mūdi futuram. Nos vero ex sacris literis edocti credimus, nihil fortuito fieri. Sed res quantumuis minutissimas divinitus gubernari Nostri quidem, sed nō Dei respeƈtu aliquid teme re et fortuito accidere dicitur. Christus ipse dicit, ne passerem quidem, quem nullæ vnquã leges defendunt, quiq; omnium insidijs est op- positus, citra Dei voluntatē cadere super ter ram. Item omnes pilos capitis nostri numera tos esse. Ipsi Gentiles crediderunt Deum fru ges, & pecora tueri, gubernare tempestates, in hoc tantum peccarunt, quod virtute Dei, alijs atq; alijs inferioribus Dijs attribuerunt. Coluerũt Cererẽ, Bachum, Floram, Robigũ, Apollinem νόμιον[?] à pascuis sic dictum. Pa- lam pabulorum vel pastorum Deam, cuise- stum vel sacra Palilia pro partu pecoris cele brarunt. Pan quoq; animalium Deus, ab eis fuit cultus. Celebrarunt Bachanalia Bacho, Robigalia Robigini, Floralia Floræ, ut illis propitijs feliciter uinũ proueniret, neq; robi- go frumenta vel arbores corrumperet, nõ in- tempestiue florerẽt. Habuerũt suas Amber- uales hostias, quæ vt ait Festus, rei diuinæ causa circũ arua ducebãtur. Ab his Pontifici suas pcessiones mutuati sunt, quib etiã agros lustrãt, nã et frugib. pecorib. tepestatib. suos deos tutelares costituerũt. At sacra scriptura testatur Deum dare & auferre pabulum pecoribus, quantò magis homini, propter quem bruta animantia, & res vniuersæ conditæ sunt, alimentum subministrat.
units.tr: Who gives snow like wool, and scatters hoarfrost like ashes. He casts forth his ice like morsels; who can stand before his cold? He sends forth his word and melts them; he makes his wind blow, and the waters flow. In the following Psalm 148: Fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy wind, which fulfil his word. Mountains and all hills, fruitful trees and all cedars. Beasts, all cattle, creeping things and winged birds. Jeremiah 14: Are there among the idols of the nations any that send rain, or can the heavens give showers? Are not you the Lord our God, whom we have waited for? For you have made all these things. There is a great number of the profane who think that famine and dearth happen by chance. They say that, as far back as memory can reach, there have always been changes of fortune: war following peace, plenty giving way to dearth, and so on, and that this change and alternation will continue until the end of the world. But we, taught by the sacred letters, believe that nothing happens by chance. Rather, even the smallest things are governed by God. It is said that something happens rashly and by chance as far as we are concerned, but not as far as God is concerned. Christ himself says that not even a sparrow, which no laws protect and which lies open to everyone's snares, falls to the ground without the will of God. Likewise, that all the hairs of our head are numbered. The Gentiles themselves believed that God protects the fruits and the cattle and governs the storms. Their only sin was that they attributed the power of God to other, lesser gods. They worshipped Ceres, Bacchus, Flora, Robigo, Apollo Nomius [νόμιον], so called from the pastures. They worshipped Pales, goddess of fodder or of shepherds, and celebrated her festival, the Palilia, for the birth of the flocks. Pan too, the god of animals, they worshipped. They celebrated the Bacchanalia for Bacchus, the Robigalia for Robigo, and the Floralia for Flora, so that by their favour the wine would come forth well, rust would not corrupt the grain or trees, and the flowers would not bloom out of season. They had their Ambarvalia sacrifices, which, as Festus says, were led around the fields for the sake of divine worship. From these the Pontiffs borrowed their processions, with which they also purify the fields; for they set up guardian gods for crops, cattle and storms. But Scripture testifies that God gives and takes away food for the cattle. How much more, then, does he supply nourishment for man, on whose account the brute animals and all things were created.

units.la: Quam diu homines nō credunt, copiam et inopiam frugum à Deo esse, nec cōuertantur {u}seria pœnitentia, ad percutientem eos, hoc flagello: neque patienter ferent hanc pœnam. Multum itaque interest scire, vnde sit fames, & caritas rerum omnium. Et hæc de primo articulo dicta sint.
units.tr: As long as men do not believe that the abundance and the scarcity of crops come from God, and do not turn to repentance toward him who strikes them with this scourge, they will not bear this punishment patiently. It therefore matters greatly to know whence come famine and the dearth of all things. And let these things be said about the first point.

units.la: II. Sequitur secundo loco quam horribilis sit hæc pœna Famem præsertim diuturnam atrox esse malum, multis argumentis & rationibus probari potest. Aliquas adducam. Cum Deus optionem faceret Dauidi regi in ter pestem, famem & bellum, pestem tanquam læuius reliquis omnibus elegit. Plæriq; enim qui peste laborant, intra paucas horas, Deo spiritum reddentes, omnibus curis, molestijs, & mortis horrore liberantur. Qui in prælijs cadunt, non diu sapè cruciantur. Quibus cū fame luctandum est, sperat subinde aliquod remedium fore præsentibus malis, ita tandē lenta & miserrima morte contabescunt. Vere ergo Ierem.cap.4. ait: Melius fuit occisis gladio, quam interfectis fame, quoniam isti extabuerunt, consumpti à sterilitate terrae. Vt fames inuentrix est multarum artium (pauperes multa excogitant, varias artes inueniunt, ut vitam honeste sustentare pos-sint) ita etiā malesuada dicitur, nam ad latro cinia furta, cædes, imposturas, usuras, & horrenda scelera stimulu addit hominibus. Horat. audacem paupertatem vocat: fames nil non audet facere. Pia ergo est sapientis Prou. 3o. petitio Duo (inquit) rogaui te, ne deneges mihi antequam moriar: Vanitatem & verba mendacia longe fac à me. Mendicitatem & diuitias non dederis mihi. Tribue tantum victui meo necessaria, ne forte satiatus, illiciar ad negandum & dicam: Quis est Dominus? aut egestate compulsus, furer, periurem nomen Dei mei. Multi quidem diuites fuerunt omnibus seculis, qui tamen opum fiducia elati, non abnegarunt Deum, tamen ea est nostra infirmitas, ut nisi nos Deus, verbo suo tanquam freno retineat, opes insolentiores reddant. Sic multi sunt qui pau-pertatem patienter ferunt, à furto abhorret, prauis affectibus resistunt: tamen ea est natura nostrae corruptio, vt latrante stomacho, quidus nobis licere putemus, furto, medacis malis artibus, vitam sustentare volumus, peccata extenuamus: egestate ac fame compulsos haec fecisse dicimus.
units.tr: II. Second, we come to how horrible this punishment is. That famine is a dreadful evil, especially when it lasts long, can be proved by many arguments and reasons. I will adduce some. When God gave King David the choice of pestilence, famine and war, David chose pestilence, as the lightest of them all. For most who suffer from plague, within a few hours, give up the spirit to God and are freed from all cares, troubles and the horror of death. Those who fall in battle are often not tormented for long. But those who must struggle with famine keep hoping from time to time for some remedy for their present evils, and so they waste away with a slow and most wretched death. Truly, therefore, Jeremiah in chapter 4 says: "It was better for those slain by the sword than for those killed by famine, for these wasted away, consumed by the barrenness of the land." As famine is the inventor of many arts (the poor devise much and discover various skills so that they may sustain life honestly), so too it is called evil-counselling, for it spurs men on to robbery, theft, murder, fraud, usury and horrible crimes. Horace calls poverty bold; hunger dares to do anything. Holy, therefore, is the petition of the wise man in Proverbs 30: "I asked two things of you; do not deny them to me before I die. Keep vanity and lying words far from me. Give me neither beggary nor riches; give me only the necessities of my sustenance, lest perhaps, being full, I be drawn to deny and say, 'Who is the Lord?', or, compelled by want, I steal and profane the name of my God." Indeed, many rich men have existed in every age who, though elated by trust in their wealth, did not deny God. Yet such is our weakness that unless God restrains us with his word, as with a bridle, riches make us more insolent. So there are many who bear poverty patiently, who shrink from theft and resist depraved desires. Yet such is the corruption of our nature that, with the stomach barking, we want to sustain life by whatever means we think permitted: theft, lying, wicked arts. We minimise our sins and say that we did these things compelled by want and hunger.

units.la: Etiamsi non solum ad victum necessaria quae habeat, sed etiā exquisitis delitijs fruatur. Tamen in illa copia rerum, non læviter afficitur (nisi plane ferreus & adamante durior sit) si videat alios fame tabescere. Si videat in plateis opifices, rusticos, operarios, aliàs strenuos, oberrare, nec habere quod agat, nec unde vitam sustentent & ex pallore vultus fame ferè enectos cognoscit: audiat eiulatus, gemitus, vagitus infantum, puerorum, mulierum non potest non graviter commoueri, & ingemiscere, miserandum hoc spectaculum acerbas opes ei reddit. Quod si ipsos quoque famem ferre oporteat, familiam denique videre famelicam, tanto maiore dolore afficiuntur. In tanta rerum inopia, pauci operaoperariorum & artificum opera utuntur, ne mo eos conducit, etsi praeter cibum nullam aliam mercedem requirant. Multos paupertatis pudet, eam quantum possunt dissimulant, de egestate sua apud vicinos, & amicos con-queri non audent, neminem habent cui fidat, qui illorum miseretur, ijsque opem ferat, in tantis angustijs paulatim apum instar suas opes consumunt, ex avena, furfure panem pinsunt, hinc inde mutuo accipiunt pecunias, oppignorant vestes, suppellectilem, domos, agros; & quid non dura paupertas facere & pati iubet? Incidunt in faeneratores, qui auxilium pollicentur, sed non praestant, ita eos exugunt, ut nulla spes sit reliqua restitutionis eorum in integrum. Aegyptij, ut sacra historia testatur, agros, & pecora fame per septennium dominante, Regi oppignorarunt. Nehem. 5. reduces ex Babilone conquerun-tur, quod liberos suas vendere compellan-tur.
units.tr: Even if a man has not only the necessities of life but enjoys exquisite delights, yet amid that abundance he is not lightly affected (unless he is utterly iron and harder than adamant) if he sees others wasting away with hunger. If he sees craftsmen, country folk and labourers, otherwise strong, wandering about the squares with nothing to do and nothing by which to sustain life, and from the pallor of their faces recognises that they are almost killed by hunger; if he hears the wailing, groaning and crying of infants, children and women, he cannot but be grievously moved and groan. This pitiable spectacle makes his wealth bitter to him. If they must also bear hunger themselves, and he sees a famished household, they are affected with still greater grief. In such scarcity of goods, few make use of the labour of workmen and craftsmen; no one hires them, even though they ask for no wage beyond food. Many are ashamed of their poverty and hide it as far as they can; they dare not complain of their want to neighbours and friends, and have no one they can trust who pities them and brings help. In such straits they gradually consume their goods like bees, grind bread from oats and bran, borrow money here and there, pawn their clothes, household goods, houses and fields. And what does hard poverty not command and make them endure? They fall into the hands of usurers, who promise help but do not give it, and they drain them so that no hope remains of restoring them to their former state. The Egyptians, as sacred history testifies, when famine ruled for seven years, pawned their fields and cattle to the king. In Nehemiah 5 those returning from Babylon complain that they were compelled to sell their sons and daughters.

units.la: Multos etiam viros pios ac probos fames cogit, ut relicto solo patrio alias sedes quaerent, quo familiam suam commodius aleret. Abrahamus cum magna effet fames in terra Chanaan in Ægyptum profectus est. Isaac orta fame in Gerar ad Abimelechum se contulit, sed Deus in somnis ei apparens monuit ne abiret in Ægyptum, sed in illis locis se contineret, quæ ei monstraturus esset. De Iacob et Iosepho nota est historia, is cum filijs fame diu durante, in extrema sua senectute ad filium in Ægyptum descendit. Elimelech cum fames esset in Israel, cum uxore & liberis in regionē Moabiticam se contulit. Helisseus Sunamitidem iubet in aliam regionem abire. Deus enim vocaturum famem, quæ septem annos duratura fit. In profanis historijs plurima exempla extant, & nonnulla etiam in nostris annalibus leguntur. Sed quid antiqua refero? Multi minime mali, neq;[?] aliqua falsa religione in festi[?] annis iam aliquot, præ fame & egestate nouas sedes quærere coacti sunt.
units.tr: Famine also compels many pious and upright men to leave their native soil and seek other homes, where they can feed their families more conveniently. Abraham, when there was a great famine in the land of Canaan, went down into Egypt. Isaac, when famine arose in Gerar, betook himself to Abimelech; but God appeared to him in dreams and warned him not to go down into Egypt, but to remain in the places he would show him. The story of Jacob and Joseph is well known: he, with his sons, in his extreme old age went down to his son in Egypt, when the famine had lasted long. Elimelech, when there was famine in Israel, betook himself with his wife and children to the land of Moab. Elisha bade the Shunammite woman go to another region, for God was going to call the famine, which was to last seven years. Very many examples exist in profane histories, and some are also read in our own annals. But why do I recount ancient things? Many men, not at all wicked, nor under any false religion, in recent years have been compelled by famine and want to seek new homes.

units.la: Plures ad extremam paupertatem & mendicitatem redacti cateruatim cum uxoribus, & liberis oberrant, in urbib. villis, & pagis stipem importunè flagitant: rusticis præsertim, qui etiam ipsi vix habent, quod edant, molesti molestisunt. Mendicitati asueti laborare nō possunt, nec volunt. Multi tamen ex his non omnino mali, oberrant, deficientibus viribus laborare nō possunt, vix cutis ossibus hæret. Pathetica plane est Ieremiæ prophetæ in Threnis quærela: Adhæsit lingua lactantis ad palatum eius in sitì, paruuli petierunt panem, et nō erat qui frangeret eis. Et mox: Cadidiores Nazaræi eius niue, nitidiores lacte rubicūdiores ebore, antiquo saphyro pulchriores. Denigrata est super carbones facies eorum, et nō sunt cogniti in plateis. Adhæsit cutis eorum ossib. aruit, & facta est sicut lignū. Exemplis & historij, rem omnem illustrabo. Anno D. 1527. cum Gallus in Mediolanensi agro bellum gereret vt Mediolanum recupe raret, ita omnis regio assiduis bellis uastata, & depopulata fuit, ut horribilis fames consequuta sit, auctum fuit in immensum tritici precium. Comeatus Argentorato & ex Helvetia supportatus fuit, omnib. alias ex æquo fame pereundū fuisset, per tota enim regione multi fame interierunt, in ipsaq; vrbe quotidie multi in plateis fame consumpti, concide*
units.tr: Many, reduced to extreme poverty and beggary, wander about in troops with their wives and children through towns, villages and hamlets, begging alms importunately. They are a nuisance especially to country folk, who themselves scarcely have enough to eat. Accustomed to begging, they neither can nor want to work. Yet many of these are not altogether wicked. They wander about, and when their strength fails they cannot labour; they scarcely have skin clinging to their bones. The lament of the prophet Jeremiah in the Lamentations is plainly pathetic: "The tongue of the sucking child cleaveth to the roof of his mouth for thirst; the young children ask bread, and no man breaketh it unto them." And soon after: "Her Nazarites were purer than snow, they were whiter than milk, they were more ruddy in body than rubies, their polishing was of sapphire. Their visage is blacker than a coal; they are not known in the streets; their skin cleaveth to their bones; it is withered, it is become like a stick" (Lam. 4.). I will illustrate the whole matter with examples and histories. In the year 1527, when the French waged war in the territory of Milan to recover Milan, the whole region was laid waste and ravaged by constant wars, and a dreadful famine followed, and the price of wheat rose immensely. Provisions were brought in from Strasbourg and from Switzerland, yet everyone else would have had to perish by famine. For across the whole region many died of hunger, and in the city itself many were daily consumed by hunger in the streets and collapsed.

units.la: Exempla fa-miis & caritatis annona. runt, non pauci gramen & herbā in ore habere conspiciebantur. Milites nostri his visis, commiseratione moti, relictis castris domum redierunt, neue cogerentur tantas miserias aspicere militiam eiurabant.
units.tr: Examples of famine and dearth of provisions. They collapsed, and not a few were seen with grass and herbs in their mouths. Our soldiers, seeing this and moved by pity, left their camp and went home; they refused to serve, since they could not bear to see such misery.

units.la: Anno 1570. & sequentibus aliquot annis in Austria etiam & per Germaniā, multi fame consumpti sunt. Item in Italia, multi interiere, alii ne eundē vitæ finē haberent, & fame tabescerent, nauarchis ad remigia operā suam obtulerunt, voluntariē id supplicij genus subierunt, quod non nisi furibus & nebulonibus infligi solet. O malesuada fames.
units.tr: In 1570 and for some following years in Austria and throughout Germany, many were consumed by famine. Likewise in Italy many perished; others, so as not to meet the same end of life and waste away with hunger, offered their labour to ship captains for the oars, and voluntarily underwent that kind of punishment which is usually inflicted only on thieves and rogues. O accursed hunger.

units.la: An. 1572. Sæuiebat in Occitana et in maritima quidem ora, soli alioqui feracissimi regione, grauissima fames: ut passim enectorum cadauera in viis obversarentur lib.10. de statu Reip.& Relig.in regno Galliæ.
units.tr: In 1572 a most grievous famine raged in Occitania and on the maritime coast, regions otherwise most fertile, so that everywhere the corpses of the dying lay in the roads (book 10 of De statu Reipublicae et Religionis in regno Galliae).

units.la: Factum saepe est in obsidionibus urbium fame cogente, ut mures, glires, canes, equos, asinos, coria ovium & boum, paleas, quisquilias diligenter perquisierint et avidissime devorarint, & ab humana tandem carne non abstinuerint, quin quod dictu horrendum est maeres liberos præ inedia comederint. Factũ est hoc in obsidione Samariæ, in prima obsidioe ỽrbis Hierosolymitanæ sub Nabuchodono|sore, et in posteriore sub vespasiano et Tito. Sancerreses anno 1573. plusquã famem Sa-guntinam passi sunt, quã plurib. describit idẽ author de Statu Reip. & Relig. in Regno Galliæ li. 10. Quanta hæc miseria sit, omnes præsertim matres, intelligũt. Exactiorem descriptionem si quis desideret legat Ioseph. de bello Iudaico l.6.c.11. Et Eusebh.hist.Eccles. l.3.c.6. qui hæc ex Iosepho excerpsit: Naucle rus scribit An.649. quarto anno regni Clodo uei tantam annonæ caritatẽ in Gallia fuisse, ut fame & inedia populus absque modo periret. Anno 839. tanta fuit fames, ut matres, fame stipulante, filios comederint.
units.tr: Very often in sieges of cities, when famine compels, people have eagerly searched out and devoured mice, dormice, dogs, horses, asses, the hides of sheep and oxen, straw and refuse; and at last they have not abstained from human flesh, but, horrible to say, mothers have eaten their own children from hunger. This happened in the siege of Samaria, in the first siege of Jerusalem under Nebuchadnezzar, and in the later one under Vespasian and Titus. The people of Sancerre in 1573 suffered more than the famine of Saguntum, as the same author describes at greater length in book 10 of the same work. How great this misery is, all mothers especially understand. If anyone desires a more exact description, let him read Josephus, Jewish War 6.11, and Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.6, who took this from Josephus. Nauclerus writes that in the year 649, in the fourth year of the reign of Clovis, there was such dearth of provisions in Gaul that the people perished without measure from famine and starvation. In the year 839 there was such famine that mothers, with hunger demanding, ate their sons.

units.la: An.808. Dira quoq; fames uniuersam Germaniam vexauit quo tempore Hatto Mogu-tinus Episcopus nefandum illud facinus in miseros rusticos panē petentes perpetrauit. Vrspergens. scribit magnam famem quæ incidit in An.898. homines se inuicem commedere persuasisse. An.1010. vniuerso ferè terrarum in orbe inaudita fames fuit.
units.tr: In 808 a dire famine also afflicted all of Germany, at which time Hatto, bishop of Mainz, perpetrated that nefarious deed against wretched peasants who were asking for bread. Urspergensis writes that a great famine which occurred in 898 persuaded men to eat one another. In 1010 a famine almost unheard of was felt throughout nearly the whole world.

units.la: Anno 1062. Terræmotus ad 8. Januarij, frequentes grandines, magna annonæ caritas, fames fuere in his regionibus. Vide quoties Deus pœnam hanc etiam superioribus annis reuocarit? hac enim pœna superstitio-sus mundus dignus erat.
units.tr: In 1062 there were an earthquake on 8 January, frequent hailstorms, great dearth of provisions and famine in these regions. See how often God has revoked this punishment, even in earlier years? For the superstitious world deserved this punishment.

units.la: Durante bello sacro quod Christiani in Syria gessere, vbiq; terrarum erat magna fames, præsertim in exercitu Christianorum: vnum aut alterum exemplum adducam. Cum Antiochia à Saracenis cingeretur, priorem vbertatem tam intollerabilis sequuta est fames, quod & ab humanis carnibus vix abstinuerunt. Otho Frising. lib. 7. cap. 4. Otho de S. Blasio. cap.34. Notandum id est illis, qui militiam mercenariam publicæ egestatis remedium fore existimant. Circa Pragam Bohemiæ Anno 284. multi homines fame mortui. Annales Dominic. Col.
units.tr: During the holy war which the Christians waged in Syria, there was great famine everywhere, especially in the Christian army; I will adduce one or another example. When Antioch was besieged by the Saracens, after the earlier abundance so intolerable a famine followed that they scarcely abstained from human flesh (Otto of Freising, book 7, chapter 4; Otto of St Blasien, chapter 34). This is to be noted by those who think that mercenary soldiering is a remedy for public want. Near Prague in Bohemia in 1284 many men died of hunger (Annales Dominic. Col.).

units.la: Anno 1313. per Bohemiam & Poloniam continuis tribus annis maxima fames fuit, quā Vrspergens. ex Chronica Polonorum lib. 4. cap. 8. his verbis describit. Anno 1312. Fames omni bello atrocior in regno Bohemiæ & Po& Poloniæ atrociter saevit, & dietim augmentata, tribus annis duravit, & plures mortales absumpsit, parentes filios, & filij parentes pro excludenda fame occiderunt. Nonnulli cadavera in patibulum actorum rapuerunt ut rugiente[?] implerent ventrem. Lupi in obvios quosq; etiam extensos balistas portantes insiluerunt & devorarunt. Meminit quoq; tam horrendæ famis, Herburtus lib.9. cap.7. Et Germanicarum rerum scriptores referunt eodem tempore famē Germaniam pervagatam esse.
units.tr: In 1313 there was the greatest famine through Bohemia and Poland for three continuous years, which Urspergensis describes from the Chronicle of the Poles, book 4, chapter 8, in these words: "In 1312 a famine more atrocious than any war raged savagely in the kingdom of Bohemia and Poland; increasing daily, it lasted three years and carried off very many mortals. Parents killed their children, and children their parents, to ward off hunger. Some snatched corpses from the gallows of the executed to fill their roaring bellies. Wolves leapt upon all they met, even those carrying crossbows, and devoured them." Herburt also mentions so horrible a famine (book 9, chapter 7). And writers on German affairs report that at the same time famine spread through Germany.

units.la: Accidit etiam non raro, ut captiui qui fame enecandi erant digitos & proprias carnes priusquam expirassent devoraverint. Sunt qui famis impatientia sibi manus intulerint. Famem pestis sequitur plerumq;, nam, & ut modo diximus, mutuo cohærent.
units.tr: It also happens not rarely that captives who were to be starved to death have devoured their fingers and their own flesh before they expired. Some, impatient of hunger, have laid violent hands on themselves. Plague usually follows famine, for, as we have just said, they cling together.

units.la: Qua de causa vero Deus tam horribili pœna puniat homines proxima concione dicemus. Deus misericors hanc pœnam avertat. Cui sit laus, & gloria in secula. Amen.
units.tr: Why God punishes men with so horrible a penalty we shall say in the next sermon. May God in mercy avert this punishment, to whom be praise and glory for ever. Amen.

units.la: DE ANNONAE CARITATE CONCIO II.
units.tr: DE ANNONAE CARITATE CONCIO II.

units.la: CAVSAE ENVMERANTVR, quibus inductus Deus, bonos pariter ac malos caritate & fame puniat.
units.tr: The causes are set out for which God is moved to punish good and bad alike with dearth and famine.

units.la: IN omnibus publicis calamitatibus quibus genus humanum subiectum, duo praecipuè consideranda veniunt, à quo & quam ob causam haec mala generi humano accidat. De his autem corruptum est mundi iudicium, causas secundas potius quàm primam & motricem causam respicit vulgus hominum, hinc fit, vt nec quid consilij capiant, nec quomodo se se gerere debeant, satillis constet. Ex his autem publicis calamitatibus peste, fame, bello, non vltima est annonae caritas & fames, de qua nobis instituta est oratio. Et proxima quidem Concione, tantae calamitatis & egestatis, veram ac primam causam, authorem & effectorem Deum esse sacrarum literarum testimonijs & exemplis probavimus. bauimus[?]. Ego sum, inquit, apud prophetam faciens pacem & creans malum, malum sci licet pœnæ non culpæ. Totum enim hoc opus non causis secundis, non rebus naturalibus, non malitiæ hominum, sed Deo tribuendum est, qui his externis mediis efficaciter vti-tur, qui impios excitat, vt nos eorum manu castiget, (non enim malitiam illis inspirat, sed ea vtitur ad nos castigandos.) Dein secundo loco incommoda tantæ pœnæ enumerauimus, hoc est, quam dira ac horrenda sit demonstrauimus.
units.tr: In all public calamities that befall the human race, two things chiefly deserve consideration: from whom these evils come upon mankind, and for what reason. Concerning these matters the judgement of the world is corrupt. The common people look to secondary causes rather than to the first and moving cause, and so they neither take sensible counsel nor know how they ought to conduct themselves. Among such public calamities (plague, famine, war), scarcity of grain and hunger are no small matter, and it is about these that our discourse has been undertaken. In the last sermon we proved, by the testimonies and examples of Holy Scripture, that God is the true and first cause, the author and the agent of so great a calamity and want. "I am," he says, "the one who in the prophet makes peace and creates evil," that is, the evil of punishment, not of fault. For this whole work is to be attributed not to secondary causes, nor to natural things, nor to the wickedness of men, but to God, who effectively uses these external means and stirs up the wicked, so that he may chastise us by their hand. (He does not inspire wickedness in them, but uses them to chastise us.) Secondly, we set out the discomforts of so great a punishment, that is, we showed how dire and horrible it is.

units.la: Sequitur vt tertio loco dicamus, quid nam Deum moueat, (qui clemens & miseri-cors est) vt tam horribili & dira pœna bonos æque ac malos, infantes perinde ac senes, vniuersas denique regiones ad-ficiat. Nec de his causis etiam sanum est mundi iuditium, sentiunt quidem omnes manum ferientis Dei, de pœna communis omnium querela est: At quia iuditio multi carent, & asinis stupidiores sunt, nec sentiunt nec intelligunt, quas ob causas id fiat, aut quomodo ex præsentibus his malis emergendum sit. Falsas fere pro veris, secundas pro primis obseruant. Vulgus omne culpam, auaritiae, malitiae, immisericordiae usurariorum, monopolarum ascribunt, hos omnes uno ore accusant: At de corruptis nostris moribus, de vitiis & sceleribus, de impunitate & licentia peccandi, magnum silentium. Cogitandum ergo Deum malitia impiorum uti, ut in nos animaduertat. Ut ergo medicus causis morbi cognitis, commodius & felicius medicinam adhibet: Ita cognitis & hic tanti mali causis, facilius & melius videbimus, quomodo nos gerere debeamus, ut haec mala euadere valeamus.
units.tr: It follows that in the third place we should say what it is that moves God, who is merciful and compassionate, to afflict good and bad alike with so horrible and dire a punishment, infants as well as old men, and whole regions. Nor is the judgement of the world sound about these causes either. All people do indeed perceive the hand of God striking them, and there is a common complaint of everyone about the punishment. But because many lack judgement and are more stupid than asses, they neither perceive nor understand for what causes this happens, or how we must get out of these present evils. They commonly take false things for true and secondary causes for primary ones. The whole crowd ascribes the fault to the greed, wickedness and lack of mercy of the usurers and monopolists; they all accuse these men with one voice. But about our corrupt morals, our vices and crimes, about impunity and licence to sin, there is great silence. We must therefore consider that God uses the wickedness of the impious to take vengeance upon us. Just as a physician, once the causes of a disease are known, applies his remedy more conveniently and successfully, so, once the causes of so great an evil are known, we shall more easily and better see how we ought to conduct ourselves so that we may be able to escape these evils.

units.la: Primò ergo oculos ad ferientem Deum conuerte, dein quid illum moueat inquire: Ita venies in tui ipsius cognitionem. Hic tamen studiosè cauendum, ne falsas causas pro veris tibi obtrudere patiaris: In his aliisq; calamitatibus omnis fere culpa in veram religionem reijcitur. Pro concione malefe-riati quidam clamant, in foro vociferantur, in conuiuijs hoc vrgent, Nouae nimirum religioni (hoc enim titulo dignantur Euange-licam licam veritatem ) hanc annonæ caritatem acceptam ferendam esse. Ex quo defectio fa-cta sit, & Divus honor denegatus, antiquus Dei cultus (sic Pontificiam religionem vocant) abrogatus, mare malorum obruisse mundum. A quibus immunes essemus, si perstetissent in avita religione, qui a nobis defecerunt. Hæc illorum sunt verba: quibus nobis odium & invidiam conflare conantur. Sed meminerint superioribus seculis Pontificios omnium istorum malorum nō fuisse immunes: Testantur exempla proxima concione adducta. Sed ad rem. Non noua hæc est querela. Regnante impio rege Achabo, diuturna erat fames in Israel: Rex indi-gnabundus, dicebat ad Heliam Prophetam, Tu ne es ille, qui conturbas Israel? authorem famis, quæ multas turbas dat, hoc ipso designat, (quo sensu Ionathan dicebat, patrem suum Saulem, turbasse populum, cum milites à cibo, abstinere iussisset.) At ille fortiter respondit. Non ego (inquit) Israelem turbavi, sed tu & domus patris tui, quandoquidē reliquisti præcepta Domini & Baalim estis sequuti. Ita postea Ioramus rex, in Helisæum confert culpam famis, quæ Samariæ tanta erat, ut matres filios suos comederent. Rex furore correptus, mittebat seruum, qui prophetam interficeret, at præmonitus à Deo vitauit. Christianis eadem obiecta sunt, vt Tertullianus, Cyprianus, Arnobius & alij qui Apologias pro Christianis scripsere, testantur. Quoties enim Deus mundum afflixit, pruina, grandine, fame, peste, bello, aquarum inundatione, aut si qua alia calamitas publica incidisset, conclamatum est contra Christianos, Ad bestias, ad bestias, ad leones, tolle sacrilegos, scelestos istos homines non fas est viuere: indigni sunt, qui lucem aspiciant. Eusebius scribit histor. Eccles. libro nono, capite septimo, Imperatorem Maximinum passim edicta sua promulgasse, quibus indicauit, omnia mala, quæ mundus hactenus perpessus fit, propter purnitiosum istum errorem nefandorum illorum hominum, ( intelligens Christianos ) accidisse, qui vbique ferè terrarum rarum obtinuerit: gloriabatur suo tempore, ideo neque bellum, neque pestem fuisse, quod simulachra colat, & Christianos supplicijs afficiat: haec autem mala omnia, vnò eodemque tempore illum obruerunt, iactantiamque eius & contumaciam in Deum, con-tumderunt[?]. Nemo itaq; miretur similes voces hodie audiri, ab impijs & profanis hominibus qui veritatis lucem, & disciplinam odio habent. Nonne Christus praedixit, suis omnia mala eventura esse?
units.tr: First, then, turn your eyes to God who strikes, and then inquire what moves him. So you will come to the knowledge of yourself. Yet here you must take careful care that you do not allow false causes to be foisted upon you in place of true ones. In this and other calamities almost all the blame is cast upon the true religion. Certain evildoers cry out before the sermon, they shout in the marketplace, they press this point at banquets: that this scarcity of grain is to be laid at the door of the new religion (for so they deign to call the evangelical truth). Because of it, they say, a defection has been made, and the divine honour has been denied, and the ancient worship of God (so they call the Papist religion) has been abolished, and a sea of evils has overwhelmed the world; we would have been free from these if those who have fallen away from us had persisted in the ancestral religion. These are their words, by which they try to stir up hatred and envy against us. But let them remember that in earlier centuries the Papists were not free from all these evils; the examples brought forward in the last sermon bear witness to this. But to the matter. This complaint is not new. Under the impious king Ahab there was a long famine in Israel. The king, indignant, said to Elijah the prophet: "Are you the one who troubles Israel?" By this he marks the author of the famine, which gives rise to many disturbances (in the same sense Jonathan said that his father Saul had troubled the people when he ordered the soldiers to abstain from food). But Elijah answered boldly: "I have not troubled Israel," he said, "but you and your father's house, since you have forsaken the commandments of the LORD and have followed the Baals. Likewise afterwards King Joram laid the blame for the famine upon Elisha, which was so great in Samaria that mothers ate their own sons. The king, seized with fury, sent a servant to kill the prophet, but being forewarned by God he escaped. The same charges were brought against the Christians, as Tertullian, Cyprian, Arnobius and others who wrote apologies for the Christians bear witness. For whenever God afflicted the world with hoar-frost, hail, famine, plague, war, floods of waters, or any other public calamity, the cry went up against the Christians: "To the beasts, to the beasts! To the lions! Away with these sacrilegious and wicked men; they are not fit to live; they are unworthy to see the light." Eusebius writes in his Ecclesiastical History, book nine, chapter seven, that the emperor Maximinus published his edicts everywhere, in which he declared that all the evils the world had suffered until then had come upon it because of that pernicious error of those abominable men (meaning the Christians), who had spread almost everywhere on earth. He boasted that in his own time there had been neither war nor plague, because he worshipped the images and punished the Christians; but all these evils overwhelmed him at one and the same time, and they crushed his boastfulness and his defiance against God. Let no one therefore be surprised that similar voices are heard today from impious and profane men, who hate the light of the truth and its discipline. Did not Christ foretell that all these evils would come upon his people?

units.la: Sacrae litera aperte & euidenter ostendunt, caritatem annonae flagellum esse Dei, quo hominum multiplicia & enormia peccata in primis superstitionem & idololatriam castigare solet. Adducta sunt nuper aliquot testimonia, audiamus & reliqua. Leuit.26. cap. dicit, Si autem non audieritis me, neque feceritis omnia praecepta ista: Et si decreta mea spreueritis, & iudicia mea abominata fuerit anima vestra, ita vt non faciatis omnia praecepta mea, & irritum faciatis pactum meum: Seretis frustra semen vestrum: nam comedent illud inimici vestri. In eandem sententiam loquitur etiam Deut.* 28. Et capite 11. eiusdē[?] libri dicit Dominus: Terra autem ad quam ingredieris possidendam, non est sicut terra Ægypti, ex qua egressi estis, in qua seminabas semen tuum, & irrigabas pede tuo, ut hortum oleris. At terra ad quam transitis, ut possideatis eam, terra montium & vallium est, de pluuia cœli bibes aquam. Est terra quam Iehouæ Deus tuus requirit, semper sunt oculi Iehoua in ea, à principio anni vsque ad extremum anni. Erit itaq;[?] si obediendo obedieritis præ-ceptis meis, quæ ego præcipio vobis hodie, ita ut diligatis Iehouam Deum vestrum, & colatis eum toto corde vestro, & tota anima vestra: dabo pluuiam terræ vestræ in tempore suo, temporaneam & serotinam, & ita colliges frumentum tuum, ac oleum tuum: & dabo herbam in agro tuo, pro iumentis tuis, commedesq; & saturaberis. Cauete ergo vobis ne forte seducatur cor vestrum, & recedatis, colatisq; Deos alienos, & incuruetis vos coram eis: unde irascatur furor Iehouæ in vos, & claudat cœlos, ac non sit pluuia, neque neque terra det fructum suum, pereatis̃q; celeriter à terra optima, quam Iehoua dat vobis. Deut. 32. cap. describitur Canticum Mosis, in quo indicat, quod Idololatria Deum ad iram provocarint, & inter alia dicit Dominus. Consumam super eos mala, sagittas meas consumam in eis, absumentur fame.
units.tr: The Holy Scriptures plainly and evidently show that scarcity of grain is a scourge of God, with which he is wont to chastise the manifold and enormous sins of men, above all superstition and idolatry. Some testimonies were lately adduced; let us hear the rest. Leviticus chapter 26 says: "But if you will not hearken to me, and do not observe all these commandments, and if you despise my statutes, and your soul abhors my judgements, so that you do not do all my commandments and make void my covenant, you shall sow your seed in vain, for your enemies shall eat it." Deuteronomy 28 speaks to the same effect. And in chapter 11 of the same book the Lord says: "But the land into which you are going to possess it is not like the land of Egypt, from which you have come out, where you sowed your seed and watered it with your foot like a garden of herbs. But the land to which you pass over to possess it is a land of mountains and valleys; it drinks water from the rain of heaven. It is a land which the LORD your God seeks; the eyes of the LORD are always upon it, from the beginning of the year to its end. So it will be, if you obey my commandments which I command you today, so that you love the LORD your God and serve him with all your heart and all your soul: I will give the rain of your land in its season, the early and the late rain, and you shall gather in your corn and your oil; and I will give grass in your field for your cattle, and you shall eat and be satisfied. Take heed to yourselves, lest your heart be deceived and you turn aside and serve other gods and bow yourselves down before them; then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and he will shut up the heavens, and there will be no rain, and the land will not yield its fruit, and you will perish quickly from the good land which the LORD gives you." Deuteronomy 32, where the Song of Moses is described, in which he shows that idolatry provoked God to anger, and among other things the Lord says: "I will heap evils upon them; I will spend my arrows upon them. They shall be consumed with hunger."

units.la: Prophetæ, Moßs ac legis interpretes, disertis & expressis verbis dicunt, repetunt & inculcant Deum punire scelera hominum, falsum Dei cultum & idololatriam, inopia & fame. Age loca evidentiora adducemus. Isaias tertio capite, minatur populo, expressò Dei mandato, se propter multiplices eius transgressiones, omne fulcrū cibi, & omne fulcrum aquæ ablaturū: vt tametsi eis cibus & potus abundè suppetant, non tamen famem sedant, sitim restinguant. Vide plura 24. cap. Ieremias cap. 5. Ecce ego adduco super vos gentem de longinquo, & comedet ea gens messem tuam, & panem tuum, comedet filios tuos & filias tuas, comedet gregem tuam & armentum tuum, comedet vineam tuam, & ficum tuam. Causas pluri-
units.tr: The prophets, Moses and the interpreters of the law say, repeat and press home in plain and explicit words that God punishes men's sins, false worship and idolatry with want and famine. Let us bring forward the more obvious passages. Isaiah, in chapter 3, by an express command of God, threatens the people that because of their manifold transgressions he will take away every support of food and every support of water, so that although bread and drink are available to them in plenty, they will neither satisfy their hunger nor quench their thirst. See more in chapter 24. Jeremiah, chapter 5: "Behold, I will bring upon you a nation from afar, and that nation shall eat up your harvest and your bread; it shall eat up your sons and your daughters; it shall eat up your flock and your herd; it shall eat up your vine and your fig tree." The causes of the many-

units.la: E bus sequenti sexto capite enumerat: legas, nam nostro seculo optime omnia conueniunt.
units.tr: ones he enumerates in the following sixth chapter. Read it, for everything fits our own age very well.

units.la: Cap. decimoquarto describitur concio quam tempore famis & penuria fructuum habuit, inter alia, causam tanti mali exponit. Nostrae iniquitates, inquit, rependunt nobis. Pseu-doprophetae tempore famis, fertiles annos, fructuum vbertatem illis pollicebantur, tempore fertilitatis dicebant, non esse metuendam sterilitatem & inopiam victus, in tan-tarum omnium abundantia. His fidem habebant Iudaei. Sic enim natura comparati sumus, vt illis fidem habeamus, qui pro-spera & felicia nobis pollicentur. Itaque propheta eis praedicit quod fame & pe-ste peri-turi sint, quicquid alij dicant. Atque id his verbis: Gladio & fame consumentur prophetae huiusmodi. Et populus cui ipsi va-ticinantur, erunt proiecti in plateis Ierusa-lem prae fame & gladio, nec erit qui sepeliat eos, ipsi inquam, vxores eorum, filij eorum, & filiae eorum, & effundam super eos ma-litiam suam.
units.tr: Chapter 14 describes a sermon which he gave in a time of famine and scarcity of crops. Among other things he sets out the cause of so great an evil: "Our iniquities," he says, "answer against us." False prophets, in a time of famine, promised fertile years and a rich harvest; in a time of plenty they said that barrenness and lack of food were not to be feared, given such an abundance of everything. The Jews gave them credence. For we are so constituted by nature that we believe those who promise us prosperous and happy things. Therefore the prophet foretells that they will perish by famine and pestilence, whatever others may say. He says it in these words: "By sword and famine shall such prophets be consumed. And the people to whom they prophesy shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem because of famine and sword, and there shall be no one to bury them: they themselves, I say, their wives, their sons and their daughters. And I will pour out their wickedness upon them."

units.la: Ezechiel in Babylone eadem docuit & prædixit quæ Jeremias in Judæa & Jerusalem, nempe Dominum effecturum, ut urbs propter ipsorum idololatriam & flagitia obsidione prematur, multi in ea fame & peste pereant. Eadem minatur illis qui iam abducti, & mox abducendi erant. Capite 4. maiori vehementia rem agit, jubet enim Deus prophetam urbem delineare super laterem, eam obsidere & toto obsidionis tempore panem ex tritico, hordeo, faba, lente, milio, siligine confecto, certo pondere vesci, aquam certa mensura bibere, loco prunarum, quibus panem coquebat, stercus humanum accipere, aut pro humano, fimum boum. Quibus omnibus, ut ipse interpretatur, significatur Deum subtracturum panis vim alendi. Hierosolymis panem certo pondere comesturos, aquam certa mensura bibituros, carituros lignis. In obsidionibus enim civitatum aut munitionum, si metuenda est fames & annonæ penuria, omnes fruges ad belli duces perferre oportet, qui eas in singula capita certo pondere & mensura partiuntur, idem de aqua fit in locis aridis, sæpe armata manu milites aquam petunt, Hierosolymis id accidit: Causam in fine capitis refert. Propterea deficient pane & a-qua, & vastabuntur vir & frater eius, & contabescent in iniquitatibus suis. Eadem cap.12. ijsdem propemodum verbis repetit. Capite 5. dixit, Idcirco sic dicit Dominus, quoniam in statutis meis non ambulastis, & iudicia mea non fecistis, quin secundum iu-dicia gentium quæ circa vos sunt non feci-stis. Idcirco sic dixit Dominus, Ecce me ti-bi, ego inquam edam in medio tui iudicia in oculis gentium faciam inquam in te, quæ non feci & quod porro nunquam facturus sum, idque propter omnes abominationes tuas. Si quidem patres comedent filios in medio tui, & filij comedent patres suos, &c. Iusto Dei iudicio hoc factum est, contra ex-pressum Dei mandatum immolabant filios suos Molocho, is erat Saturnus (de quo sa-crificio plura scribit author noster Homil. 61.in 16. Ezechielis.) Erat ergo pæna ta-lionis. Et paulo post, Erisque opprobrio & blasphe& blasphemiæ, castigationi & stupori gentibus quæ circum te sunt, quum edidero in te iudicia in furore, in exæstuatione, & in increpationibus æstus, ego Dominus loquutus sum. Quum misero sagittas famis malas in eos, quæ sunt ad vastandum, & quas ego immissurus sum ut perdam vos, & famem adijciam super vos, & confringam in vobis baculum panis, &c. Sagittas famis vocat, bruchos, erucas, locustas, & id genus frugum pestes, item pruinam, grandinem, rubiginem, &c. Adde his propolas monopolas, qui fruges recondunt, nec ante venum exponunt, quàm precium valde auctum sit, aliquando etiam eas corrumpunt & adulterant. Sic Dicit Dominus Deus, Percute manu tua, & concute pede tuo, & dic, Ach, super omnes abominationes domus Israel, qui cadent gladio, fame & peste. Qui longe abest[?], peste morietur, qui prope gladio cadet: reliquus autem & obsessus fame morietur, compleboque furorem meum in eis. Et cognoscetis quod ego sum Dominus, quum fuerint vulnerati eorum in medio idolo-rum suorum per circuitum altarium eo-rum,&c. Sequenti septimo capite, rursum praedicit, propter abominationes & scelera ipsorum, magnam in populo fore afflictio-nem. Foris gladius, pestis atq;[?] fames intus: qui in agro est gladio interibit, & qui in ci-uitate hunc devorabit fames & pestis. Et aliquot interiectis verbis, Diuites alloqui-tur quibus poenam quoque minatur, illi ex aliorum egestate rem suam faciebant, & sterilibus annis ad quaestum faciendum abu-tebantur, alijsque esurientibus, ipsi luxurio-sa & magnifica conuiuia instruebant. Qui & nostrorum divitum mores sunt. Argen-tum suum, inquit, in plateas abijcient, & aurum eorum in disiectionem erit: argen-tum eorum & aurum eorum non poterit eos liberare in die furoris Domini: animam suam non satiabunt, neque viscera sua im-plebunt, eo quod offendiculum iniquitatis suae fuit: Diuites se contra omnia pericula animae & corporis satis munitos esse confi-dunt. Prouerbiorum decimo capite, Opes diuitiis sunt ciuitas fortitudinis eius, hoc est, ut milites confidunt munitionibus, ita illi suis opibus: sed spe sua frustrabuntur, veniet tempus, quo vna cum aliis pauperibus, quorum ærumna hactenus parum afficiebantur, fame peribunt. In obsidionibus diuitum sæpius peior est conditio, miles tormentis argentum extorquere solet. Cap. 14. Rursum pœnitere nescijs quatuor plagas minatur, gladium, famem, pestem, & nocentes bestias. De fame in hanc sententiam loquitur. Fili hominis si terra peccauerit contra me præua ricando præuaricationem (מעל maal perfidiam & defectionem significat) extendam manum super eam, & confringam baculum panis eius, immittam in eam famem, & succidam ex ea homines et iumentum, etsi fuerint tres illi viri in medio eius, Noe, Daniel & Iob, ipsi in iustitia sua liberabunt animas suas dicit Dominus Deus.
units.tr: Ezekiel in Babylon taught the same things and foretold what Jeremiah had foretold in Judea and Jerusalem, namely that the Lord would bring it about that the city, because of their idolatry and shameful deeds, would be pressed by siege, and that many in it would perish by famine and pestilence. He threatens the same to those who were already led away and those who were soon to be led away. In chapter 4 he deals with the matter with greater vehemence, for God orders the prophet to draw the city upon a brick, to besiege it, and throughout the whole time of the siege to eat bread made of wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt, by a fixed weight, to drink water by a fixed measure, and, in place of the coals with which he baked the bread, to take human dung, or, instead of human, cow dung. By all these things, as he himself explains, it is signified that God will withdraw the power of bread to nourish. The people of Jerusalem will eat bread by weight, drink water by measure, and be without wood. For in the sieges of cities or fortresses, if famine and scarcity of provisions are to be feared, all the grain must be brought to the commanders of the war, who divide it among each head by fixed weight and measure. The same happens with water in dry places, where soldiers often seek water with armed hand. This happened at Jerusalem. He gives the cause at the end of the chapter: "Therefore they shall lack bread and water, and a man and his brother shall be wasted, and waste away in their iniquities." The same thing in chapter 12 he repeats in almost the same words. In chapter 5 he said: "Therefore thus says the Lord, because you have not walked in my statutes and have not done my judgments, nor have you done according to the judgments of the nations that are around you. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you; I, I say, will execute judgments in the midst of you in the sight of the nations; I will do in you what I have not done and what I will never do again, and this because of all your abominations. Indeed fathers shall eat their sons in the midst of you, and sons shall eat their fathers," and so on. This happened by the just judgment of God, since, contrary to the express command of God, they offered their sons to Moloch, who was Saturn (concerning which sacrifice our author writes more in Homily 61 on Ezekiel 16). There was therefore a punishment of retaliation. And a little later: "And you shall be a reproach and a blasphemy, a chastisement and an astonishment to the nations that are around you, when I shall have executed judgments upon you in fury, in heat, and in rebukes of wrath; I the Lord have spoken. When I send upon them the evil arrows of famine, which are for destruction, and which I will send to destroy you, and I will add famine upon you, and break in you the staff of bread," and so on. He calls the arrows of famine the locusts, caterpillars, grasshoppers, and that kind of pests of crops; likewise frost, hail, mildew, and so on. Add to these the forestallers and engrossers, who store up grain and do not put it on sale until the price has greatly risen, and sometimes even spoil and adulterate it. "Thus says the Lord God: Strike with your hand and stamp with your foot, and say, Alas, for all the abominations of the house of Israel; they shall fall by sword, famine and pestilence. He who is far off shall die of pestilence, he who is near shall fall by the sword, and he who remains and is besieged shall die of famine; and I will spend my fury upon them. And you shall know that I am the Lord, when their slain lie in the midst of their idols around their altars," and so on. In the following seventh chapter he again foretells that, because of their abominations and their wicked deeds, there will be great affliction among the people. "Sword without, pestilence and famine within: he who is in the field shall fall by the sword, and he who is in the city, famine and pestilence shall devour him." And after some intervening words he addresses the rich, threatening them also with punishment; they made their wealth out of the want of others, and abused the barren years to make gain, and while others starved they set up luxurious and magnificent feasts. These are also the manners of our rich. "They will cast their silver into the streets," he says, "and their gold shall become a thing of contempt; their silver and their gold shall not be able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the Lord; they shall not satisfy their souls nor fill their bowels, because it was a stumbling block of their iniquity." The rich trust that they are sufficiently fortified against every danger to soul and body. Proverbs, chapter 10: "Riches are the strong city of the rich," that is, as soldiers trust in their fortifications, so they trust in their wealth; but their hope will be frustrated; the time will come when they, together with other poor people, whose distress had hitherto touched them little, will perish by famine. In the sieges of the rich the condition is often worse; the soldier usually extorts silver by torture. Chapter 14. Again, he threatens four plagues to those who will not repent: sword, famine, pestilence, and noxious beasts. About famine he speaks to this effect: "Son of man, if the land sins against me by committing a trespass (the word maal [מעל] means perfidy and defection), I will stretch out my hand upon it, and break its staff of bread, and send famine into it, and cut off from it man and beast, even though those three men, Noah, Daniel and Job, were in its midst; they by their righteousness shall deliver their own souls, says the Lord God."

units.la: Quod autem Ezechiel præ reliquis prophetis hanc pœnam tanta vehementia verborum minatur, causa hæc est, quod res Iudæorum pessimo in loco erant: nullis minus, monitis mouebantur, erant omninò contumaces, ideo toties repetit & eandem rem subinde vrget. Et paucis quidem verbis multa complectitur, causam efficientem seu authorem, Deum esse digito monstrat, causas quæ eum impellunt ostendit: formam quòd subtrahit vim alendi: Effecta, homines, iumenta, diuites & pauperes peribunt.
units.tr: Why Ezekiel threatens this punishment with such vehemence of words beyond the other prophets is this: the affairs of the Jews were in the worst state. They were moved least of all by warnings and were utterly obstinate; therefore he repeats it so often and presses the same matter again and again. In a few words he embraces much: he points out with his finger that God is the efficient cause or author; he shows the causes which move him; as to the form, that he withdraws the power of nourishing; the effects are that men, beasts, rich and poor will perish.

units.la: Nunc progrediamur ad minores prophetas. Hoseas ca.4. longum catalogum scelerum recenset, propter quæ Deus populum same et alijs malis castigaturus sit. Sic autem loquitur. Audite verbum Domini filij Israe lis, quoniam lis est Domino cum habitatoribus huius terræ. Quia neq; veritas, neq; beneficentia neq; notitia Dei est in terra. Peie rare, mentiri, occidere, furari, mæchari eruperunt (hoc est cumulatim regnant) & sanguines sanguines tetigerunt. Propterea lugebit ipsa terra, & deformabuntur omnes habitatores in ea, vnà cum bestia agri, & volucre cæli, quin & pisces maris coficientur. Verumtamen non est quispiam qui aut expo-stulet, stulet, aut reprehendat, quin populus meus sic se habet, ut qui litiget cū sacerdotib. etc. Et ca. 9. Ne læteris Israel ad exultationem ut gentes, quia scortatus es à Deo tuo, & dilexisti mercedem propter omnia horrea fru-menti. Horreum & torcular non pascet eos, & mustum fallet eos. Non habitabunt in terra Domini, sed revertetur Ephraim in Ægyptum, atque in Assyriam, & comedent immundum.
units.tr: Now let us go on to the minor prophets. Hosea, ch. 4, recounts a long catalogue of crimes on account of which God would punish the people with famine and other evils. He speaks thus: "Hear the word of the LORD, you children of Israel, for the LORD has a controversy with the inhabitants of this land. Because there is no truth, no kindness, and no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing, lying, murder, theft and adultery have broken out (that is, they reign on every side), and blood has touched blood. Therefore the land itself will mourn, and all who dwell in it will waste away, together with the beasts of the field and the birds of the heavens; even the fish of the sea will be taken away. Yet no one will protest or rebuke, since my people is like those who strive with the priests," etc. And in ch. 9: "Do not rejoice, Israel, with exultation like the nations, for you have played the harlot against your God and loved a reward on every threshing floor of grain. Threshing floor and winepress will not feed them, and the new wine will fail them. They will not dwell in the land of the LORD, but Ephraim will return to Egypt, and they will eat unclean food in Assyria."

units.la: Amos 4.cap. exprobrat populo, quod pe-regrinationes religionis ergò, in Bethel in-stituerint, idololatricis cultibus sese pollue-rint. Idcirco dicit Dominus. Ego vobis dedi munditiem dentium, etc. quem locum nuper citavi. Sensus est. Non opus habebunt den-tifricijs, quibus carnes, quæ dentibus adhæ-sissent, elicerent, vix panem atrum habere poterunt.
units.tr: Amos, ch. 4, rebukes the people because they set up pilgrimages to Bethel for the sake of religion and defiled themselves with idolatrous worship. Therefore the Lord says: "I have given you cleanness of teeth," etc., a passage I quoted recently. The sense is this: they will have no need of toothpicks to draw out the flesh that had stuck between their teeth, for they will scarcely be able to have black bread.

units.la: Ex his testimonijs sacrarum literarum, sa-tis superq, constat, caritatem & famem pœnam esse scelerum, in primis idololatriæ, & falsi cultus falsorum Deorum.
units.tr: From these testimonies of Holy Scripture it is abundantly clear that dearth and famine are the punishment of sins, above all of idolatry and of false worship of false gods.

units.la: Atq; hæc quidem in genere, & præsertim de enormibus sceleribus dicta sunt. Nunc quaedam in specie, ut loquuntur, dicenda sunt.
units.tr: These things have been said in general, and especially about enormous sins. Now certain things must be said in particular, as they say.

units.la: Hoc est, Quomodo Deus peculiaria quaedam peccata, hoc flagello castigarit. Multi enim quia non sunt manifestis sceleribus contaminati, nec idololatrae, nec superstitiosi, ideo putant ipsos hanc poenam non esse meritos, indignos esse qui haec patiantur. At hic cogitandum, ipsos non carere vitio: ideo merito cōmunem subire poenam. Per species ergo enumerabo peculiaria quaedam peccata, quibus expresse et diserte Deus minatur famem. Ierem. 11.capit. scribit suos populares in Anathoth mandasse sub poena capitis, ne cōcionaretur, hanc audaciam dicit Deus, se penuria rerū & samie velle ulcisci: hit[?] verbis: Ideo sic dicit Dominus de viris Anathoth, qui quaerunt animam tuam, & dicunt, ne prophetes in nomine Domini, ne moriaris in manibus nostris: idcirco sic dicit Dominus exercituum: Ecce ego visitabo eos, iuuenes morientur gladio, filij autem & filiae eorum morientur fame, ut nulli fiant reliqui, quia adducam calamitatem super cines[?] Anathoth, annū visitationis eorum. Iustum autem es[?] & ut si homines pretiosum animæ cibum, verbum Dei aspernentur, Deus cibum corporis eis subtra hat. Vide Amos 8. cap.
units.tr: That is, how God has punished certain peculiar sins with this scourge. For many, because they are not stained with manifest crimes, are neither idolaters nor superstitious, therefore think that they have not deserved this punishment, and that they are unworthy to suffer these things. But here one must consider that they are not free from fault, and so they rightly undergo the common punishment. I will therefore enumerate by species certain peculiar sins for which God expressly and plainly threatens famine. In Jeremiah, ch. 11, we read that his fellow countrymen in Anathoth ordered him, under pain of death, not to preach. God says he will avenge this audacity by a lack of goods and by famine, in these words: "Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life and say, 'Do not prophesy in the name of the LORD, lest you die by our hands': therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: Behold, I will visit them; the young men shall die by the sword, and their sons and daughters shall die by famine, so that none of them remain, for I will bring disaster upon the men of Anathoth, the year of their visitation." It is also just that, since men despise the precious food of the soul, the word of God, God should withhold from them the food of the body. See Amos, ch. 8.

units.la: Multi quidem audiunt verbum, consulunt proph. sed eorum dictis fidē non habent, hunc uerbi Dei contemptū fame ulciscitur Deus. Iere.42.c. Urbe deleta à Nabuchodonosore, reliquiæ cōsulebant Ierem. utrũ in Ægyptū proficisci deberent, nec ne: cūq; disuaderet, illi nihilominus ad iter sese accingebant: diser te itaq; dicit Propheta in Ægypto fame periturus[?]. Consilia bona ex verbo Dei petita, hodie quoq; à nobis repudiantur. Digni ergo sumus, ut petentes panem, repudiamur.
units.tr: Many indeed hear the word and consult the prophets, but do not trust their words; God avenges this contempt of his word with famine. Jeremiah, ch. 42: when Nebuchadnezzar had destroyed the city, the remnant consulted Jeremiah whether they ought to set out for Egypt or not; and when he dissuaded them, they nonetheless prepared themselves for the journey. The prophet therefore plainly says that they will perish by famine in Egypt. Good counsels sought from the word of God are rejected by us today as well. We are therefore worthy that, when we seek bread, we be refused.

units.la: Privati quoq; commodi studium, Deū ad-iram provocat. Cum res nostras curamus, parum solliciti de gloria Dei, & propagatione verbi ipsius. Israelitæ ex Babilone patriæ restituti, privatas ædes splendidè ædificabãt: domus D. nulla ratio habita fuit: idcirco Deus pœnam eis per Aggæū cōminatur dicēs: Diligeter perpedite vias vestras. Seminastis multum, & parū infertis, commeditis sed non ad satietatem bibitis, sed non ad ebrietatem: induimini, ita tamen, ut nemo calefiat, & qui se ipsum pro precio elocat, recipit mercedem in saculum pertusum. Et mox. Respicitis ad multum, & ecce parum, quodque in domum infertis, in illud ego infio, ob idscilicet, dicit Dominus exercituū, quod domus mea adhuc deserta est, vos autem curritis, ut quisque domum suam habeat. Idcirco cœli super vos rorem non dant, nec terra prouentum suum. Ego quoque vocaui siccitatem super terram, & super montes, super frumetum & vinum, super oleum, & super vniuersum quod terra profert, super hominem, & super iumentum & super vniuersum laborem manuum.
units.tr: The pursuit of private advantage also provokes God to anger. When we look after our own affairs, we are little concerned for the glory of God and the propagation of his word. The Israelites, restored to their country from Babylon, built their own houses splendidly, and no account was taken of the house of the LORD. Therefore God threatens them with punishment through Haggai, saying: "Consider carefully your ways. You have sown much and brought in little; you eat, but not to satiety; you drink, but not to drunkenness; you clothe yourselves, but so that no one is warm; and he who hires himself out for wages receives his wages in a bag with holes." And soon after: "You look for much, and behold, little; and what you bring into the house, I blow away. Why? says the LORD of hosts, because my house is still deserted, while you run, each to have his own house. Therefore the heavens over you withhold their dew, and the earth its produce. I have also called for a drought upon the land, upon the mountains, upon the grain and the wine, upon the oil, and upon all that the earth brings forth, upon man and beast and upon all the labour of your hands."

units.la: Quod Deus propter periurium & oppressionem pauperum, cum aliis poenis, tum caritate annonæ homines castiget, ostendit insignis illa historia, quæ 2.Sam.21.cap.extat. Fame dominante tribus annis, consulebat Dauid Dominum quænam tāti mali causa esset, is respondebat famem: eam nāq; gras-sari propter Saulem eiusque domum, quod miseros Gibeonitas (quibus temporibus Io-sue, & ipse, & seniores interposito iuramento pacem promiserant) oppressisset. Non autem est dubitandum quin Saul scelus suum ita defenderit, ut vulgò putaretur iniuste fecisse. Deus ostendit pœnam hanc non ante auferendam, donec Gibeonitis, qui superuerant, fuisset satis factum. Dauid itaque interrogabat Gibeonitas quomodo possent placari. Illi postulabant Saulis filios sibi tradi: quod cum fieret, septem ex ipsis in crucem a-fixi [?] sunt, & ita fames cessauit.
units.tr: That God chastises men with dearth of food, along with other punishments, on account of perjury and the oppression of the poor, is shown by that notable history in 2 Sam., ch. 21. When famine raged for three years, David consulted the LORD as to what was the cause of so great an evil. He answered that it was famine, and that it was raging on account of Saul and his house, because he had oppressed the wretched Gibeonites, to whom Joshua and the elders, in former times, had promised peace under an oath. Nor is there any doubt that Saul defended his crime in such a way that it was commonly thought he had acted unjustly. God showed that this punishment would not be lifted until satisfaction had been made to the Gibeonites who had survived. David therefore asked the Gibeonites how they might be appeased. They demanded that the sons of Saul be handed over to them; when this was done, seven of them were hanged on a cross, and so the famine ceased.

units.la: Cur vero, dicis, filij vel nepotes, scelerís patrís sui vel avi pœnas luunt? Haud dubie, eum moribus suis referebant, ut vulgò dicitur, mali corvi, malum ouum.
units.tr: But why, you say, do sons or grandsons pay the penalties for the crimes of their father or grandfather? Undoubtedly because they followed their fathers' ways, as the common saying goes: a bad crow, a bad egg.

units.la: Insatiabilis quoque habendi cupido fame punitur. Nam Isaias capite quinto queri-tur, quòd in vinea Domini tantum omphaces provenerint, & inter alia dicit. Væ his qui copulant domum domui & agrum agro continuant, donec locus deficiat. Num vos soli habitabitis in terra? In auribus Domini exercituum (obtestor) si non domus multæ magnæ & pulchræ desolatæ erunt, ut nemo inhabibet. Porro vinearū decem iugera reddent Batum unum, & Homer sementis reddet Epha. Nam si malignus est proventus frugum, famem sequi necesse est. Ierem.34. cap.legimus: Regem & populum quasi conspiratione facta seruos & ancillas Israelitas, quasi iuxta legem manumittere debebant, manu misisse quidem, postea autem retraxisse in seruitutem. Idcirco Deus annonæ caritatem & famem eis comminatur. Pauperes & serui non inclementer tractadi sunt: semper enim cogitandum est illos Deum habere in cœlis. Dominus apud Michæam 6. capit.dicit. Sunt ne adhuc in domo thesauri impietate congregati, & modius deficiens, detestatus Domino? Nunquid iustificabo stateram impiam, & sacculum ponderum dolosorum? Cuius urbis diuites repleti sunt iniquitate, & inhabitatores eius loquuti sunt mendacium, & lingua ipsorum fraudulenta in ore ipsorum. Ego quoq; ægrotare faciam te, percutiendo te, desolabo te propter peccata tua. Tu comedes, & non saturaberis: tu se-minabis minabis & non metes: tu calcabis olivas: sed non unges te oleo, & mustum sed non bibes vinum.
units.tr: Insatiable greed for possessions is also punished by famine. For Isaiah, in chapter 5, complains that in the vineyard of the Lord only wild grapes have come forth, and among other things he says: "Woe to those who join house to house and add field to field, until there is no room left. Will you alone dwell in the land? In the ears of the LORD of hosts (I call him to witness), surely many houses, great and fair, shall be desolate, without inhabitant. Indeed, ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath, and a homer of seed shall yield an ephah." For if the yield of the crops is meagre, famine must follow. In Jeremiah, ch. 34, we read that the king and the people, by a kind of conspiracy, had to set free their Israelite menservants and maidservants, as the law required, and had indeed set them free, but afterwards took them back into bondage. Therefore God threatens them with dearth and famine. The poor and the servants must not be treated harshly, for one must always remember that they have God in heaven. The Lord says in Micah, ch. 6: "Are there still treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and a short measure that is accursed? Shall I acquit the man with false scales and a bag of deceitful weights? Its rich men are full of violence, its inhabitants speak lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth. Therefore I also will make you sick, striking you down, and I will lay you waste because of your sins. You shall eat, but not be satisfied; you shall sow, but not reap; you shall tread olives, but not anoint yourselves with oil; and you shall press the must, but not drink wine."

units.la: Superbiam puniri caritate annonae testis est hist. 2. Sam. 14. c. ubi scribitur Dauide ex mera superbia nummerasse legitur populum, & de populi multitudine gloriatū esse. Deus igitur optionem ei dedit inter famem, pestē, & hostilem insectationem. Nam uno horū flagellorum ipsum Dauidem castigare de-creuerat.
units.tr: That pride is punished by dearth is witnessed by the second history, 2 Sam., ch. 14, where it is written that David, out of sheer pride, numbered the people, and boasted of the multitude of the people. God therefore gave him a choice between famine, pestilence and hostile pursuit. For he had decided to chastise David himself with one of these scourges.

units.la: Deum Ebrietatem, & crapulam fame castigare, intelligitur ex Ioele propheta, qui in primo cap. iubet ebrios lugere: ingentē enim exercitum vēturum[?], qui omnes vites exscindat, ut deniceps vino caituri sint. Ac si dicat, vestra ebrietate prouocastis iram Dei, ut posthac aquae potu vos cōtētos esse oporteat. Quanquam in calidis illis regionibus sæpe ne aquam quidem salubrem habeant, quasi[?] sitim restinguant.
units.tr: God punishes drunkenness and gluttony with famine: this is clear from the prophet Joel, who in the first chapter bids drunkards weep, because a great army is coming that will strip all the vines, so that they will henceforth have to drink water. It is as if he were saying, "By your drunkenness you have provoked the anger of God, so that from now on you must be content with water to drink." Yet in those hot regions they often do not even have wholesome water, so as to quench their thirst.

units.la: Item si decimæ, & alia pensiones maligne persoluuntur, quibus Dei cultus conseruari debet, vel quibus pauperes alendi sunt Deus caritate annonae, homines punit. Nam apud Malachiam frugum copiam eis promittit, si haec debita bona fide persoluant.
units.tr: Likewise, when tithes and other dues are paid grudgingly, though they should maintain the worship of God or feed the poor, God punishes men with dearth. For through Malachi he promises them an abundance of fruits, if they pay these dues in good faith.

units.la: Si evoluamus veteres historias a Prophetarum temporibus ad nostra usq; tempora, inveniemus tantam aliquoties fuisse omnium rerum caritatem, ut multi fame extincti sint. Interea legimus omnia fuisse corruptissima, & principes, & subditos suum officium neglexisse.
