In Actis Apostolorum legitur sub Claudio Imperatore, magnam fuisse famem, cuius Suetonius & Dion quoque mentionem faciunt. Ob quas autem causas Deus tantam famem in mundo illis temporibus graßari passus sit, inde constat, quod Claudius Tiberius homo impius, ebrius, libidinosus, gulosus rerum potiebatur, quem per ludibrium milites Biberium dixere: qui ut Suetonius refert, ignotissimum quaesturae candidatum nobilissimis antepositus, ob epotam in conuiuio, propinante se, vini amphoram: nam honores, publica officia egregiis vini potoribus & gulosis mandabat. Plerumque autem fit, ut quales sint principes, tales etiam sint aulici, & subditi ipsorum. Mundus tali principe dignus. Apostoli hinc inde Euãgeliũ prædicabãt, quibus multi Iudæorum et Gentiũ cõtradicebant, quo minus eam amplecterentur. Quã ob causam Deus & fame & alijs calamitatibus eos afflixit. Eusebius scribit lib.9. Eccles.hist.7. & 8.ca. Imperante Maximino, qui crudeliter cõtra Christianos sæuiebat, tantam fuisse annonæ caritatem, vt etiam opulenti homines in plateis conciderint, inedia extincti sint, & à canibus dilacerati: Iustum hoc Dei fuit iu-dicium: nam non multo ante plurimos Chri-stianos bestijs lacerandos obiecerat. Hoc loco non est necesse sigillatim referre, quando, quoties & quas ob causas Deus hoc flagello mortales afflixerit. Exempla in proxima concione adducta sunt. Quid proximis elap-sis quadraginta annis factu sit, quantum re-rum prætia aucta sint, interim quæ flagitia grassata, necdum grassari desinant, nemo est qui nesciat. Habemus itaq; præcipuas causas, ob quas Deus omnibus seculis annonæ penuriam immisit.
units.tr: If we go through the ancient histories from the times of the prophets down to our own, we shall find that at various times there was such a scarcity of all things that many died of hunger. Meanwhile we read that everything had become thoroughly corrupt, and that both rulers and subjects had neglected their duty. In the Acts of the Apostles we read that under the emperor Claudius there was a great famine, which Suetonius and Dio also mention. The reasons why God allowed so great a famine to rage through the world in those times are clear enough: Claudius Tiberius, an impious, drunken, lustful and gluttonous man, held power. The soldiers mockingly called him Biberius (the Tippler). As Suetonius reports, he preferred a most obscure candidate for the quaestorship to the noblest men, because the candidate had drained a jar of wine at a banquet when he was toasted. He entrusted offices and public duties to outstanding wine-bibbers and gluttons. It usually happens that such as the rulers are, such also are their courtiers and subjects. The world is worthy of such a prince. The apostles everywhere preached the gospel, and many Jews and Gentiles opposed them, so that they would not embrace it. For this reason God afflicted them with famine and other calamities. Eusebius writes in the ninth book of his Ecclesiastical History, chapters 7 and 8, that under the emperor Maximinus, who raged cruelly against the Christians, there was such a scarcity of food that even wealthy men collapsed in the streets, died of starvation, and were torn apart by dogs. This was a just judgment of God, for not long before he had thrown very many Christians to be torn by wild beasts. It is not necessary here to recount one by one when, how often and for what causes God has struck mortals with this scourge; examples were given in the previous sermon. Everyone knows what happened in the forty years just past, how much the prices of goods have risen, and what crimes have been rife and have not yet ceased to be rife. We therefore have the chief causes for which God has sent scarcity of food in every age.

units.la: Si nunc nostros mores diligenter examinemus, inveniemus flagitia illa, quae Deus populo suo exprobrat, passim tam esse vulgaria, ut vix sperari possit, aliqua poenarum mitigatio. Morbus ita invaluit, ut remedij nulla fere spes nobis relinquatur. Deus bone quantus est contemptus verbi Divini? quam rari sunt qui conciones quotidianas audiunt? quam pauci admonitiones ex verbo Dei profetas, secum perpendunt? Deus exuscitat nos ostentis & portētis in cœlo & terra, quorum statim obliviscimur. Ante paucos annos cœlum ardere visum: Cometas, stellas crinitas, chasmata varia & huiusmodi portenta plurima non sine horrore conspeximus, vidimus eluviones aquarum, incredibiles grandines, insolitas procellas, terræmotus, & alia mi-randa: quotus quisq[?] his rebus commovetur? Sunt qui hæc omnia propter crebritatem securè contemnant, & aperte negent irati Dei signa esse, fausta esse omina dicant. Quot modis, quam frequenter quam temere divinum Dei nomen profanatur? ex levitate, & prava quadam consuetudine, multi frequenter edmodum venerandum Dei nomē quasi ornatus gratia quotidianis suis sermonibus inserunt, idq; nulla cogente etiam necessitate. Horrendæ execrationes, deierationes, impiæ deuotiones, quotidie audiuntur. At nemo exhorrescit, nemo est, qui peccantes ex præscripto legum officij admoneat, ut proniterram osculentur, hanc enim multam temere iurantibus maiores nostri irrogarunt: Iusiurandi parua est religio. Inuidia, odio & simultatibus omnes ordines laborant. Cædes quis horret? cum cæde, effusione sanguinis, militia mercenaria, multi maximū quæstum faciunt. Vagæ libidines, stupra, incestus & adulteria impune patrantur: risum non lachrimas mouent. Ethnicis prudentioribus hac in re profaniores sumus, qui huiusmodi scelera abominati sunt. Luxus vestiū, leuitatem, & molliciem animi prodit. Quotidie noua genera vestium inueniuntur. Gallicum, Hispanicum, Italicum vestitum, simiarum instar imitamur: Quorum etiam mores cum vestibus assumpsimus. Peccatur autem hîc non à iuuenibus tantum, sed etiam à profectioris ætatis hominibus, à senibus quos hæc leuitas omnino dedecet. An non ex-auro, argento, holoserico, & aliis prætiosis rebus contextis vestibus induuntur ij quos minime decet? Interim quot ege ni frigent, qui non habent, quibus induantur, & tegan-tur. Ebrietas, quam ante non paucos annos omnes detestati sunt, nunc omnes ordines, om-nes sexus infecit. De avaritia quid dicam? Illa passim nemini fere obstante, regnat, & cum radix sit omnium malorum, pessimos fru-ctus edit. Hinc enim tanquam ex fœtido son-te promanarunt, usurae, monopolia, variae & inaudita artes, (imposturas rectius dice-res) quas in mutandis, & corrumpendis mo-netis, in omnibus contractibus, in emendo & vendendo exercent. Veris & circumcisis Judaeis Christiani isti longe sunt deteriores & astutiores: vulgo quidem male audiunt, incircumcisi Judaei vocantur, & apud ma-gnates in honore sunt, & ad Reip. guberna-cula soli fere adhibetur. O tempora o mores. Ad vos qui talia patratis me conuerto, quid tandem vobis proderunt iniustæ hæ opes, quas aliorum magno cum damno corrasistis? Malè partis opibus non gaudet tertius hæ-res. Hæredibus ergo nil nisi peccandi mate-riam relinquetis. Considerate, quid Christo venienti ad iudicium responsuri sitis, qui dictorum, & factorum à vobis rationem exiget. Sed quid verbis opus? quod nam peccatum, quodnam flagitium est, quod non impunè hodie committatur? cuius neminem etiam pudeat? Si non in omnibus locis omnia patrantur, tamen in aliquibus, ita altè radices egerunt, ut vix spes reliqua sit alicuius emendationis.
units.tr: If we now examine our morals carefully, we shall find that those vices which God reproaches his people for are so widespread everywhere that scarcely any relief from punishment can be hoped for. The disease has so taken hold that almost no hope of a remedy is left to us. Good God, how great is the contempt of the Word of God! How rare are those who hear the daily sermons! How few ponder with themselves the admonitions drawn from the Word of God! God rouses us with portents and wonders in heaven and on earth, and we forget them at once. A few years ago the sky was seen to burn; we have seen comets, bearded stars, various gaping apparitions and very many portents of this kind, not without horror; we have seen floods of waters, incredible hailstorms, unusual gales, earthquakes and other marvels. How few are moved by these things! There are those who, because of their frequency, scornfully disregard all these signs and openly deny that they are signs of God's wrath, calling them lucky omens. In how many ways, how often and how rashly is the divine name of God profaned! Out of levity and a depraved habit, many people very often insert the most venerable name of God into their everyday speech, as if for ornament, and this without any compelling necessity. Dreadful curses, oaths and impious imprecations are heard daily. Yet no one shudders; there is no one who, according to the prescribed law of his office, reminds the offenders to kiss the ground prone, for our ancestors imposed this fine on those who swore rashly. The sanctity of an oath has become slight. Envy, hatred and enmities trouble all ranks. Who shudders at murder? Many make the greatest profit from slaughter, bloodshed and mercenary soldiering. Wandering lusts, debaucheries, incest and adulteries are committed with impunity; they stir up laughter, not tears. In this respect we are more profane than the more prudent heathens, who abhorred such crimes. The luxury of clothing betrays levity and softness of mind. Every day new fashions of clothing are invented; we ape the French, Spanish and Italian dress, like monkeys, and along with their clothes we have taken on their manners. And this sin is committed not only by the young but also by men of more mature age, by old men whom such frivolity utterly disgraces. Are not those clothed in gold, silver, pure silk and other precious fabrics who least deserve them? Meanwhile, how many needy people are cold, who do not have clothes with which to be dressed and covered! Drunkenness, which not many years ago everyone detested, now infects all ranks and all sexes. What shall I say of avarice? It reigns everywhere, with almost no one opposing it, and since it is the root of all evils, it bears the worst fruits. From it, as from a fetid source, have sprung usury, monopolies, and various unheard-of arts (or rather trickeries), which they practise in debasing and corrupting coinage, and in all contracts, in buying and selling. Compared with the true circumcised Jews, these Christians are far worse and more crafty. Among the common people they indeed have a bad reputation; Jews are called uncircumcised, yet among the great they are held in honour, and they are almost the only ones admitted to the helm of the commonwealth. O the times! O the manners! To you who commit such things I turn: what will these unjust riches, which you have scraped together to the great loss of others, ultimately profit you? "Ill-gotten wealth does not please the third heir." You will therefore leave your heirs nothing but matter for sin. Consider what you will answer when Christ comes to judgment, who will demand an account of your words and deeds. But why need words? What sin, what crime is there that is not committed today with impunity? What is there that no one is even ashamed of? If everything is not committed in every place, yet in some places the roots have struck so deep that scarcely any hope of amendment remains.

units.la: Quin adeo corruptum est iudicium mundi, ut iam vitia virtutum nominibus ornen-tur: fœnerator frugalis, ebrius hilaris, prodi-gus liberalis dicitur. An ne putas hæc semper impunita fore? Nequaquam. Aliàs Prophetarum oracula, imo Dei ipsius commina-tiones, vanæ essent. Quod cogitare quidem, nedum dicere Christiano homini nefas est. Sed age omnes ordines hominum examine-mus, vel obiter tantum: hic miram videbis corruptionem, & fateberis nos hac & longe quidem graviore pæna dignos esse. Nō ergo iniustitiæ accusandum esse Deum.
units.tr: Indeed, the judgment of the world is so corrupted that now vices are adorned with the names of virtues: a usurer is called thrifty, a drunkard cheerful, a spendthrift generous. Do you think these things will always go unpunished? By no means. Otherwise the oracles of the prophets, indeed God's own threats, would be empty. To think this, let alone to say it, is wicked for a Christian. But come, let us examine all the ranks of men, even if only in passing: here you will see a remarkable corruption, and you will confess that we deserve punishment, and a far heavier one. Therefore God is not to be accused of injustice.

units.la: Multi ministrorum negligenter officio suo fungūtur, adhæc vitæ sunt dissolutæ, ebrieta ti, ambitioni aut auaritiæ dediti sunt. Multi ex magistratu aspirant quidem ad altiores gradus, interim bonas leges non tuentur, priuato potius quam publico commodo student, non coereent scelera, tanta seueritate, quanta debebant: multa in opulētiorum gratiam, contra ius & fas, dicunt & faciunt, volunt hac ratione inuidiam declinare. Coniuges mutua inter se exercent odia, & simultates, perpetuis rixis, pugnis certant, liberos male educunt, illos nec castigant, nec ab alijs eos castigari volunt, malo exemplo corrumpunt, scurriliter in illorum præsentia loquūtur: non tantum authoritatem ministrorum verbi Dei extenuāt, sed & ipsum verbū Dei proterue contemnunt, his auditis liberi pertinatiores redduntur, nec Deum timent, nec verbum Dei audiunt, nec castigationes ferunt, nec parentes colunt, & obseruant, cur illos colerent, cum nec Deum colant? quod parentum culpa factum est. Vsitata querela est, pueros indies deteriores fieri, sed hoc fit vitio parentum, & senum, qui cū iuniores ad virtutem & pietatem hortari deberent, eos ad scelera pelliciunt. Ludi & artium magistri officium suum negligenter faciunt. Ut multa paucis complectar omnes sexus, aetates, & ordines hominum corrupti & depravati sunt, nec reformationis spes est.
units.tr: Many ministers perform their office carelessly; moreover, they live dissolute lives and are given to drunkenness, ambition or avarice. Many of the magistrates aspire indeed to higher positions, yet they do not uphold good laws; they pursue private advantage rather than the public good; they do not restrain crimes with the severity they ought; they say and do many things against right and law for the favour of the wealthier, wishing by this means to avoid unpopularity. Spouses exercise mutual hatreds and enmities between themselves, they contend with constant quarrels and blows; they bring up their children badly, neither punishing them nor wanting them punished by others; they corrupt them with bad example and speak coarsely in their presence; they not only diminish the authority of the ministers of the Word of God, but also shamelessly despise the Word of God itself. Children, having heard these things, become more obstinate: they fear neither God nor the Word of God, they heed no correction, they do not honour and obey their parents. Why should they honour them when they do not honour God? This is the fault of the parents. It is a common complaint that children grow worse every day, but this happens through the fault of parents and elders, who, when they ought to exhort the young to virtue and piety, entice them to crimes. Schoolmasters and masters of the arts carelessly perform their duty. To sum up many things in a few words: men of every sex, age and rank are corrupted and depraved, and there is no hope of reformation.

units.la: Ne mireris ergo, cur Deus tam diuturna fame nos exerceat, graviora meriti sumus.
units.tr: So do not wonder why God afflicts us with such a long famine; we have deserved worse.

units.la: Si vero caritas annonae, et fames, (obijcis,) est poena peccati, cur ab hac poena pij ac fideles non sunt immunes? Certum enim est omnibus temporibus multos pios & bonos viros famem pertulisse, ut nihil jam dicam de Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo quos hinc inde migrare fames compulit, de quibus proxima concione plura diximus. Nonne diuturna illa fame, qua Deus Israelitas Achabi tempore afflixit, multi quoque pij viri afflicti sunt? Ipse enim Deus Heliae affirmat 7000. adhuc viros superesse qui genua Baali non flexerint, hoc est, qui externis gestibus nullum ei honorem detulerint. Abscondit Abdias prophetas in speluncis, quos ex aula regis aluit. De Paulo extat 1+ Cor. 11. quod famem & sitim pertulerit. Aliquot ex sanctis martyribus, etiam nostris temporibus, fame à tyrannis necatisunt. Author Epistolae ad Hebraeos dicit, multos ex fide in solitarijs locis,in speluncis, vallibus, montibus, vitam traduxisse: vbi procul dubio cum fame conflictati sunt. Respondemus ad hæc: Etiam fideles esse peccatores:corrupta enim natura in sepulchrum vsq; eos commitatur. Etsi non prolabantur in magna scelera,quod etiam interdum fit,tamen sunt socordes,non assidue audiunt sacras conciones, vt deberent,non resistunt malo vt possent,neminem enim volunt offendere, bona non promouent tanto studio,quanto deberent. Itaque mirã-dum non est, Deum publicis calamitatibus eos vexare. Etenim si Deus summo cum ip-sis iure agere vellet, æternæ condemnationi essent obnoxij.
units.tr: But if dearth and famine (you object) are a punishment for sin, why are the godly and faithful not exempt from this punishment? It is certain that in every age many pious and good people have endured famine, not to mention Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, whom famine drove hither and thither, and of whom we spoke at length in the last sermon. Were not many godly men also afflicted in that long famine with which God struck the Israelites in the time of Ahab? God himself assures Elijah that 7,000 men remained who had not bowed the knee to Baal, that is, who had paid him no honour by outward gestures. Obadiah hid the prophets in caves and fed them from the king's court. Concerning Paul we read in 1 Cor. 11 that he suffered hunger and thirst. Some of the holy martyrs, even in our own times, have been put to death by tyrants through hunger. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews says that many lived by faith in desert places, in caves, valleys and mountains, where without doubt they struggled with hunger. We reply to this: the faithful too are sinners, for corrupt nature accompanies them to the grave. Even if they do not fall into great crimes, which sometimes happens, yet they are slack, they do not hear sacred sermons as often as they ought, they do not resist evil as they could, for they are unwilling to offend anyone, and they do not advance good works with the zeal they should. So it is no wonder that God afflicts them with public calamities. Indeed, if God wished to deal with them by strict right, they would be liable to eternal condemnation.

units.la: Hæc nondum,inquis, mihi satis faciunt, nam si annonæ penuria & fame idololatria & scelera castigantur: his pœnis in primis obnoxij esse debebant, qui reliquis sunt peiores & sceleratiores. Etsi pij suos nœuos ha-beant, tamen dolet eis, vellent, se illos posse excutere, infideles vero nihil solliciti sunt de emendatione vitæ, non satis est ipsis, quod ipsi Deum quotidie offendunt, vellent alios quoq; peccare, nihilq; ferunt indignius, quam si vel ipsi nefaria patrare non possint, aut alios ad ea non incitare. Non tamen plus affliguntur fame, quam ipsi fideles, imò tem-pore famis, suas habent artes quibus non so-lum famem effugiunt, sed magnas opes colli-gunt, & pijs hominibus oneri sunt. Pij mal-lent fame perire, quàm artibus illis, quibus impij vtuntur, vitæ necessaria comparare: non tamen potior est piorum, quam impio-rum hac in parte conditio. Hæc tentatio, o-mnibus seculis homines valde turbauit. Mul-ti hinc collegerunt, Deum non curare res hu-manas: perinde ei esse, siue hoc, siue illud fa-ciamus. Malach.3. & 4. scribit multos in has impias voces erupisse, recte vel perperā agere, perinde esse. Si quis iniuste agit, non punitur, si quis iuste, non afficitur præmio. Sciendum est hoc loco, maximum esse discrimen[?] pij & impij in simili paena: item, Deum non solum ad puniendum peccata hominum (quanquam peccata princeps causa sunt omnium malorum) sed alias atque alias etiam ob causas, famem, bellum, pestem, & alias afflictiones hominibus immittere. Duo illi latrones, quorum unus ad dextram, alter ad sinistram Christi filij Dei in cruce pendebant, eodem supplicij genere affecti sunt: attamen magna inter ipsos est disparitas, ille patienter ferebat omnia, & Jesum Messiam esse confitebatur: hic impatienter ferebat dolores, & contumelia ipsum afficiebat. Deus multas habet causas, ob quas suis plures interdum afflictiones immittit, quàm aliis. Ex multis paucas ad nostram consolationem colligemus.
units.tr: "These arguments," you say, "still do not satisfy me. For if scarcity of food and famine punish idolatry and crimes, then those who are worse and more wicked than the rest ought above all to be liable to these punishments. Although the godly have their blemishes, they grieve over them and wish they could shake them off; but the unbelievers are not at all anxious about amending their lives. It is not enough for them that they offend God every day; they want others to sin too, and they can bear nothing more indignantly than being unable to commit wickedness themselves or to incite others to it. Yet they are not more afflicted by famine than the faithful themselves; indeed, in time of famine they have their own arts by which they not only escape hunger but gather great wealth, and they are a burden to pious people. The pious would rather perish by hunger than obtain the necessities of life by those arts which the impious use. Still, the condition of the godly is no better than that of the impious in this respect." This temptation has greatly troubled men in every age. Many have concluded from it that God does not care for human affairs, and that it makes no difference whether we do this or that. Malachi 3 and 4 writes that many have burst out into these impious words: to act rightly or wrongly is all the same; if anyone acts unjustly he is not punished, and if anyone acts justly he gains no reward. We must note here that there is the greatest difference between the godly and the impious under a similar punishment; also that God sends famine, war, pestilence and other afflictions upon men not only to punish sins (although sins are the chief cause of all evils), but also for other and various reasons. The two robbers, one hanging at Christ's right hand and the other at his left, the Son of God, were subjected to the same kind of punishment, yet between them there was a great difference: the one bore everything patiently and confessed that Jesus was the Messiah; the other bore his pains impatiently and reviled him. God has many causes for which he sometimes sends more afflictions upon his own than upon others. Of the many, we shall gather a few for our consolation.

units.la: Primum Deus nos fame & aliis aerumnis ad agnitionem peccatorum veramq; poenitentiam incitat. Etenim quum pij à Deo aliquibus aerumnis affliguntur, statim causas inquirunt. Quum David videret caritatem annonae non cessare, consulebat Dominum, cur ita populo suo irasceretur? Mox audiebat (ut supra diximus) propter Gabaonitas id accidere. Fideles aliquando incidunt in varios errores & scelera, nec pos-sunt verbo Dei in via revocari, donec Deus afflictionibus aliquibus eos emolliat. Ex 2. Amos Prophetæ audivimus, Deum dicere, quòd tametsi populum cibi inopia & potionis afflixerit, nondum tamen ad ipsum reversus sit, idq; [?] repetit. Unde colligimus, Deum famem ideo terris immittere, ut homines ad ipsum convertantur. Quemadmodum equos si incitato cursu feruntur, aut à via exorbi-tent, fræno retrahimus, ita Deus nos fame alijsq; [?] ærumnis in viam retrahit. Si puer aliquis fugam meditetur, aut jussus scholam frequentare nolit, mittuntur nuntij, qui eum de via retrahant: ita Deus suos habet nuntios, famem, morbos, qui nos ad Patrem nostrum & Præceptorem reducant.
units.tr: First, God, by famine and other troubles, stirs us up to the recognition of our sins and to true repentance. For when the godly are afflicted by God with some troubles, they at once inquire into the causes. When David saw that the dearth of food did not cease, he consulted the Lord as to why he was so angry with his people; and straightway he heard (as we said above) that this came about on account of the Gibeonites. Believers sometimes fall into various errors and sins, and cannot be called back to the way by the Word of God until God softens them by some afflictions. We have heard from the second chapter of the prophet Amos that God says that although he afflicted the people with lack of food and drink, they had still not returned to him; and he repeats this. From this we gather that God sends famine upon the earth so that men may be converted to him. As we draw in horses that are carried away in a headlong course, or that stray from the road, by the bridle, so God draws us back into the way by famine and other troubles. If a boy plans to run away, or refuses to attend school when ordered, messengers are sent who bring him back from his path; so God has his messengers, famine and sickness, which lead us back to our Father and our Teacher.

units.la: Deinde Deus fame & alijs afflictioni-bus probat & examinat fidem nostram erga ipsum, & charitate erga proximos nostros, item patientiam nostram. Sæpenumero putamus nos præclara fide præditos esse, sin verò multa aduersa nobis obtingant, tune ex-perimur, quàm sit necessarium, ut cum Apos-tolis clamemus: Domine adauge nobis fidē.
units.tr: Second, God, by famine and other afflictions, tests and examines our faith towards himself, our love towards our neighbours, and likewise our patience. Very often we think we are endowed with excellent faith, but when many adversities befall us, then we learn how necessary it is to cry out with the apostles: "Lord, increase our faith."

units.la: Petrus ibat super lacum, iubente Christo, cæterùm quum sentiret ventum validum, ex-territus cæpit demergi, ut Domini manu apprehensus confirmandus esset, Matth.14. cap. Deus experiri vult quo pacto nos geramus erga proximos nostros, expectando solutionem debitorum, dando mutuum, donando, & alijs in rebus. Experiri vult, quàm patienter crucem feramus. Multa nobis pollicemur de patientia nostra, si res aduersa nobis obtingant, sed quum ingruunt, sumus im-patientes, & tum demum rectè intelligimus, quàm simus imbecilles. Miles qui aciem nunquam vidit, multa sibi promittit de sua for-titudine, sed si videat instructum armis ex-ercitum, si audiat bombardarum tonitrua, expauescit & trepidat. Deus quidem nouit nostram infirmitatem priusquam crucem imponat, tamē ne confidentiores simus, vult ut nos ipsi alijque nostram cognoscant imbe-cillitatem. Multi confidenter satis dicunt, fame potius mori vellem, quam furtum aut latrocinium cōmittere. Sed quid fames pos-sit nondum experti sunt, tandem autem vident ac sentiunt cum Iuspirijs[?], quanta sit nostra infirmitas, quid non tentaremus, ni po-tenti sua manu nos Deus retraheret.
units.tr: Peter walked upon the lake at Christ's command, but when he felt the strong wind, terrified, he began to sink, so that, grasped by the Lord's hand, he might be strengthened (Matth. 14). God wishes to test how we behave towards our neighbours, in waiting for debts to be paid, in lending, in giving, and in other matters. He wishes to test how patiently we bear the cross. We promise much about our patience if adverse things befall us, but when they press upon us we are impatient, and only then do we rightly understand how weak we are. A soldier who has never seen battle promises himself much about his own courage, but if he sees an army drawn up in arms and hears the thunder of the cannons, he is terrified and trembles. God indeed knows our weakness before he lays the cross upon us; yet, so that we may not be overconfident, he wills that we and others should come to know our weakness. Many say quite confidently, "I would rather die of hunger than commit theft or robbery." But they have not yet experienced what famine can do, and at last they see and feel, with the Iuspirij, how great our weakness is, and what we would not attempt, unless God drew us back with his mighty hand.

units.la: Præterea his afflictionibus futura mala præuenire quodammodo vult, hoc est pro-hibere ne in graviora scelera ruamus: Veluti peritus medicus ægroto dat προφυλακτικά[?] pharmaca, ne in morbum incidat, ad quem procliuem esse sentit: ita Deus scit quomodo nos affecti simus. Infligit itaq; nobis varias afflictiones, ne in scelera ruamus, sed cogite-mus, hæc vel illa, malè tibi cesserunt, caue itaque tibi: multis peccatis iam ante Deum offendisti, quibus si hoc accedat, grauius te ca-stigabit. Germani prouerbio dicunt, pueros ustos igne expauescere: ita si quis in magnis fuit malis, cauet ne suo vitio in maiora in-cidat. Quomodo nos in affluentia annonæ gera-mus, non opus est quod multis annotemus.
units.tr: Moreover, by these afflictions God wishes in some measure to forestall future evils, that is, to prevent us from falling into greater sins. As a skilful physician gives prophylactic [προφυλακτικά] medicines to a patient, so that he does not fall into the disease to which he feels him inclined, so God knows how we are disposed. Therefore he inflicts upon us various afflictions, lest we fall into sin; and we should consider: "This or that has turned out badly for you; take care, then. You have already offended God by many sins, and if this is added to them he will chastise you more severely." The Germans say in a proverb that children burnt by fire are afraid of it; so if anyone has been in great trouble, he takes care lest by his own fault he fall into greater ones. How we behave in the abundance of food there is no need to note at length.

units.la: Est & alia causa ob quam Deus fame & alijs malis suos exercet, nempe ut ardentius orent. Experimur enim nostro exem-plo, nos si nullis exerceamur malis, remissio-res esse in precibus, si abundantiam victus habeamus plærunque proteruiores euadere. Prospera fortuna non possumus recte uti. Sin fame alijsq; malis exercemur, ardenter precibus instamus. Necessitas enim nobis quodammodo serias preces extorquet. Si quis abundat cibo & potu, non tam diligen-ter gratias agit Deo pro eius beneficijs, quàm ardenter esuriens abipso petit, ut iterum ei necessaria ad victum suppeditare velit: pro alijs quoque orat, quos fame scit la-borare: postea si Dominus eum liberet, serio & ardenter gratias agit, precaturq; ut à se & alijs famem depellat: deniq; esurientibus & famelicis compati nouit.
units.tr: There is also another cause for which God exercises his people with famine and other evils, namely, that they may pray more fervently. For we experience in our own case that if we are exercised by no troubles, we are more lax in prayer, and if we have an abundance of food we generally become more wanton. We cannot use prosperous fortune rightly. But when we are exercised by famine and other evils, we press on in prayer with fervour, for necessity in some measure wrings earnest prayers from us. If someone has plenty of food and drink, he does not give thanks to God for his benefits so diligently as he who, hungry, earnestly asks of him that he would again be willing to supply what is necessary for his sustenance; he also prays for others whom he knows to be suffering from hunger; afterwards, if the Lord delivers him, he gives thanks seriously and fervently, and prays that God would drive away famine from himself and from others; and finally he knows how to feel compassion for the hungry and the famished.

units.la: Adhoc quoq; fames & aliæ afliones conferunt, quod humiliamur sub potenti manu Dei. Nostra caro insolescit & imitatur Sa-thyrionis pelles, quas negant in fundo arcæ vestibus refertæ, quiescere, sed sursum niti: ita nos sumus elato animo, neque satis nos ipsos cognoscimus. Quare Deus rebus ad-nersis versis domat nostram carnem, & cristas contundit. Docet nos quibus indigeamus, & quam necessaria nobis sit gratia ipsius. Vniuersum genus hominum si omnes suas vires coniungeret, & artes adhiberet, non possent vel culmum producere, vel vuam[?] creare, interim tam insolenter se gerunt, ac si non omnia ex liberalitate Dei acciperent. Deo subtrahente manu, res nostrae non aliter habent, quàm liberorum, quos primum incedere, aut illorum quos natare docemus, quum primum manum ab eis retrahimus, illi concidunt in terram, hi verò in fundum mergun-tur. Hæc tamen ante non expendimus quam Deus cruce nos exerceat.
units.tr: Moreover, famine and other afflictions also serve to humble us under the mighty hand of God. Our flesh grows proud and imitates the skins of the sathyrion, which, when laid at the bottom of a chest full of clothes, will not lie still but strain upward. So we are high-minded and do not know ourselves well enough. Therefore God, by adverse circumstances, tames our flesh and breaks its pride. He teaches us what we lack and how necessary his grace is to us. If the whole human race joined all its strength and applied all its skill, it could not make a single stalk grow or create a grape, yet people behave so insolently, as if they did not receive everything from God's generosity. When God withdraws his hand, our affairs are no different from those of children whom we teach to walk or to swim: as soon as we take our hand away, the first fall to the ground and the second sink to the bottom. Yet we do not weigh these things until God exercises us with the cross.

units.la: Præterea Deus fame aliisq; his ærumnis in suis fidelibus futuræ vitæ desiderium accendit & contemptum huius ærumnosæ vi-ta docet, ut tandem ad meliorem aspirent. Nam si ex animi nostri sententia omnia succederent, nemo hinc migrare & mundum deserere vellet, de altera & meliori vita parum solliciti essemus. Nam in tot malis miserijs & calamitatibus quibus expositi sumus in tanta malitia, inuidia & insidijs ho-minum, quas quotidie experimur, tamē praesentis vitae desiderio tenemur eamq; maximi facimus, quid quaso ergo facturi essemus, si hic nihil aduersi nobis accideret? Speramus quotidie res nostras meliori loco futuras, at vana spe fruimur. Experientia docet eas quotidie fieri deteriores. Qui ergo vitae lon-gaevitatem, spe melioris conditionis optant, perinde sentiunt ac qui vestes longo vsu me-liores fore opinantur. Vita nostra nil nisi mi-seriarum[?] vallis est, vt vulgari prouerbio dicitur, Caelebs si viuas, de te tantum sollici-tus es, Vxorem si duxeris, duplex iam tibi cura imminet: si tuis moribus non est apta, miserrima hæc est vita, si infæliciter pareat, augentur curae, Cognatos si habeat, eosque diuites, non affines sed dominos habebis. Si pauperes, hic tibi necesse est vt illarum quoq; inopiae subuenias, si numerus liberorum au-geatur, augentur & curae ac labores, & quo sunt adultiores, eo plura tibi illorum nomine ferenda sunt. Quod si tu & illi rebus neces-sarijs destituantur, iam te tandem serio vi-tæ huius tæ huius tædet pigetque, at futuræ vitæ de-siderium in te accenditur, in qua cibo & potu non indigemus: sed miserijs & molestijs omnibus exantlati, angelis similes erimus: In his ergo angustijs hanc tecum rationem inire soles, Moriendum tibi tandem est[?], quo citius eò melius, ita tandem liberaberis multis miserijs. Vltimo loco fideles suos quos fame alijsq; ærumnis exercet, patientiæ exemplum omnibus alijs proponit. Pij cum illorum patientiam constantiam & fidem cernunt, hinc quoque consolationem petunt, & spem auxilij diuini accipiunt: hanc enim rationem ineunt: Deus illis adfuit spiritu suo sancto, vt omnia patienter ferre potuerint, igitur tibi quoq; aderit vt famem & durissima quæq; patientia vincas. Rursum si pios ac probos abiecto & pusilli esse animo videt, inde naturæ nostræ imbecillitatem melius cognoscunt. Impij ex piorum afflictionibus colligere debent, quid de ipsis futurum sit, si Deus ita filios suos castiget. Si hæc in viridi ligno fiunt, quid fiet in arido? Omnes deniq; ex piorum fame & egestate vehementer iram Dei contra peccata hominum colligere & obseruare debent: cum tanta seueritate in electis suis, corruptam naturam, & minora etiam peccata puniat, quid de illis fiet? Hæ ferè sunt causæ, ob quas Deus pios homines fame, priuatis publicisq; calamitatibus inuoluat & exerceat. Sed hæc de finalibus causis annnotasse sufficiant. Orandus Deus ut in hac cruce veram patientiam largiatur. Illi debetur benedictio, gloria & potestas in æ-ternum. Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, through famine and other such hardships God kindles in his faithful a desire for the future life and teaches them to despise this troubled life, so that at last they may aspire to a better one. For if everything turned out according to our wishes, no one would want to leave here and depart from the world, and we would be little concerned about another and better life. Amid so many evils, miseries and calamities to which we are exposed, and the great malice, envy and snares of men which we experience every day, we are still held by love of the present life and value it highly. What, I ask, would we then do if nothing adverse happened to us here? We hope every day that our affairs will be in a better state, but we enjoy an empty hope. Experience teaches that they grow worse every day. Those who wish for a long life in hope of a better condition think just like those who suppose that clothes will get better with long use. Our life is nothing but a valley of miseries, as the common proverb says: "If you live single, you are anxious only about yourself; if you take a wife, a double care now hangs over you; if she is not suited to your character, this is a most wretched life; if she bears children unhappily, your cares increase; if she has relatives, and they are rich, you will have them not as kin but as masters; if they are poor, you must also relieve their want; if the number of children grows, cares and labours increase, and the older they grow, the more you must bear on their account." But if you and they are deprived of necessities, then at last you seriously grow weary of this life and are disgusted with it, and a desire for the future life is kindled in you, where we shall have no need of food and drink, but, having endured all miseries and troubles, shall be like angels. In these straits you are wont to make this reckoning with yourself: you must die at last, and the sooner the better; so at last you will be freed from many miseries. Lastly, God sets before all others, as an example of patience, the faithful whom he exercises with famine and other hardships. When the pious see their patience, constancy and faith, they also take comfort from this and receive hope of divine help, for they reason thus: God was present with them by his Holy Spirit so that they could bear everything patiently; therefore he will also be present with you, so that you may overcome famine and all the harshest trials by patience. Again, when the pious and upright are seen to be cast down and of fainthearted spirit, from this they better recognize the weakness of our nature. The impious ought to gather from the afflictions of the pious what will become of themselves if God chastises his sons in this way. If these things are done in the green wood, what will be done in the dry? Finally, everyone ought to gather from the famine and want of the pious how great is God's anger against the sins of men: since he punishes with such severity even the lesser sins of corrupt nature in his elect, what will become of others? These are almost the causes for which God involves and exercises pious men with famine and private and public calamities. But it is enough to have noted these things concerning the final causes. God is to be prayed to, that he may grant true patience in this cross. To him be blessing, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO III.
units.tr: CONCIO III.

units.la: QVO PACTO TAM DIVITES quàm pauperes se famis tem-pores gerere debeant.
units.tr: IN WHAT MANNER BOTH THE RICH AND THE POOR OUGHT TO CONDUCT THEMSELVES IN TIMES OF FAMINE.

units.la: UT peritus medicus primo causas & grauitatem morbi ægro osten-dit, dein quid ei facto opus sit præscribit, & medicinam adhibet: Eadem in cõmuni hoc quasi morbo, publica scilicet re-rum omnium penuria & fame, spirituali me dico obseruanda sunt. Nimirum homines inducat, ut sentiant grauitatem calamita- tis, & Deum authore esse agnoscant, Deum enim peccatis suis commouisse, ut hac grauì pœna eos coerceat, denique officij sui omnes ex æquo admoneat: hoc est, doceat, quo pa- sto se in omnibus afflictionibus, siue priuatæ illæ sint, siue publicæ gerere debeant. Hæc methodus in hac de fame tractatione à nobis hactenus obseruata est. Prima concione pro bauimus Deum authorem esse, copiæ & ino- piæ, dein exemplis grauitatem huius pœnæ demonstrauimus: Altera concione diximus, peccata nostra causam esse mouentem: nos peccatis nostris hanc pœnam commeruisse. Præterea causas finales indicauimus. Nunc quarto loco dicendum, quomodo nos in tanta penuria & fame tam erga Deum, quàm er- ga proximum gerere debeamus: Et ut ordi- ne procedamus, primo audiemus, quod nam Ecclesiæ Christianæ in hac calamitate ossi- cium sit. Dein quid Magistratui, Conciona- toribus, Patribus familiâs, diuitibus & ege- nis omnibus & singulis faciendum sit.
units.tr: As a skilled physician first shows the sick man the causes and seriousness of his disease, then prescribes what must be done and applies the remedy, so in this common sickness, namely the general scarcity of all things and famine, spiritual remedies must be observed. That is, he must lead people to feel the seriousness of the calamity and to acknowledge that God is its author, since God has been moved by their sins to restrain them with this heavy punishment; and finally he must admonish all equally of their duty, that is, teach them how they ought to conduct themselves in all afflictions, whether private or public. This method has so far been observed by us in this treatment of famine. In the first sermon we proved that God is the author both of plenty and of scarcity, and then by examples we showed the seriousness of this punishment. In the second sermon we said that our sins are the moving cause, and that we have deserved this punishment by our sins. Besides, we have indicated the final causes. Now, fourthly, we must say how we ought to behave, in such great scarcity and famine, both towards God and towards our neighbour. And to proceed in order, first we shall hear what the duty of the Christian Church is in this calamity. Then what must be done by the magistrate, the preachers, the heads of households, the rich and all and each of the poor.

units.la: Ante omnia autem pij & fideles ne de-sperent, quasi Deus ita peccatis ipsorum of-sensus, vt nullus sit auxilij & misericordiae locus reliquus.
units.tr: Above all, let the pious and faithful not despair, as if God were so offended by their sins that no place for help and mercy remained.

units.la: Solomon in hac sua precatione inter cae-teras fideles admonet, vt tempore famis peccata sua quibus iram Dei provocarint agnoscant deplorent, emendent, seriam poeniten-tiam agant. Deut.30.dicitur: Si cōuersi fue-ritis, &c. Nec satis est cessare a malo, sed & bonum est faciendum. His enim malis Deus ad viam pietatis nos revocat. Sed a re-bus etiam licitis in tanta publica calamita-te abstinere debemus. Ioel.2. 1.Cor.7.cap.
units.tr: In this prayer of his, Solomon admonishes the faithful, among other things, that in time of famine they should acknowledge and lament the sins by which they have provoked the anger of God, amend them, and do earnest repentance. It is said in Deut. 30: "If you shall be converted," etc. Nor is it enough to cease from evil, but good must also be done. For by these evils God calls us back to the way of godliness. But in so great a public calamity we ought to abstain even from things that are lawful. Joel 2; 1 Cor. 7.

units.la: Dein iubet nos confiteri nomen Domini, hoc est, cognoscere peccatum & iudicium Dei. Quod nos punit, iustitia eius requirit, bonitati vero eius ascribendum, quod nos non penitus euertit. Etenim si secundum me-rita nos tractaret, non temporarijs tantùm, sed & æternis afficeret pœnis. Non ergo illum iniusticiæ, sed nos ipsos accusare: laudare vero debemus, & prædicare eius iusti-tiam & misericordiam. Sunt qui omnium malorum malorum causas, non in sua peccata, sed in usurarios, sagas, multi etiam in nouam religionem coniciant, illis dira imprecantur. Nos factis digna patimur.
units.tr: Then he bids us confess the name of the Lord, that is, to acknowledge our sin and the judgement of God. That he punishes us, his justice requires; that he has not utterly destroyed us must be ascribed to his goodness. For if he dealt with us according to our deserts, he would punish us not only with temporal but also with eternal punishments. Therefore we must accuse not his injustice but ourselves; rather we ought to praise and proclaim his justice and mercy. There are some who ascribe the causes of all evils not to their own sins but to usurers, witches, and many even to the new religion, and they call down dreadful curses upon them. We suffer what our deeds deserve.

units.la: Præterea nos Deum per Christum orare iubet, nimirum ut graues tempestates auer-tat. Templum Solomonis typus quodammodo Christi eiusque Ecclesiæ fuit. Cum ergo petit ut fideles in hoc templo orantes exaudire velit, perinde dictum est, ac si petat, universam Ecclesiam, per Christum Iesum ad Deum Patrem clamantem, exaudire dignetur.
units.tr: Besides, he bids us pray to God through Christ, namely that he may turn away the heavy storms. The temple of Solomon was in some sense a type of Christ and of his Church. Therefore, when he asks that he would be willing to hear the faithful praying in this temple, it is said just as if he asked that he would deign to hear the whole Church crying out to God the Father through Jesus Christ.

units.la: Deum autem solum invocandum hinc constant, quod Solomon in hac sua oratione inter cætera dicit: Illum solum corda hominum cognoscere. Frustra ergo invocamus illos, qui corda nostra non intuentur. Preces ferè omnes in corde fiunt. Raro expressis verbis oramus: Sæpe autem tam sumus per-turbati, ut conceptis verbis orare non possimus. In primis cum nobis hinc migrandum est, vox nos deficit. Frustra ergo preces funduntur ad illos, qui nos non audiunt, qui non intelligunt nec sciunt, quae nobis sint neces-saria, quique nec bona conferre nec mala avertere possunt. Paulus dicit Rom.10. Il-lum invocandum, in quem credimus, in solum autem Deum credimus. Is ergo solus est invocandus. Dein nec praeceptum, nec exempla invocationis Sanctorum, nec etiam pro-missiones habemus. Quod ex Ezechiele ad-ducunt, elumbe plane est, ut postea dicetur. Pontificij ad Litanias tanquam ad sacram anchoram in his calamitatibus confugiunt: Sed merum est humanum inventum. Gregorius Magnus maiorem ut vocant, ante festum Marci instituit, circa annum 590. Triduanas vero processiones ante festum ascensionis Claudianus Mamertus Viennensis Episcopus invenit: Sed cum verbo Dei pugnant, in his enim Angeli, Patriar-chae, Martyres, Confessores, Virgines, viduae invocantur & obtestantur, ut pericula & calamitates omnes avertant: quae tamen solus Deus avertere potest.
units.tr: That God alone is to be invoked follows from what Solomon says in this prayer, among other things: that he alone knows the hearts of men. It is in vain, then, that we invoke those who do not look upon our hearts. Almost all prayers are made in the heart; we seldom pray in express words. Indeed we are often so disturbed that we cannot pray in set words; above all, when we must depart hence, the voice fails us. It is therefore in vain that prayers are poured out to those who do not hear us, who do not understand or know what we need, and who can neither confer good things nor avert evils. Paul says in Rom. 10 that we should invoke him in whom we believe; but we believe in God alone. He alone, then, is to be invoked. Further, we have neither a command nor examples of invoking the saints, nor even promises. What they adduce from Ezekiel is utterly feeble, as will be said later. The Papists flee to the litanies in these calamities as to a sacred anchor; but it is a mere human invention. Gregory the Great instituted the so-called greater litany before the feast of Mark, about the year 590. The three-day processions before the feast of the Ascension were devised by Claudianus Mamertus, bishop of Vienne; but they fight against the word of God, for in them angels, patriarchs, martyrs, confessors, virgins and widows are invoked and besought to avert all dangers and calamities, which yet God alone can avert.

units.la: Quae vero petenda sunt a Deo? Ne jux-ta nostra merita nos tractare, sed poenam hanc vel auertere vel saltem mitigare velit, patientiam, vitæ emendationem & pietatis studium concedat, Christus iussit nos panem quotidianum petere, hoc est, ea quæ ad terrenæ & cœlestis vitæ sustentationem faciunt.
units.tr: But what are we to ask of God? That, not dealing with us according to our merits, he may be willing either to avert this punishment or at least to mitigate it, and that he may grant patience, amendment of life and zeal for godliness. Christ commanded us to ask for our daily bread, that is, those things which serve the sustenance of earthly and heavenly life.

units.la: Et vt vno verbo dicam, pœnitentia nobis agenda est, hoc est, agnoscenda & confitenda sunt nobis peccata, inuocandus est Deus per Christum vt nobis ignoscat, atque id firmiter nobis credendum est. Prætereà licitis honestisque medijs ( de quibus posteà ) vti licet, & patienter omnia ferenda sunt quæ nobis imminent, donec nos liberare dignetur, quod dum fit, cauendum nobis est ab omnibus ijs rebus, quæ Deo displicent, illis verò studere quæ & ipsi placent, atque ita vera pœnitentia iram Dei declinare, & in vijs eius ambulare debemus.
units.tr: And to say it in one word: repentance is to be done by us, that is, we must acknowledge and confess our sins, God must be invoked through Christ that he may forgive us, and this we must firmly believe. Besides, we may use lawful and honest means (of which later), and all that hangs over us must be borne patiently until he deigns to free us. While this is being done, we must beware of all those things which displease God, and must rather strive for those things which please him; and so by true repentance we ought to avert the anger of God and walk in his ways.

units.la: Sed & alia loca sacrarum literarum monent in huiusmodi calamitatibus hac via procedendum esse. Israelitæ, à Palæstinis cæsi, & capta arca, Samuel illos admomonet, ut 1. Sam. 2. cap. scribitur, ut resipiscant & vero corde ad Dominum reiectis idolis convertatur, hoc si fiat Deum illis propitium fore, & eventus, promissiones veras esse probavit: Licet ibi de bello loquatur, quid prohibet tamen quo minus etiam de fame intelligamus. Dan. 9. Peccavimus & iniquè fecimus, impie egimus & desciuimus deflectendo etiam à praeceptis tuis et iudiciis tuis. Neq; obedivimus servis tuis Prophetis, qui tuo nomine locuti sunt ad reges nostros, principes nostros, patres nostros & ad totum populum terrae. Fatetur ergo omnes cuiuscunq; sint ordinis peccasse. Etsi quidam graviùs peccarint, neminem tamen excepit. Nō dicit, haec mala huic vel illi accepta sunt ferenda, sed omnes etiam in vitio esse confitentur. Vide Amos 4. Ioel. 1. & 2. cap.
units.tr: But other passages of Holy Scripture also admonish that in calamities of this kind this path must be followed. When the Israelites were slain by the Philistines and the ark was taken, Samuel admonished them, as is written in 1 Sam. 2, that they should repent and, with a true heart, turn to the Lord, putting away their idols; if this were done, God would be propitious to them, and the outcome proved his promises true. Although there he speaks of war, what prevents us from understanding it also of famine? Dan. 9: "We have sinned and done wickedly, we have acted impiously and revolted, turning aside even from your precepts and your judgements. Nor have we obeyed your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes, our fathers and to all the people of the land." He therefore confesses that all, of whatever rank they are, have sinned. Although some have sinned more grievously, he excepts no one. He does not say that these evils are to be borne as deserved by this or that person, but all confess that they too are at fault. See Amos 4; Joel 1 and 2.

units.la: Hoc fecere omnes viri pij & religiosi tempore famis: non desperarunt de gratia & auxilio divino, non abnegarunt fidem: nec imposturis & iniquis rationibus paupertati consulere voluere. Luc. 15. Filius prodigus, typus generis humani, sua culpa in illas angustias gustias redactus fuit, ut in magna fame porcis pascendis præficeretur, & in tanta penuria, desiderabat implere ventrem suum si-liquis, quas edebant porci, & nemo ei dabat. Sed in se reuersus paternam domū repetijt. Quum autem adhuc longe abesset, vidit eum pater ipsius, ac misericordia motus est, & accurrens incidit in collum eius, et osculatus est eum. Dixit autem ei filius: Pater peccaui in cœlum & aduersum te, neq; amplius sum dignus, vocari filius tuus. Ita & nos Deo supplices esse debemus.
units.tr: All pious and religious men have done this in time of famine: they did not despair of grace and divine help, they did not deny their faith, nor did they wish to provide for themselves by deceit and unjust devices. Luke 15: the prodigal son, a type of the human race, was brought by his own fault into those straits, so that in a great famine he was set to feed swine, and in such want he longed to fill his belly with the husks that the swine were eating, and no one gave him any. But coming to himself, he returned to his father's house. While he was still far off, his father saw him, was moved with compassion, ran and fell on his neck and kissed him. And the son said to him: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son." So we too ought to be suppliant before God.

units.la: Sin vero neq; Deum neq; verbum eius cu-ramus de emendada vita non sumus sollici-ti, non ardenter oramus, mirum non est ma-ledictione Dei nos premi. Iacob.4. Pugnatis & bellatis, non tamen obtinetis, propterea quod non petitis. Petitis & non accipitis, eo quod male petatis, ut in voluptates vestras insinuatis. Ezech.14. docet, piorū etiam in-tercessiones fore irritas, nisi pœnitentiam agant homines. Etsi fuerint tres illi viri in medio eius, Noe, Daniel & Iob, ipsi iustitia sua liberabunt animam suam. Eadem fere verba loquitur Ierem.15. Sistarent Moses & Samuel coram me, non esset animus meus ad populum istum, eijce eos à facie mea, vt egrediantur etc. Sed quo? [?] respondit propheta. Qui ad mortem (inquit Deus) ad mortem, & qui ad gladium, ad gladiū, et qui ad famē, ad famem etc. Iudæi multum cofidebant intercessioni sanctorum. Tot, dicebant, (ut ad illum locum Ezech. homil.53. author noster annotauit) in Iudæa, in exilio, boni viri & religiosæ fœminæ quotidie ardentes preces pro conseruatione regni & reductione exulū effundentes, haud dubie exaudiuntur, proin-de nō est vt nobis à Prophetarum minis metuamus. Deus autem refellit per prophetam vanā hanc spem. Esto (inquit) duo illi egregij viri pro vobis intercedant, tamen quod vos attinet, nulla erit vtilitas, etc.
units.tr: But if we neither care for God nor for his word, do not concern ourselves with amending our lives, and do not pray earnestly, it is no wonder that we are oppressed by the curse of God. James 4: "You fight and wage war, yet you do not obtain, because you do not ask. You ask and do not receive, because you ask amiss, that you may spend it on your pleasures." Ezekiel 14 teaches that even the intercessions of the godly will be in vain unless men repent. "Even if those three men, Noah, Daniel and Job, were in the midst of it, they would deliver only their own souls by their righteousness." Jeremiah 15 speaks almost the same words: "If Moses and Samuel stood before me, my mind would not be toward this people; cast them out of my sight, that they may go forth," etc. But to what end? the prophet answers. "Such as are for death, to death; and such as are for the sword, to the sword; and such as are for famine, to famine," etc. The Jews put much confidence in the intercession of the saints. "So many," they said (as our author noted on that passage of Ezekiel, homily 53), "in Judea and in exile, good men and religious women, pouring out fervent prayers every day for the preservation of the kingdom and the return of the exiles, are undoubtedly heard; therefore we need not fear the threats of the prophets." God, however, refutes this vain hope through the prophet: "Even if those two excellent men," he says, "intercede for you, yet as far as you are concerned there will be no advantage," etc.

units.la: Ex his colligimus aliorum intercessiones pro te otioso et inpœnitenti nil prodesse. Ideo Ierem.7. Prophetæ dicit Deus: Ne oraueris pro populo isto, nec leuaueris pro eis clamorem, etc. Sic Samuelem pro Saule impœni-tenti orantem reijcit Deus. Si piorum tibi preces preces nil proderunt, quid impiorum & su-perstitiosorum hominū prodesse poterunt, qui non nisi mercede conducti orant? quiq3 [?] etiam ipsis pro quibus orant longe sunt deteriores? Ite si piorū in his terris preces impijs nil pro-sunt, quid cœlitū, qui his curis & molestijs li-berati sunt, illis profuturas existimandū est? Ridiculi ergo sunt Papistæ qui his ex locis invocationē Divorum colligere volunt. Con-ditionalis enim propositio nil ponit in esse.
units.tr: From these things we gather that the intercessions of others do nothing for you if you are idle and unrepentant. Therefore God says to the prophet in Jeremiah 7: "Do not pray for this people, nor lift up a cry or prayer for them," etc. So God rejects Samuel praying for the unrepentant Saul. If the prayers of the godly profit you nothing, what can the prayers of the ungodly and superstitious men profit, who pray only when hired for wages? And who are, moreover, far worse than those for whom they pray? Again, if the prayers of the godly in this earth do nothing for the wicked, must we suppose that the heavenly ones, who are freed from these cares and troubles, will profit them? Therefore the Papists are ridiculous who wish to draw the invocation of the saints from these passages. A conditional proposition does not establish anything as existing.

units.la: Nam ut Zuinglius in illum locum Ierem. re-ctè annotavit, Si starent enim,ait,non stant & interpellant. Est enim prosopopoeia, ac si diceret, Si nūc superstites essent Noe & Iob, & se interponerent,manebo tamen inexora-bilis: Dein Danielis qui adhuc in vivis erat mentionē facit. Non ergo hoc vult Prophe-ta mortuos in cœlis pro hoc populo intercede-re. Sed ab impossibili argumentatur. Velim etiam mihi dicat Papistæ an fuerint patres ante Christi adventū in has terras,in cœlus? Negabunt utiq3. Nam in limbo patrum de-tentos fuisse dicunt. Interim eos nō pudet hoc argumento uti. In summa in his publicus plagis pœnitentiam precibus coniungamus.
units.tr: For, as Zwingli rightly noted on that passage of Jeremiah: "If they stood," he says, "they do not stand and intercede." It is a prosopopoeia, as if he said: "If Noah and Job were now alive and interposed themselves, I would still remain unyielding." Then he mentions Daniel, who was still alive. Therefore the prophet does not mean that the dead in heaven intercede for this people, but argues from the impossible. I would also like to ask the Papists whether the fathers were in heaven before Christ's coming into this land? They will certainly deny it, for they say the fathers were held in the limbo of the fathers. Yet they are not ashamed to use this argument. In sum, in these public plagues let us join repentance with prayers.

units.la: Nunc singulos sigillatim officij sui admonebo.
units.tr: Now I will admonish each one separately of his duty.

units.la: Primo pius Magistratus, omnia illa, propter quae supra diximus, Deum nos annonae caritate aliisq; poenis affligere, pro virili sub movere debet. Sublatis causis tollitur esse-ctus. Dauid hac in parte fideliter officio suo functus est, cū enim tribus integris annis fa-mes duraret, diligenter inquirebat, cur Deus populo suo irasceretur: & cognita causa, eam tollit, ut nuper diximus, atq; ita hac ratione Deus placatus & populus ei reconciliatus est. Multum hic peccatur à Principibus vi-ris, qui suo more vivunt, libidinibus & voluptatibus indulgent, interim nulla cura e-genorum, subditorum, tanguntur, non inqui-runt imò ne cogitant quidem quae nam famis aliarumque publicarum calamitatem causae esse possint, & quo nam pacto ira Dei placari debeat. Magistratum etiam decet bonis legibus & severitate poenarum obviam ire iis rebus, quibus subditi ad paupertatem re-diguntur, ut sunt alea, luxus in cibo, potu, ve-sticu[?], etc. Iuvenes coercendi sunt, ne opes pa-ternas ternas turpiter prodigalitate perdant: prin-cipiis obstandum, Nam ut ille ait:
units.tr: First, the godly magistrate ought, as far as he is able, to remove all those things on account of which we said above that God afflicts us with dearth of grain and other punishments. When the causes are removed, the effect is removed. David discharged his duty faithfully in this matter: when famine lasted for three full years, he diligently inquired why God was angry with his people; and having learned the cause, he removed it, as we said a little while ago, and so by this means God was appeased and the people reconciled to him. Princes and powerful men sin greatly here, who live after their own fashion, indulge their lusts and pleasures, and meanwhile are moved by no concern for the poor and their subjects; they do not inquire, indeed they do not even think, what causes there may be for famine and other public calamities, and how the wrath of God ought to be appeased. The magistrate should also, by good laws and severity of punishments, check those things by which subjects are reduced to poverty, such as gambling, extravagance in food, drink, clothing, etc. Young men must be restrained, lest they shamefully squander their fathers' wealth through prodigality; one must withstand beginnings, for as that poet says:

units.la: Quid juvat amisso claudere septa grege?
units.tr: What good is it to close the fold after the flock is lost?

units.la: Veteres habuerunt leges sumptuarias, quas hodie quoque utile esset revocari, ne tot homines ad mendicitatem redigerentur. Ad hac monopolis, propolis, fœneratoribus, & aliis qui omnium rerum ad vitam sustentandam necessariarum, precia gravant, frænum injicere debent, ut pauperes omnia viliore pretio sibi comparare possint. Hac de re insigne extat exemplum, Nehem.5.cap. Exor-ta fame variæ querelæ pauperum contra divites audiebantur, quòd fœnus exercerent, liberosq; & res eorum sibi vendicarent, quodq; conditio eorum non melior esset, quàm in captivitate sub ethnicis fuisset. Res ad seditionem gravissimam spectare videbatur. In his turbis Nehemias bonam navabat operam: etenim zelo ardens, quomodo rebus afflictis succurreret, consilium capiebat. Non dicebat, frustrà hoc saxum voluo, non sine vitæ periculo his malis mederi potero: sed increpabat proceres, quòd rem non seriò tractarent. Comitia congregabat, in quibus debitores & creditores conparerent, argumentis aliquot diuites à suo proposito abducebat. Primùm dicebat, Nos (nempe Esdras, Zorobabel & ego) populũ ex captiuitate reduximus, proinde vos iugum eis non denuò debetis imponere. Deinde dicit, Gentes lætarentur si hæc viderent: si verò Deum timeretis, hæc non faceretis: proponit eis suum exeplũ, quòd nihil ab eis postulet, quod ipse nõ sponte facturus sit: iubet ut pauperib. per usuras adepta restituant, nepe agros, vineas, domos, itē pignora & alia. His rationib. tantũ effecit, ut imperata facerent. Hodie quoq; si pij magistratus officio suo non desint, multũ possunt efficere. Romani, & alij habuerunt annonæ præfectos, qui dimissis passim frumetarijs ad frumentum coëmendũ anonæ subuenirët. Solomonẽ tales habuisse 1. Reg. 4. legitur. Utile quoq; fuerit magistratũ fertilib. annis frugum aceruos reponere, ut postea fame ingruente, agricolis cõmodato dare fruges possint, ut sementẽ faciat, et ne in foro precĩu immodicè augeatur. Quũ rex Pharao ex Iosepho intelligeret, ligeret,postea septe annos fertiles,totidè steriles uèturos,utileq; fore si frugũ thefaurũ colligeret,cõstituebat ipsum œconomũ,qui fruges conseruaret et reponeret, id nisi fecisset,multos postea fame perire necesse fuisset. Eufeb. Eccl.hist.2.l. 12.ca.scribit de Helena gentis Adiabenorum regina, quòd in fame quæ Iu-dæa pressit,frumetũ ab Ægyptijs cõparatũ, egenis distribuerit. Ioseph.quoq; illius rei meminit.In illa fame quæ incidit in an.649.cuius in 1.cõcione mentione fecimus,celebratur à Nauclero Regis Clodouæi erga egenos li-beralitas,testũ quod argeteũ erat(inqt)à te-plo martyrũ auferri et p loci Abbate Agul-stetũ indigetib.et peregrinis distribui iubet? Sed et in pfanis historijs ethnicorũ quoq; co-mẽdatur liberalitas erga egenos. Gillias A-grigentinus apud Valeriũ Maximũ li. 4.c. 8.Pauperibus alimẽta & subsidia,uirginib. pauperibus doues[?] dabat,& Gedensiũ equites quingentos ui tẽpestatis ad ipsum propulsos fouit,et ita liberalis erat,ut et Agrigentina ciuitas omnis & uicinæ getes ex eius opib.in getes caperẽt utilitates. In nostris analib.memorabile liberalitatis erga egeos exép,extat
units.tr: The ancients had sumptuary laws, which it would be useful to revive today as well, so that so many men are not reduced to beggary. Moreover, monopolists, forestallers, usurers, and others who raise the prices of all things necessary for sustaining life must be curbed, so that the poor can procure everything for themselves at a cheaper price. There is a notable example of this matter in Nehemiah 5. When famine broke out, various complaints of the poor against the rich were heard: that they practised usury, took their children and their property for themselves, and that their condition was no better than it had been under the heathen in captivity. The matter seemed to threaten the gravest sedition. In these disturbances Nehemiah did good work: burning with zeal, he took counsel how to help the afflicted. He did not say, "I shall roll this stone in vain; I cannot remedy these evils without danger to my life," but he rebuked the nobles for not handling the matter seriously. He called an assembly, at which debtors and creditors appeared, and with several arguments he drew the wealthy away from their purpose. First he said: "We (that is, Ezra, Zerubbabel and I) have brought the people back from captivity; therefore you ought not to impose the yoke on them again. Next he says: "The nations would rejoice if they saw these things; but if you feared God, you would not do them." He sets before them his own example, that he asks nothing of them which he himself would not willingly do; he orders that they restore to the poor what they had gained through usury: namely fields, vineyards, houses, also pledges and other things. By these arguments he so far prevailed that they did what was commanded. Today too, if godly magistrates do not fail in their duty, they can achieve much. The Romans and others had prefects of the grain supply, who, sending out grain-buyers everywhere to purchase corn, came to the aid of the supply. We read that Solomon had such men, 1 Kings 4. It would also be useful for the magistrate in fruitful years to store heaps of grain, so that afterwards, when famine threatens, they may be able to lend grain to the farmers, that they may make seed, and so that the price is not immoderately raised in the market. When King Pharaoh understood from Joseph that seven fruitful years would be followed by seven barren ones, and that it would be useful to gather a treasury of grain, he appointed him steward, to preserve and store the grain; had he not done so, many would necessarily have perished afterwards by famine. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2, chapter 12, writes that Helena, queen of the people of Adiabene, during the famine that pressed Judea, bought grain from the Egyptians and distributed it to the needy. Josephus also mentions this event. In that famine which fell in the year 649, of which we spoke in the first sermon, Naucler celebrates the liberality of King Clodoveus toward the needy, since he ordered that the silver which was (he says) taken from the temple of the martyrs be distributed by the abbot of the place to the indigent and to strangers. But liberality toward the needy is also commended in the profane histories of the heathen. Gellias of Agrigentum, in Valerius Maximus book 4, chapter 8, gave food and support to the poor, and dowries to poor maidens, and he cherished five hundred Gedensian horsemen who had been driven to him by a violent storm, and he was so generous that the whole city of Agrigentum and the neighbouring peoples derived benefit from his resources. In our annals there is a memorable example of liberality toward the needy.

units.la: Erat Nicolaus nobilis à Kizingen[?] homo ad miraculum usque avarus & sordidus. Is Episcopatum Constantiensem adeptus erat Anno 1343. vel ut alij supputant 1335. Neq; hoc opimo Pontificatu avaritia sedari po-tuit. Nam hinc inde variis artibus ingen-tes corrasit opes. Sed ecce miram & inaudi-tam sexiò hominis mutationem. Erat anno 1343. & 1344. magna fames & rerum pe-nuria per universam superiorem Germa-niam. Is comportatis suis opibus libera-liter utitur. Nam duobus illis annis, ter sin-gulis septimanis pulmento & pane benignè aluit 3000. interdum 4000. sæpius etiam 4500. homines, qui ex vicinis regionibus Constantiam confluebant. Vix cessauit fa-mes, moritur benignus præsul in arce sua, cui Castrum nomen est: Inde Constantiam usq; à maxima pauperum multitudine funus du-citur: ita suam erga alitorem gratitudinem pio hoc officio testabantur. Imitanda hæc exempla sunt principibus, præsulibus & Re-buspublicis. Multi quidem libenter inopiam subditorum suorũ subleuarent: sed in eorum facultate non est positum: non enim omne frumentum in suos distribuere possunt, quum quid futurum sit nesciant. Sæpe ex commeatus inopia urbes hostibus dedere oportet. Legimus de Phalari tyranno quòd hoc stratagemate munitissima Sicilia loca occuparit: simulato enim cū oppidanis fœdere, fruges eis seruandas dedit. Curans interim, ut granaria in quibus cōdebantur, pluuia admitterét, & sic inutiles redderentur. Illi fiducia depositi apud se tritici, proprio abutebātur. Tyrannus itaq; obsessos, cōmeatus inopia ad deditionem cōpulit. Sunt homines qui uno die omnia proferenda putāt, neq; cogitāt quòd maiore periculo postea illis caredum sit. Solomon Proue. 6. formicarum exemplo docet quāta sedulitate, cura et industria fruges ad futurā necessitatem reponere et colligere debeamus. Quem locum author noster plurib. tractat & explicat in Cōmentarijs suis quos in Pro. Solomonis edidit. Vrbs Tigurina hoc nomine laudanda est,quòd non solùm quotidie multis pauperibus, ex bonis publicis ad uictum et amictum necessaria suppeditat: sed & ciuibus suis fame dominante, tolerabili pretio frumē tum vendit, vt farciat eorum inopiam, & vt exteri quoque in publico foro fruges viliori pretio habere possint. Argetoratū vrbs ornatissima, hodie quoq; à multis celebratur, quòd in illa annonæ caritate, quæ fuit anno Dom. 1517. item 1529. aliisq; teporibus, suis ciuibus, & etiam peregrinis fruges liberaliter distribuit: suisq; ciuibus, aliisq; quos fames adipsos compulerat, quotidie alimoniā suppeditauit.
units.tr: There was a noble man, Nicholas, from Kizingen, a man of wonderful avarice and meanness. He obtained the bishopric of Constance in the year 1343, or, as others reckon, 1335. Yet avarice could not be quelled even in this rich pontificate; for he amassed great wealth here and there by various arts. But behold the wonderful and unheard-of change in the man. In the years 1343 and 1344 there was a great famine and shortage of goods throughout upper Germany. He, using his riches generously, fed with soup and bread, three times each week, 3000, sometimes 4000, and often even 4500 people who flocked to Constance from the neighbouring regions. Scarcely had the famine ceased when the generous prelate died in his stronghold, which is called Castrum. From there his funeral was led to Constance with a very great multitude of the poor; thus by this pious duty they bore witness to their gratitude toward their benefactor. These examples are to be imitated by princes, prelates and commonwealths. Many would gladly relieve the want of their subjects, but it is not within their means: they cannot distribute all the grain among their own people, since they do not know what will happen. Often through lack of supplies cities must be surrendered to enemies. We read of the tyrant Phalaris that by this stratagem he seized the most fortified places of Sicily: pretending an alliance with the townspeople, he gave them grain to keep, and meanwhile saw to it that the granaries in which it was stored admitted rain, and so made them useless. They, trusting in the wheat deposited with them, were themselves abused by it. So the tyrant, with his besieged enemies driven by want of supplies, forced them to surrender. There are men who think everything should be brought out in one day, and do not consider that they will afterwards have to go without, with greater danger. Solomon, Proverbs 6, teaches by the example of the ants with how much diligence, care and industry we ought to store up and gather grain against future need. Our author treats and explains this passage at length in his commentaries which he published on the Proverbs of Solomon. The city of Zurich is to be praised for this, that not only does it daily supply many poor people from public goods with what is necessary for food and clothing, but also, when famine is raging among its citizens, it sells grain at a bearable price, to relieve their want, and so that strangers too may be able to obtain grain in the public market at a cheaper price. The city of Strasbourg, a most distinguished city, is still praised by many today, because in that dearth of grain which was in the year 1517, likewise in 1529, and at other times, it distributed grain generously to its own citizens and also to strangers, and daily supplied food to its citizens and to others whom famine had driven to it.

units.la: Adhæc magistratus officium est, curare vt publicæ eleemosynæ rectè distribuātur. In pagis Ecclesiæ aliquot, suos quoq; habent annuos reditus: utile igitur fuerit à procuratoribus illorum, ratione accepti & expensi exigere, ne dum diuites opibus illis vtuntur, aut ex illis belluantur, pauperes cibo, victuq; fraudētur. Multis in locis statis dieb. panes distribuuntur pauperibus, quam eleemosynā vulgo Spendam vocant. Deriuatur, vel à Germanica voce, quæ expendere significat, vel à Græco vocabulo σπένδω, quod est, libo, vel sacrifico, & σπονδὴ libamen.
units.tr: Moreover, it is the duty of the magistrate to see that public alms are distributed properly. Several churches in the villages also have their own annual revenues. It would therefore be useful to require accounts of receipts and expenditure from their stewards, so that the rich do not enjoy those funds or feast on them while the poor are cheated of food and sustenance. In many places bread is handed out to the poor on fixed days, an alms that people commonly call the Spenda. It is derived either from the German word that means to spend, or from the Greek σπένδω, which means to pour a libation or to sacrifice, and σπονδὴ, a libation.

units.la: Neq; parum retulerit, vt magistratus pauperes peres ad certos labores cogat, veluti ad publica aedificia extruenda, et alia, neq; otiosos ferat. Item vt ualidos mendicos, qui laborare nolunt, ditione sua pellat, ne oneri sint agri-colis & alijs. Saepe enim fit, vt illi obseruent absentiam virorum in villis solitarijs, minis-que adigant familiam illorum, vt carnes suil-las, & alia eis conferant. Tales instar lupo-rum prosequendi sunt, vt laboriosi & verè pauperes melius necessaria habere possint. Tempore Apostol. eleemosynae collectae sunt, quibus tempore famis, fidelium in dissitis locis paupertas posset subleuari. Paulus non dedignatus est pauperibus Hierosolymitanis afferre eleemosynam, quam in Macedonia & Achaia fideles collegerant. Diligenter in suis Epistolis Ecclesias hortatur, vt sibi pauperes commendatos habeant.
units.tr: It is also of no small importance that the magistrate compel the poor to work at fixed tasks, such as building public edifices and other things, and that he not tolerate idlers. Likewise he should drive out of his territory the able-bodied beggars who refuse to work, so that they are not a burden to the farmers and others. For it often happens that they watch for the absence of the men on isolated farms and, by threats, force the household to hand over their salted meats and other things. Such people must be chased off like wolves, so that the industrious and truly poor can more easily have what they need. In apostolic times alms were collected, by which in a time of famine the poverty of the faithful in distant places could be relieved. Paul did not disdain to bring alms to the poor of Jerusalem, which the faithful in Macedonia and Achaia had collected. In his Epistles he diligently urges the churches to keep the poor commended to them.

units.la: Ministri Ecclesiae, populū sibi commissum pro cōcione docere debet ex verbo Dei quod fertilitas sit Dei donū: item quas ob causas Deus famem immittat: inuitare eū debent ad poenitentiam, pauperes confirmare & erigere, diuites adhortari, vt largas eis elemosynas conferant. Deũite serió precari debent, ut pauperib. sit propitius, eosq; clemen-ter respiciat. Ierem. enim quum audiret populum fame affligendum, pro eo apud Deũ intercedebat. Amos 7. c. quû ex visione intelligeret famem imminere, orabat Deum, ut populo propitius esset, suisq; ardentibus precib. famem auertebat. Iacob 8. ca. dicit: deprecationem iusti efficacem, multum valere. Adducit exemplum Heliae, qui precibus suis cæ-lum clauserit & aperuerit. Cyrillus tempo-re famis ut succurreret egenis, preciosa vasa distraxisse legitur. Ministri igitur, praeser-tim illi quibus bonorum Ecclesiasticorum administratio commissa est, suo officio non desint.
units.tr: The ministers of the Church ought to teach from the Word of God, in their sermons, the people committed to them: that fertility is a gift of God; likewise for what reasons God sends famine. They ought to invite the people to repentance, to strengthen and raise up the poor, and to exhort the rich to give generous alms to them. They must also earnestly pray that God be gracious to the poor and look on them with mercy. For when Jeremiah heard that the people were to be afflicted with famine, he interceded for them with God. Amos, chapter 7, when from a vision he understood that famine was impending, prayed to God that he would be gracious to the people, and by his fervent prayers he turned the famine away. James 8 says that the prayer of a righteous man avails much and is effective. He cites the example of Elijah, who by his prayers shut and opened the heavens. It is recorded that Cyril, in a time of famine, sold his precious vessels in order to help the needy. Ministers, therefore, especially those to whom the administration of church goods has been entrusted, must not fail in their duty.

units.la: Patresfamiliâs & matresfamiliâs, liberis & domesticis suis inculcare debent, quòd cibum & potû ex Dei manu accipiat, quodq; omnibus moriendum esset fame, si Deus manum suam clauderet: à teneris annis instillare quasi debent liberis suis, ut quando ad mensam accedunt, vel ab ea recedunt, Deo pro cibo & potu gratias agant.
