units.tr: Fathers and mothers of families ought to impress upon their children and household that they receive food and drink from the hand of God, and that all would have to die of hunger if God closed his hand. From their tender years they ought, as it were, to instil into their children that when they come to the table or rise from it, they should give thanks to God for their food and drink.

units.la: Divites in primis tempore famis pauperi-bus consulant: ideo enim Deus ipsos opib.in-struxit,ut alijs quoq; manu porrigant,quod multis modis fieri potest. Si habeas colonos quorum laboribus vineæ et agri non respon-dent, ne importunè eos urgeas ad solutionem debitorum. Incolas ædium tuarum ne vexes, nec pretium augeas, cogitans eos vix maximis laboribus panem, vestes, ligna, vedū[?] alia sibi comparare. Alios debitores ne ultra modū urgeas, ut tibi satisfaciant, præsertim si multos liberos habeat, et nō suo vitio ad paupertatem sint redacti: Mercenarijs persolue debitam mercedē: plus illis dato quàm petāt, si videas eos esurire. Elargire tuas eleemosynas illis quos nostri rerū necessariarum penuria laborare. D.Pau.1,Tim.6.hortatur di-vites, ut sibi in cœlis thesaurum colligant, & in pauperes sint liberales & benefici. Deus tuas opes auget sua benedictione, si ad victum & cultum corporis necessaria pauperibus distribuas. Superioribus aliquot seculis multi idola ex pretiosa materia fecerunt, sacrificia eis obtulerunt, suspenderunt anathemata, putantes hæc Deo grata esse: nunc vero certo scimus ex verbo Dei, Deo obsequium præstari sit vivis simulachris, hoc est, pauperibus, vestes, cibi, pecuniæ offeratur, aliaq; necessaria, ut labori suo possint incumbere. Obijcis, te non posse tantum elargiri alijs, quantum vel les. [?] Minue itaq; luxum in conuiuijs, vestib. suppellectili, & alijs in rebus. Institue conuiuia iuxta Christi doctrinam pauperibus & famelicis. Amos propheta in divites illos invehitur, quibus nō dolebat quod Ioseph atterebatur, hoc est, quòd populus cū fame & egestate conflictabatur, ipsi securi interim voluptatibus indulgebant. Ex quorū numero erat dives ille epulo, qui tantum abdominis suo natus, indies belluabatur, de quo Lucas decimosexto, Rectius fecit Carolus Magnus Imperat. qui solebat domi pauperes aliquot alere ut pauper tatis imagine ante oculos posita, summæ fortunæ moderari, Christique & Apostolorum meminisse, insuesceret. Quòd si tibi molestum est pauperes invita-re in domum tuam, dato eis ut domi suæ cum liberis vel atro pane satiari possint. Deus bone quantum vini effunditur ab ebriosis hominibus, quantum vini bibunt ab aliis a-dacti, quo pauperes recreari possent, ut idonei essent perferendis laboribus? Religio tibi esset si aliquem impelleres, ut vel terun-cium alteri surriperet: at adigens alterum ad ebrietatem, Deum non metuis? Consi-dera[?] quanta sit hominum illa cæcitas. De elee-mosyna quid sit, quæ eius sint species, quis e-largiri eam debeat, cui, quid, quantum, quo-modo: item de vitiis eleemosynæ, & alia quæ de hac materia disputari solent, non est necesse, ut hoc loco à nobis multa afferan-tur: plurimi enim hac de re copiose scripse-runt.
units.tr: The rich above all should look after the poor in a time of famine, for God has therefore endowed them with wealth so that they may also stretch out a hand to others, which can be done in many ways. If you have tenants whose labours do not yield a return from your vineyards and fields, do not press them too hard for payment of their debts. Do not harass the occupants of your houses, nor raise the rent, reflecting that they can scarcely obtain bread, clothing, wood and other necessities for themselves even with the greatest labour. Do not press other debtors beyond measure to satisfy you, especially if they have many children and have been reduced to poverty not through their own fault. Pay your hired workers their due wages; give them more than they ask if you see them going hungry. Bestow your alms on those who suffer from a lack of the things they need. The apostle Paul, in 1 Tim. 6, urges the rich to lay up for themselves a treasure in heaven, and to be generous and beneficent to the poor. God increases your wealth with his blessing if you distribute to the poor what is necessary for their sustenance and the care of their bodies. In past centuries many people made idols of precious material, offered sacrifices to them, and hung up votive offerings, thinking these things pleasing to God; but now we know for certain from the Word of God that service is rendered to God when things are offered to the living images, that is, to the poor: clothing, food, money and other necessities, so that they may apply themselves to their labour. You object that you cannot give to others as much as you would like. Then reduce the luxury at your feasts, in clothing, household furnishings and other matters. Hold banquets for the poor and hungry in accordance with the teaching of Christ. The prophet Amos rails against those rich men who were not grieved that Joseph was being worn down, that is, that the people were struggling with hunger and want, while they themselves, careless, indulged in pleasures. Of their number was that rich man who feasted, who, born only for his belly, grew fat day by day, of whom Luke speaks in chapter 16. Charles the Great, emperor, acted more rightly, who used to feed some poor people at home, so that with the image of poverty set before his eyes he might moderate his great fortune and be trained to remember Christ and the apostles. But if it is troublesome to you to invite the poor into your house, give them the means to be fed at home with their children, even on black bread. Good God, how much wine is poured out by drunken men, how much wine is drunk by those driven to it by others, wine with which the poor could be refreshed and made fit to bear their labours! Would it not be a matter of conscience for you if you were to induce someone to snatch even a little loaf from another? Yet by forcing another into drunkenness, do you not fear God? Consider what blindness this is in people. As to what alms are, what kinds there are, who ought to give them, to whom, what, how much and in what manner; likewise concerning the vices of almsgiving, and other matters that are customarily debated on this subject, there is no need for us to bring forward much here, for very many have written abundantly on this matter.

units.la: Divites diligenter cavent, ne difficul-tate annonæ ad spoliandos pauperes, qui-bus auxilio esse debent, utantur, eosque sua crudelitate in exilium pellant. Sunt enim homines qui famis tempore de au-genda re sua familiari, non sine iniuria proximi cogitent: quumque de peccatis suis cogitare deberent, quibus fames & alia mala attrahuntur, ipsi cogitant de augendis rerum pretijs: quos Deus puniet. Prouer.11. Ei qui comprimit frumentum , maledicet populus: benedictio autem super frumentum vendentis. Quidam dant operam, ut præfenti pecunia instructi, obæratorum & famelicorum prata, vineas, domos, sylvas & alia bona sibi vendicent: charitas postulat ut eis succurrant, ne vendere omnia sit necesse. Opes his artibus collectæ, fœlices & diuturnæ non erunt. Experimur opes iuste partas sæpe diffluere, quid nobis de illis promittere-mus, quæ dolis, fraudibus & scelere partæ sunt? Cogitet quisque breui, Deo, qui falli non potest, accepti & expensi rationem esse reddendam. Audi quid Deus in lege sua dicat, Leuit.25. Si attenuatus fuerit frater tuus, nutaueritq; manus eius iuxta te, sustentabis eum, tam peregrinum quam indigenam, ut viuat tecum. Non accipies ab eo usuram vel incrementum: sed timebis Deum tuum, ut viuere possit tecum frater tuus. Pecuniam tuam non dabis illi ad usuram, neque pro incremento dabis illi frumentum tuum. Ego Dominus Deus vester, qui eduxi vos de terra Ægypti, vt darem vobis terram Chanaan & essem vobis in Deum. Amos Propheta clamat cap.8. contra illos qui penuria rerum ad pauperum oppressionem abutuntur: Audite istud qui absorbetis pauperem, & qui facitis cessare pauperes de terra, dicentes: Quando transibit messis, vt vendamus frumentum: & sabbathum, vt aperiamus frumentū, minorem faciamus mensuram Epha, & maiorem faciamus Siclum, atq; peruertamus stateras dolosas: vt acquiramus argento inopes, & pauperem propter duo calceamenta, atque quisquilias frumenti vendamus. Iurauit Dominus per magnificentiam Iacob, si oblitus fuero in perpetuū operum eorum. An non super isto contremiscet terra, & lugebit omnis qui habitat in ea? ascendet enim tota ipsa quasi fluuius, expelletur & operietur vt fluuius Ægypti. Hoc est, vt Munsterus annotat, sicut Nilus sua inundatione omnia quae in eo natant, in planiciem terrae euomit, ita isti euomentur de terra sua.
units.tr: The rich should take great care not to use the scarcity of grain to plunder the poor, whom they ought to help, and by their cruelty drive them into exile. For there are people who, in a time of famine, think about increasing their household wealth, not without injury to their neighbour; and when they ought to be thinking about their sins, through which famine and other evils are brought on, they instead think about raising the prices of goods: God will punish them. Proverbs 11: The people will curse him who withholds grain, but a blessing is upon him who sells it. Some take pains, having money in hand, to seize meadows, vineyards, houses, woods and other goods from the indebted and the hungry; charity requires that they help them, so that they do not have to sell everything. Wealth gathered by these arts will not be happy or lasting. We see that goods justly acquired often slip away; what should we promise ourselves from those gained by deceit, fraud and crime? Let each consider that before long he must render an account of receipts and expenditures to God, who cannot be deceived. Hear what God says in his law, Leviticus 25: If your brother becomes poor, and his hand falters beside you, you shall support him, both the stranger and the native, that he may live with you. You shall not take usury or increase from him; but you shall fear your God, that your brother may live with you. You shall not give him your money at interest, nor give him your grain for increase. I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, to give you the land of Canaan and to be your God. Amos the prophet cries out in chapter 8 against those who abuse the scarcity of goods to oppress the poor: Hear this, you who swallow up the poor, and who make the needy cease from the land, saying: When will the new moon pass, that we may sell grain; and the sabbath, that we may open the grain? Let us make the ephah smaller and the shekel larger, and let us pervert the deceitful balances; that we may buy the weak with silver, and the poor for a pair of sandals, and sell the refuse of the grain. The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob: surely I will never forget any of their works. Shall not the land tremble for this, and everyone who dwells in it mourn? The whole of it shall rise up like a river, and be cast out and submerged like the river of Egypt. This means, as Munster notes, that just as the Nile by its flood casts out everything that swims in it onto the plain of the earth, so these men shall be cast out of their land.

units.la: Possem hic plurima in medium afferre exempla divitū eorum, qui erga egenos im-misericordes fuere, at à Deo graviter puniti sunt, sed quia adhuc recenti memoria sunt, & eorum commemoratio odiosa est, ideo su-persedeo. Audiamus potius Christi de his ultimam sententiam, quam venturus ad iudicium, pronuntiabit: Facta enim separatio ne dicet rex iis qui ad dextram ipsius erunt, Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete regnū paratum vobis à iactis fundamentis mundi. Esurivi enim, & dedistis mihi quo vescerer: sitivi, & dedistis mihi potum: hospes eram, & collegistis me: nudus, & amicivistis me: ægrotavi, & invisistis me: in carcere eram, & venistis ad me. Non missas, non peregrina-tiones votivas commendabit. Quid respon-suros putas usurarios, monopolas, qui ne unum quidem misericordiae opus praestiterunt? Tantum enim abest, ut famelicū cibarint, ut etiam cibum & potum subtraxerint, eò ipso quod rerum pretia nefarijs suis artibus auxerunt, peregrinos non modò non excepe-runt hospicio, sed concives suos nefarijs suis artibus in exilium pepulerunt. Ad extremā egestatem & mendicitatem eos redegerunt. Nudos non modò non operuerũt, sed suis debitoribus, qui soluendo non erant, vestes detraxerunt & culcitrã sub capite abstulerũt. Si maritus soluendo non erat, uxor ex dote soluere cogebatur. Ægrotos nõ cõsolati sunt, sed augendo rerum pretia multos in graues morbos coniecerunt, effecerunteq; ut multi fa me contabescerent. Captiuos non modò non uisitarunt, uerũ etiã debitores suos nulla urgente necessitate in uincula coiecerunt. Vos alloquor diuites inhumanos, quaso verba hæc summi iudicis, voluite & reuoluite in animis uestris, fidem habeatis his verbis nec ne perinde est, nam uestro magno damno tandem uera esse experiemini. Ratū enim erit illud Solom. Præstat parum habere in timore Domini, quã ingẽtes thesauros in trepidatione.
units.tr: I could cite many examples of rich men who were merciless to the poor and were severely punished by God. But since these are still within recent memory, and recalling them is hateful, I will pass them over. Let us instead hear Christ's final sentence, which he will pronounce when he comes to judgment: "For when the separation is made, the king will say to those on his right hand, 'Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you took me in; naked and you clothed me; I was sick and you visited me; I was in prison and you came to me.'" He will not commend masses or votive pilgrimages. What do you think the usurers and engrossers will answer, who did not perform even one work of mercy? So far were they from feeding the hungry that they even took away food and drink, precisely because by their wicked arts they raised the prices of goods. They not only did not receive strangers into their homes, but by their nefarious arts they drove their fellow citizens into exile and reduced them to utter want and beggary. They not only did not clothe the naked, but stripped their debtors, who could not pay, of their clothes, and took the mattress from under their heads. If a husband could not pay, his wife was forced to pay from her dowry. They did not console the sick, but by raising prices they threw many into grave illness and caused many to waste away with hunger. They did not visit the captives, but even threw their debtors into chains with no pressing necessity. I address you, inhuman rich men: I beg you, turn over and over in your minds these words of the supreme judge. Whether you believe them or not makes no difference, for at great cost to yourselves you will at last find them true. For what Solomon said will come to pass: "Better is little with the fear of the Lord than great treasures with trouble" (Prov. 15.).

units.la: Iniustas & male partas opes infaustas esse memorabile Achani exemplū docet, quod extat Ios.7.ca. Occupata urbe Hierichuntina, Achan ducentos Siclos argenteos, palliū Babylonicū & uirgam auream vel vt alij uertunt laminā, pugionem ex anathemate suffuratus est: cogitabat haud dubie se absq; testibus peccare, sibi ac liberis hoc furtum profuturum: sed iusto Dei iudicio revelatum est, ipse cum filijs & filiabus, item iumentis suis atque omnibus quae habebat eductus & crematus fuit. Sed hic difficultas occurrit, quod Deus cum patre liberos quoque occidi voluit. Solutionem malo ipsius authoris quam nostris verbis afferre. Ea institutae narrationi optimè cōueniunt: sic scribit Ho-mil.33.in lib.Josue. De liberis huius Achani, statui non potest, an conscij fuerint sacrile-gij, quod pater eorum commisit nec ne: sed sive conscij fuerint, sive minus, Deus non de-bet iniustitiae accusari. Nam quod Acha-nem unà cum liberis exuri iussit, multas & graves ob causas fecit. In primis autem voluit ut hinc colligeremus, illos malè liberis suis consulere, qui opes iniustas cumulant.
units.tr: The memorable example of Achan, in Joshua 7, shows that unjust and ill-gotten wealth brings misfortune. When the city of Jericho had been taken, Achan secretly took two hundred silver shekels, a Babylonian cloak and a golden bar (or, as others render it, a plate), and a dagger from the accursed things. He no doubt thought he sinned without witnesses, and that this theft would profit himself and his children. But by God's just judgment it was revealed, and he was led out with his sons and daughters, likewise with his beasts and all that he had, and burned. Here, however, a difficulty arises, that God wished the children to be killed along with the father. I prefer to give the solution in the author's own words, which fit this narrative well. Thus he writes in Homily 33 on the book of Joshua: "Concerning the children of this Achan, it cannot be determined whether they knew of the sacrilege their father committed or not. But whether they knew of it or less so, God is not to be accused of injustice. For in ordering Achan to be burned together with his children, he acted for many and serious reasons. Chiefly, however, he wished us to gather from this that those who heap up unjust wealth provide badly for their children."

units.la: Multa sunt quae hominem ad colligendum malus artibus divitias stimulant: quidam enim Deo diffidentes, iustis viis se non asse-quuturos sperant ad vitae usum necessaria, convertantur itaque ad malas artes. Alii vero verò non contenti rebus necessarijs, etiam quæ ad voluptatem & luxum pertinent, habere desiderant. Plurimi verò commodis liberorum & nepotum consultum volentes, per fas & nefas opes congerunt, quibus illi postea vtantur. Cura quidem & solicitudo pro liberis moderata non damnatur, sed quæ modum excedit, & cum diffidentia coniuncta est. Tales enim homines, si exerceant honestam aliquam artem: tamen nimiùm pe tunt pro suis laboribus, plerumq; verò ad artes impias se applicant, furtis, sacrilegijs, peculatu, sese polluunt. Sed quis tandem erit exitus? Haud dubiè Achan, quoque suis liberis prospicere voluit, sed hac via quam se quuntur est, diris flammis eos obiecit. Ita hodie quoque, qui illicitis vijs liberis consulere volunt, et se et liberos suos grauissimis malis inuoluunt. Illi enim mortem parentum, veluti vultures cadauer, expectant: deinde opibus illis vti nesciunt, sed in suam perniciem conuertunt. Parentes enim eorum colligendis thesauris intenti, nō curarunt vt liberos suos rectè educarent. Crates Thebanus misratus est illam hominum stultitiam, quod opes tanta cura coacervarent, quas postea liberis relinquerent, quorum interim nullam rationem haberent, neque darent operam, ut recte eis uti possent. Quid autē opes in manu stulti aliud sunt, quam gladius in manu furentis? Quid prodest habere varia instrumenta, quorum usum nescias? Experimur opes iustē partas, saepē nimis instar diffluere, quid igitur de iniustē partis nobis promitteremus? Multa proverbia vulgò iactantur de iniustis opibus, quorum veritatem eventus comprobat, quale est illud. Male partum, male disperit: item,
units.tr: Many things drive a man to gather riches by wicked arts. Some, distrusting God, hope that they will not obtain by just ways what is needed for living, and so they turn to evil arts. Others, however are not content with necessities, but desire to have even what pertains to pleasure and luxury. Very many, wishing to provide for the advantage of their children and grandchildren, heap up wealth by right and wrong, for those children to use afterwards. Care and concern for children is indeed not condemned when it is moderate, but what exceeds the measure and is joined with distrust is another matter. Such people, even if they practise some honest trade, demand too much for their labours, and very often they apply themselves to impious arts, polluting themselves with thefts, sacrileges and embezzlement. But what, finally, will be the outcome? Achan no doubt wished to provide for his children too, but by the road he followed he exposed them to dreadful flames. So today also, those who wish to provide for their children by unlawful ways involve both themselves and their children in the gravest evils. For the children wait for their parents' death like vultures waiting for a carcass; then they do not know how to use those riches, but turn them to their own ruin. Their parents, intent on heaping up treasure, did not take care to bring up their children rightly. Crates of Thebes marvelled at that folly of men, that they should pile up wealth with such care, to leave to their children, of whom meanwhile they took no account and made no effort to ensure they could use it rightly. What, indeed, are riches in the hand of a fool but a sword in the hand of a madman? What good is it to have various tools whose use you do not know? We often see justly gained wealth dwindle away quickly; what then can we promise ourselves from unjustly gained wealth? Many proverbs are commonly repeated about unjust riches, and experience confirms their truth, such as that saying: "What is badly gotten is badly lost"; likewise:

units.la: De male quaesitis, nō gaudet tertius hæres, &c.
units.tr: "Of ill-gotten goods the third heir takes no joy," and so on.

units.la: Micheas 6.cap. opes fraude & scelere partas, igni comparat, quod etiam iustē partas, atq; ipsos possessores absumant. Multæ gnomæ extant in Prouerbijs Salomonis contra opes iniustē collectas, quæ omnia nobis veternum excutere deberent. Præstat exiguas, aut omnino nullas opes habere iustē, quàm ingentes malè partas. Quare si quàm optimè consultum vis liberis, ne compares opes do-lis & lis & fraudibus, nō enim maiore damno eos afficies, quàm hac via opes colligendo: recte instituę liberos, non solùm verbis, sed etiam vitæ exemplo. Semperā hoc triste Achani supplicium, veluti speculum inspicito. Non enim est quod putemus Deum nimis seuerè cum eo egisse, cum videamus illa seueritate paucos admodum à vitijs auocare. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Micah 6 compares wealth gathered by fraud and wickedness to fire, which consumes even what was justly gained, and the possessors themselves. Many sayings in the Proverbs of Solomon are against wealth unjustly collected, and all of them ought to shake us out of our drowsiness. It is better to have little, or nothing at all, justly, than great wealth ill-gotten. Therefore, if you wish your children to be provided for as well as possible, do not procure wealth by tricks and frauds. You will not harm them more by any other means than by gathering wealth in this way. Bring up your children rightly, not only by words but also by the example of your life. Always look upon this sad punishment of Achan as a mirror. For there is no reason to think that God dealt too severely with him, since we see that with such severity very few are called back from their vices. Thus he.

units.la: Pauperes quod attinet, qui vnà cum liberis & vxoribus cum fame conflictantur, & illi officij sui admonendi sunt, quomodo erga Deum & homines se gerere debeant.
units.tr: As for the poor, who struggle with hunger together with their children and wives, they too must be reminded of their duty, of how they ought to conduct themselves towards God and men.

units.la: Primò crucem hanc diuinitus sibi impositam tam patienter ferant. Inquies facile quidem dictu, sed non factu est. Fateor, caro enim nostra vix adduci potest, vt famem patien-ter ferat. Nam, vt Cato dicebat: Venter caret auribus. Famelici non patienter se ossi-cij admonere patiuntur, non de officio, sed de cibo loquentes libenter audiunt, potius quid edant, quam quid faciant solliciti sunt. Sed vt patientiores simus, cogitandum nobis est, non fortuito, vel inscio Deo nobis hæc contingere: sed diuinitus copiam & inopiam mitti, vt pluribus nuper diximus. Dein sciendum est Deum vota & suspiria famelicorum nō la-tere. Etiamsi nos fame premat, tamen pater noster est, vt oratione Dominica & Symbo-lo Apostolico confitemur, ideo nos paterno animo castigat vt emendet, non vt perdat. Qui fructus sint crucis fidelium, proxima cō-cione dictum est, nimirum vt ad pœniten-tiam nos vocet, pietatis studium & ad preces nos excitet. Cogitandum quoq; tibi est, te non solum nec etiam primum esse, nec ul-timum fore qui hæc perferat. Christus ipse nostra causa esurijt, Paulus & alij viri pij (de quibus aliâs) famem quoq; pertulerunt. Promittit deniq; nobis Deus quòd supra vi-res nos tentare nolit. Nullus pater tam cru-deli animo erga filium affectus est, vt ei o-nus viribus granius imponat, ita vt sub eo succumbat, aut eum fame perire patiatur cū ei posset succurrere. Multò minus Deus qui plus quam paterno erga nos animo affectus est, hoc faciet. Quin vis[?] in igne, aqua, captiuitate & fame nobis gratia & auxilio suo aderit, & cum ei visum fuerit, varias habet rationes, quibus suos ex malis eripere potest.
units.tr: First, let them bear this cross laid upon them by God so patiently. You will say this is easy to say but not to do. I admit it, for our flesh can scarcely be brought to bear hunger patiently. For, as Cato used to say, the belly has no ears. The hungry do not patiently allow themselves to be reminded of their duty; speaking of food rather than of duty, they gladly listen, and they are more anxious about what they will eat than about what they do. But that we may be more patient, we must consider that these things do not happen to us by chance or without God's knowledge, but that abundance and scarcity are sent by God, as we said at length recently. Next, you must know that God does not overlook the prayers and sighs of the hungry. Even if hunger presses us, he is nevertheless our Father, as we confess in the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed; so he chastises us with a fatherly mind in order to correct us, not to destroy us. What fruits the cross brings to the faithful was said in the sermon last week: namely, that it calls us to repentance and stirs us to zeal for godliness and to prayer. You must also consider that you are neither the first nor the last to endure this. Christ himself hungered for our sake, and Paul and other godly men (of whom elsewhere) also suffered hunger. Finally, God promises us that he will not allow us to be tried beyond our strength. No father is so cruel in his feelings toward a son as to lay a burden on him heavier than his strength, so that he sinks under it, or to let him perish of hunger when he could help him. Much less will God, who is disposed toward us with more than a fatherly mind, do this. Indeed, in fire, water, captivity and famine God will be present to us with his grace and help, and when it pleases him he has various means by which he can rescue his own from evils.

units.la: Pauperes denique erga Deum & homi-nes se recte gerant. Erga Deum, ab illis re-bus studiose sibi caueant, quibus ira Dei provocatur, ut nobis famem immittat, incum-bat pijs precibus & alijs pietatis exercitijs.
units.tr: Finally, the poor should conduct themselves rightly towards God and towards men. Towards God, let them carefully guard themselves against those things by which the wrath of God is provoked so that he sends us famine, and let them devote themselves to pious prayers and other exercises of piety.

units.la: Erga eos, qui ipsorum egestatem sublevant, grati sint: sunt adhuc multi viri boni, qui mutuo dando, donando, fideiubendo, ero-gando eleemosynas, misericordiam & beneficentiam suam testantur. Quare si non es soluendo, obnixe orato creditorem, ne te ni-mis urgeat. Dein si ad certum tempus ex-pectat, quae promittis fideliter praestato.
units.tr: Towards those who relieve their want, let them be grateful. There are still many good men who show their mercy and kindness by lending, giving, standing surety, and bestowing alms. Therefore, if you cannot pay, earnestly beg your creditor not to press you too hard. Then, if he waits for a fixed time, faithfully do what you have promised.

units.la: Hic enim multum a debitoribus pecca-tur, &c. Multi paupertatem & multitudi-nem liberorum praetexunt, quum satisfaciendum est creditoribus, interim dies noctesq; pergraecantur.
units.tr: For here debtors sin greatly, etc. Many plead poverty and the number of their children, when they ought to be satisfying their creditors, and meanwhile they spend their days and nights in gambling.

units.la: Pauperes item iustis & legitimis medijs & rationibus utantur, ut ex fame emer-gere possint: laborent manibus suis & potius statim cibum quaerant, quam quod illicitis artibus egestati suae consulere velint. Satan non quiescit, sed obambulat famelici leonis instar, ut famelicos ad quævis scelera, puta ad seditionem, furta, latrocinia, scortationes, lenocinia stimulet, & ita turpi quaestu victum quaerant. Sed huiusmodi diabolicae suggestiones non sunt audiendæ. Proba matrona, si à procis tentetur, illos repudiat & reijcit. Ita nos quoque insultus hosce repudiare debemus. Christum quoque cum 40. dies in deserto ieiunasset, & tandem esurijsset, tentauit diabolus, sed ipse diabolum gladio verbi Dei profligauit. Paulus Rom.8. scribit: Nec angustiam, nec famem, nec rerum caritatem nos à charitate Christi separare posse. Saguntinos fideliores decet esse: illi potius fame perire voluere, quàm Romanis socijs & confœderatus fidem fallere. Ita nec nos à Deo summo principe famis impatientia deficiamus. Patriarchae, ut prima concione pluribus diximus: fame coacti, sedes potius, quam religionem mutare voluere. Hodie id nobis diligenter observandum est: Multi in hac dura fame egenos religionem mutare iubent, si velint ut ipsis succurratur. Est autem & illud res pessimi exempli, si & ipsi pauperes erga pauperiores sunt in-humani.
units.tr: Likewise, let the poor use just and lawful means and methods so that they can rise out of famine. Let them labour with their own hands and seek food at once, rather than wish to provide for their want by illicit arts. Satan does not rest but prowls like a hungry lion, to goad the hungry into every kind of crime, such as sedition, theft, robbery, fornication, and procuring, so that they seek a living by shameful gain. But such diabolical suggestions must not be heeded. A virtuous matron, if tempted by suitors, rejects and spurns them. So we too ought to repudiate these assaults. When Christ had fasted forty days in the wilderness and at last grew hungry, the devil tempted him, but he himself routed the devil with the sword of the word of God. Paul writes in Romans 8: that neither distress, nor famine, nor the nakedness of things can separate us from the love of Christ. The Saguntines ought to be more faithful: they preferred to perish by famine rather than break faith with their Roman allies and confederates. So too we must not fail our supreme Prince, God, through impatience at famine. The patriarchs, as we said at length in the first sermon, when compelled by famine, chose to change their dwelling rather than their religion. Today we must carefully observe this: many, in this harsh famine, command the needy to change their religion if they want help. Moreover, it is also a matter of the worst example if the poor themselves are inhuman towards those poorer than they are.

units.la: Meminerint etiam pauperes, ut si fertiles anni Deo annuente redierint, rem familiarem diligenter administrent, non omnia turpiter ut ante solebant, profundant, sed frugalitate sibi mature prospiciat[?]. Est enim ut vulgo dicitur: Parsimonia magnum ve-ctigal. Item & illud diligenter considerent: Sera est in fundo parsimonia. Multi malè ratiocinantur, Nosodochia & Xenodochia in hunc usum constructa sunt, ut illic egeni alantur. At consultius esset ita rei familiari prospicere, ut hac misera consolatione opus non haberent. Nam qui reditus sui rationem nō habet, eum egere tandē dura necessitas cogit.
units.tr: Let the poor also remember that, if by God's assent fruitful years return, they should manage their household affairs carefully, not squander everything shamefully as they used to, but provide for themselves early by frugality. For, as the common saying goes: thrift is a great revenue. Likewise let them consider this carefully: thrift comes too late when it is at the bottom of the barrel. Many reason badly: hospitals for the sick and for strangers have been built for this purpose, so that the needy may be fed there. But it would be wiser to provide for one's household affairs so that they would have no need of this wretched consolation. For the one who takes no account of his income, harsh necessity at last compels to be needy.

units.la: Ex his intelligitur, quid omnibus & singulis, in publica hac calamitate facto opus sit. Si qui sint viri pij qui non sperant emendationem, ipsi interim officio suo fideliter fungantur: non aliorum exempla imitari debent. Si Noe, Loth, alijq; voluissent corrupti mundi exemplum sequi, cum illo quoque perijssent. Nam & electos ac pios in extremis angustijs conseruare potest & solet.
units.tr: From this it is understood what must be done by everyone and each one in this public calamity. If there are any pious men who do not hope for amendment, let them meanwhile faithfully discharge their duty; they ought not to imitate the examples of others. If Noah, Lot, and others had wished to follow the example of a corrupt world, they would have perished with it. For he both can and is wont to preserve the elect and the pious even in the greatest distress.

units.la: Vltimo nunc loco, consolationis vice audiamus suauissimas Dei promissiones, quibus pijs auxilium suum offert. Pollicetur nanque si verbum illius audiuerimus & in vijs eius ambulauerimus, se velle nos famis tempore alere. Vt enim Deut.28.contemptoribus verbi sui famem minatur, ita vicissim populo suo pollicetur, si audierint verbum eius, & mandata eius obseruauerint, se thesaurum aperturum benignitatis suæ, opportuno tempore daturum pluuias, & benedicturum laboribus manuum ipsorum. Leuit. 26. Terram producturam[?] fruges & fructus, & pane satiandos esse: lege totum caput. Salomon in præsenti capite, vt nuper diximus, hoc in primis agit in dedicatione templi, quod Deum orat, vt orantes & clamantes ad se benigne exaudire velit, & expressis quidem verbis promisit Dominus Solomoni se benignus auribus ex fide preces ad se clamantium auditurum. Elephaz in libro Iobi rectè dicit cap.10. In fame Dominus te conseruat seruat à morte, & in bello à gladio. Prouer. 1o.cap. [?] Dominus animam iusti non sinit esurire. Quæ verba author noster pie & docte in Comment. suis expendit. Hæc gnome(in-quit) dulcissimam consolationem contra tentationem de victu continet. Vix autem maior est tentatio. Semper enim veremur, ne fame pereamus: & quanto morti sumus vi-ciniores, tanto magis hac cura tangimur. Augent in nobis hoc malum, peruersa mundi studia, & impia prouerbia, quæ circum-fert de parandis diuitiis per fas & nefas. Nisi vero repugnemus huic tentationi, ad impias vias conuertimur, quibus victum paremus, & in magna scelera ruimus, in furta, rapinas, latrocinia, sacrilegia, proditi-tiones: multi relinquunt uxores & liberos, atque in desperationem interdum incidunt. Hæc igitur sententia, & aliæ similes, dili-genter expendendæ sunt, vt contra pericu-losissimam tentationem, conscientias munimus. Et mox: Iustum vocat, qui fiduciam suam in Deo ponit, qui scit se ab eo seruari ac gubernari, suamq; vocationem sectatur, qui, vt Christus dicit, Regnum Dei quaerit, eiusq; iustitiam, &c. Haec ille. Psalmo 37. dicit regius propheta: Tempore periculoso iusti non cōfunduntur, & fame oriente aluntur: Et mox, Iunior fui & senui, & non vidi iustum derelictum, nec semen eius quaerens panem. Licet iusti sint misericordes & liberales, libenterq; mutuum dent, tamen posteris illorum nil deerit. Rursum Psalm.33. Ecce oculi Domini super timentibus eum, & ad eos qui expectant pietatem eius, vt à morte animam eorum liberet, & nutriat eos fame. Item Psalm.34. Temerarij & audaces homines fame affliguntur, obseruan tibus autem Dominum nihil deerit. In Prophetis multa passim extant testimonia, quae ostendunt Deum populo suo, si ad ipsum conuertantur, gratiam suam conferre velle, & vbertatem rerum omnium dare. Vide Ose. 2. Ioelis 1. & 2. Amos 2. Zach.8. Malach. 3. quibus in locis ostendit Dominus se facile posse & velle frugum calamitatem resarcire, si conuertantur. Zach.10. Petite pluuias & dabitur vobis. Matth.6. pluribus prohibet solicitam & anxiam curam de victu & amictu, quin primo & ante omnia quaerentibus regnum Dei haec omnia pollicetur.
units.tr: Last of all, let us now hear, by way of consolation, the most sweet promises of God, by which he offers his help to the pious. For he promises that if we hear his word and walk in his ways, he will be willing to feed us in the time of famine. For as in Deut. 28 he threatens famine to those who despise his word, so in turn he promises his people that, if they hear his word and keep his commandments, he will open the treasury of his goodness, give rain in due season, and bless the labours of their hands. Lev. 26: the land will yield its crops and fruits, and they will be satisfied with bread; read the whole chapter. Solomon in the present chapter, as we said recently, deals chiefly with this in the dedication of the temple, where he prays God that he would be willing to hear graciously those who pray and cry out to him; and the Lord, in express words, promised Solomon that he would graciously listen with his ears to the prayers of those who cry out to him in faith. Eliphaz in the book of Job rightly says, cap. 10: In famine the Lord preserves you from death, and in war from the sword. Proverbs, chap. 10 [?]: the Lord does not allow the soul of the righteous to hunger. Our author weighs these words piously and learnedly in his Commentaries. This saying, he says, contains a most sweet consolation against the temptation concerning food. Yet scarcely any temptation is greater. For we always fear lest we perish by hunger, and the nearer we are to death, the more we are troubled by this care. Perverse pursuits of the world and impious proverbs, which are current about acquiring riches by right and wrong, increase this evil in us. Unless we resist this temptation, we are turned to impious ways by which to obtain food, and we rush into great crimes: into theft, plunder, robbery, sacrilege, betrayal; many abandon wives and children, and sometimes fall into despair. Therefore this sentence, and others like it, must be carefully weighed, so that we may fortify consciences against this most dangerous temptation. And soon after: he calls righteous the one who places his trust in God, who knows that he is kept and governed by him, and pursues his calling, who, as Christ says, seeks the kingdom of God and his righteousness, etc. Thus he. In Psalm 37 the royal prophet says: In a time of peril the righteous are not confounded, and in the rising of famine they are fed. And soon after: I have been young and have grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging for bread. Although the righteous are merciful and liberal, and willingly lend, yet nothing will be lacking to their posterity. Again, Psalm 33: Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, and upon those who hope in his mercy, to deliver their soul from death and to feed them in famine. Likewise Psalm 34: Rash and bold men are afflicted by famine, but nothing will be lacking to those who seek the Lord. In the Prophets there are many testimonies scattered about which show that God wills to bestow his grace on his people and to give abundance of all things, if they turn to him. See Hosea 2, Joel 1 and 2, Amos 2, Zechariah 8, Malachi 3, in which places the Lord shows that he can easily and is willing to make good the calamity of crops, if they turn. Zechariah 10: Ask for rain and it will be given to you. Matthew 6: he forbids in many words anxious and troubled care about food and clothing, and promises all these things to those who seek first and above all the kingdom of God.

units.la: Hæ non nudæ sunt promissiones, sed eas privatis & publicis exemplis illustrauit & confirmauit. Permultos tempore famis mirabiliter aluit, plures etiam malis eripuit. Pauca quædam ex multis audiamus. Mo-sem quadraginta dies & totidem noctes sine omni cibo & potu, diuina sua virtute in monte Sinai conseruauit. Heliam ad torrentem Carith, in solitudine ministerio coruorum ma-ne & vespere panes & carnes afferentium aluit. Sic carniuora animalia si necessitas postulat mandante Deo homini seruiunt. Idem ad viduam Sareptanã missus, illa panem quem unicum habebat petenti dedit, eoq; absumpto certam sibi mortem imminere videbat. Is ergo a Domino precibus impetrauit, ut cadus farinæ & olei lecythus nunquam deficeret, quoad fames grauissima quæ triennium integrum durauit, cessauit. Citatur hoc exemplum à Domine Luce 4. viduis inprimis consolationi seruit. Mox cum minas Iesabellis fugeret in deserto ab Angelo cibum & potum accipit, cuius virtute 40. diebus & totidem noctibus ad mon-tem Horeb profectus est.
units.tr: These are not bare promises; he has illustrated and confirmed them by examples, both private and public. He miraculously fed very many in time of famine, and also rescued many from evils. Let us hear a few of the many. He preserved Moses for forty days and as many nights without any food or drink by his divine power on Mount Sinai. He fed Elijah at the brook Cherith in the wilderness by the ministry of ravens bringing him bread and flesh morning and evening. So carnivorous animals, when necessity demands, serve man at God's command. The same Elijah, sent to the widow of Zarephath, she gave him the bread she had, the only one she possessed, when he asked for it, and seeing that once it was used up certain death was hanging over her. He therefore obtained from the Lord by prayer that the jar of meal and the flask of oil should never fail, until the most severe famine, which lasted a full three years, ceased. This example is cited by the Lord in Luke 4, and served chiefly as a consolation for widows. Soon afterwards, when he was fleeing the threats of Jezebel into the wilderness, he received food and drink from an angel, by whose strength he went forty days and as many nights to Mount Horeb.

units.la: Publica quoque exempla ad nostram cō-solationem plurima extant. Deus cum educeret populum suum ex Ægypto miraculose illos in deserto 40. annis aluit & conseruauit, ita ut ne vestes quidem eorum attritae fuerint. Manna à cœlis dedit quotidie, prohibuit, ne plus colligerent, quam in diem suf-ficeret. Cum non haberent dulces aquas, Mosem petram percutere iubet, aqua assa-tim profluebat, ita ut iumenta quoque pota-re potuerint. Tandem cum Manna pertæsi essent, & peterent carnes, dat illis quoque miraculose. Nā ut scriptura loquitur: Profectus est ventus à Domino, qui abripiens coturnices à mari disiicens eos ad castra circumquaque spatio itineris diurni fere duobus cubitus [?] in superficie terrae. Et surgens populus colligerunt toto illo die & tota nocte, toto denique sequenti die coturnices, quique parum collegit, collegit decem Homer (est decima pars Ephae.) Samaritanos, qui iu-bente Propheta Helisaeo hosti dedere no-lebant, contra opinionem eorum liberavit.
units.tr: Public examples of comfort are also abundant. When God led his people out of Egypt, he miraculously fed and sustained them in the wilderness for forty years, so that even their clothes did not wear out. He gave them manna from heaven every day, and forbade them to gather more than would suffice for the day. When they had no sweet water, he bade Moses strike the rock, and water flowed out so abundantly that the beasts could drink as well. At last, when they were weary of the manna and asked for meat, he gave them that too, miraculously. For, as Scripture says: "A wind went out from the LORD, which brought quails from the sea and let them fall by the camp, about a day's journey on every side, about two cubits above the surface of the earth. And the people rose up and gathered quails all that day and all that night, and all the next day; and he who gathered least gathered ten homers (a homer is the tenth part of an ephah)." He also delivered the Samaritans, who, at the command of the prophet Elisha, were unwilling to surrender to the enemy, contrary to their expectation.

units.la: Dux quidam, qui prophetae dictis fidem adhibere noluit, vidit equidem haec, sed à populo oppressus tanta Dei benignitate frui non potuit 2. Reg. 7. In novo Testamento Chri-stus turbas mirifice aluit. Matthei 14. quinque panibus, & duobus piscibus, ingentem multitudinem hominum cibavit. Matthei 15. septem panibus & paucis pisciculis, qua-tuor ferè millia cibavit, & septem cophini fragmentorum sublati sunt. Item Ioann. 6. Hoc autem miraculum ideo toties repetit, ut inde solidiorem consolationem petamus.
units.tr: A certain captain, who refused to give credence to the prophet's words, indeed saw these things, but, trampled by the people, could not enjoy so great a kindness of God (2 Kings 7). In the New Testament Christ marvellously fed the crowds. In Matthew 14 he fed a huge multitude of men with five loaves and two fish. In Matthew 15 he fed about four thousand with seven loaves and a few small fish, and seven baskets of fragments were taken up. Likewise in John 6. He repeats this miracle so often so that we may seek from it a firmer consolation.

units.la: Inquies: Si nostris quoque temporibus idem Christus faceret. Facit, sed oscitantes non observamus. Rationem quaeso ineas, quibus tibi opus sit, & vicissim quid lucreris, senties singularem erga te Dei benedi[?]tionem: potest enim & vult nobis benedice-re, si ipsum inquam obseruamus & colimus: sin vero neque Deum, neque verbum ipsius curamus, in precibus negligentes sumus nec de vitæ emendatione sumus soliciti, mirum non est, in tanta securitate perpetua nosfa[?] me laborare.
units.tr: You will say: "If Christ did the same in our times?" He does, but we do not notice, being careless. Please consider what you need, and in turn what you gain; you will feel God's singular blessing toward you. For he can and will bless us, if, I say, we observe and worship him; but if we neither heed God nor his word, are negligent in prayers, and are not anxious about amending our lives, it is no wonder that in such a continual security we suffer [the text here is garbled].

units.la: Sæpius etiam memoria nostra in extre-ma inopia rerum quidam sine omni cibo per aliquot tempus conseruati sunt. Fateor in-terdum hic quoque imposturas commissas fuisse. Certum tamen est vere hæc non mul-tos ante annos facta fuisse. Sic apud Intersyluanos Heluetios, Frater Nicolaus, no-stræ gentis verus Propheta, sine omni victu & potu unum & 20. annos vixit. Angelo quam homini similior. Quo miraculo Deus haud dubiè nostram gentem docere voluit, si consilio F. Nicolai obtemperauerimus (fuit id, vitare peregrinorum Principum fœdera, & pensiones annuas, et fugere mercenariam militiam) velle & posse illum nos in his mo-tanis regionibus, perinde ac ipsum alere conseruare. Non opus vt his artibus victu quaeramus.
units.tr: Very often, too, within our own memory, some people have been kept alive for a time without any food in extreme want of things. I admit that deceptions have sometimes been practised here as well. Yet it is certain that these things truly happened not many years ago. Thus among the Intersylvan Swiss, Brother Nicholas, a true prophet of our nation, lived for twenty-one years without any food or drink, more like an angel than a man. By this miracle God undoubtedly wished to teach our nation that, if we obey Brother Nicholas's counsel (it was to avoid the alliances of foreign princes and their annual pensions, and to flee mercenary soldiering), he is willing and able to nourish and preserve us in these mountain regions just as he did himself. We have no need to seek our food by these arts.

units.la: Relatum quoque est in fastos, Friderici Austriaci Imperatoris insigne & prudens factum. Is in Comitijs Coloniae habitis, quò magna multitudo hominum confluebat, numerare iussit homines pariter & panes, veritus nimirum ne in tanta hominum multitudine prae inopia comitia soluerentur. Diligenti quidem inquisitione facta, multitudinem hominum numerum panis longe superare deprehendit. Crastina relatum est, plures etiam panes superfuisse. Nos non obseruamus iuditia diuina.
units.tr: It is also recorded in the annals of a notable and prudent deed of Frederick, Emperor of Austria. At the diet held at Cologne, to which a great multitude of people flocked, he ordered the people and the loaves to be counted, fearing, of course, that the assembly might break up for lack of food in so great a crowd. After a careful inquiry was made, he found that the number of people far exceeded the number of loaves. On the next day it was reported that even more loaves had been left over. We do not observe the judgements of God.

units.la: Extat & in Stumpfij annalibus memorabile exemplum auxilij diuini in extrema fame. Anno 849. erat maxima fames in Germania, in qua multi miserè perierunt. Apud Turingos quidam sedes cum vxore & liberis fame coactus mutare voluit: cùm transfiret syluam famis rabie efferatus, filium interficere & comedere meditatur, iam iam conceptum facinus perpetrare voluit, subitò[?] Deo ita prouidente, duos lupos ceruam discerpentes cōspicit, è vestigio lætus manus abstinet, & à fera lupos abigit & carnibus ferae cum liberis vescitur. Sigebertus refert ad annum 851.
units.tr: Also in Stumpf's annals there is a memorable example of divine help in extreme famine. In the year 849 there was a great famine in Germany, in which many perished wretchedly. Among the Thuringians a certain man, compelled by hunger, wished to move his home with his wife and children. As he crossed a forest, driven mad by the rage of hunger, he planned to kill and eat his son, and was about to carry out the crime already conceived, when God, providing so, suddenly showed him two wolves tearing apart a deer. Straightaway, glad, he refrained his hand, drove the wolves from the beast, and ate the flesh of the deer with his children. Sigebert reports this under the year 851.

units.la: Anno Domini 1570. In Bauaria frumentum pluit, ex quo multi panes pinsuerunt. Voluit in illa rerum inopia auxilij sui spem facere. Idem factum est in regno Neapolitano, Anno Domini 722. & apud Vascones anno 828.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1570, grain rained down in Bavaria, from which many people baked bread. In that scarcity of things he wished to give them hope of his help. The same happened in the kingdom of Naples in the year of the Lord 722, and among the Vascones in the year 828.

units.la: Etsi vero hæ promissiones verissimæ sint, non tamen ita accipiendæ sunt, quasi omni cruce cariturisimus[?]. Prophetæ & Apostoli & Christus quoque famem experti sunt. Deus enim quando & quomodo ei visum fuerit, sua dona distribuit. Esurire nos permittit, ut ardentiores in precibus simus. Præterea etsi negat terrena, nobis tamen maiora dat dona, fidem, patientiam & spem.
units.tr: Although these promises are most true, they are not to be taken as though we were to be free of every cross. Prophets, apostles, and Christ himself also experienced hunger. For God distributes his gifts when and how it seems good to him. He allows us to hunger, so that we may be more fervent in prayer. Moreover, although he denies us earthly things, he nevertheless gives us greater gifts: faith, patience, and hope.

units.la: Utque finem tractationi huic tandem imponam, Christus Matthæi vigesimoquarto, Lucæ vigesimo primo, prædixit, ultimis tempotemporibus famem extremi & jam jam futuri judicii signum fore. Jubet nos capita levare & bono animo esse, atque ita nos comparare, ut coram tribunali eius apparere valeamus, & cum ipso omnibusque electis, ex fame aliisque miseriis liberati, vitam æternam ingrediamur.
units.tr: And so that I may finally bring this discourse to an end: Christ, in Matthew 24 and Luke 21, foretold that famine would be a sign of the last times and of the extreme and now imminent judgement. He bids us lift up our heads and be of good cheer, and so to prepare ourselves that we may be able to appear before his tribunal, and with him and all the elect, freed from famine and other miseries, enter into eternal life.

units.la: SVb imperio Maximini & Licinij persequtorū Christianæ religionis, fames fuit tāta, ut ūna tritici mēsura bis mille et quingentis Atticis venderetur. Factum inde est, ut per ciuitates infinita hominū multitudo fame cōsecta, mortua sit: maior vero ꝑ vicos & agros pestileti[?] morbo: Alij vero quæ charissima & pretiosissima haberent pro tenuis-simo cibo ditioribus vendebant: alij possessionibus suis paulatim diuenditis, ad extremā egestatem redacti sunt. Quidā modicas graminis minutias mandentes, & lethiferis herbis promiscuò vescentes, valetudinem corruperunt. Nonnullæ etiam per ciuitates nobiles fœminæ adextremam inopiā redactæ, ad agros mendicandi gratia se receperunt. Et alij quidem viribus exhausti, velut examina simulachra, huc illuc vacillantes, nutantesq; et collabantes in medijs plateis pro-cidebant: cidebant: supiniq, palmis extensis, ut pauxillum sibi cibi porrigeretur, supplicitèr orabant atque in extremis constituti, animā que agentes, esurire se clamabant, ad hanc e-tiam vocem perferendam vix valentes. Sic igitur in medio foro, et per angi portus, mortua ac nuda cadauera pluribus diebus inhumata & proiecta, miserabile videntibus spectaculum exhibebant. Cùmque & canum cibi nonnulli fierent, ob eamque causam potissimùm aliqui canes interficerent, veriti ne rabidi facti[?], ad vorandos, & laniandos homines conuerteretur, &c.
units.tr: Under the rule of Maximinus and Licinius, the persecutors of the Christian religion, there was such a famine that one measure of wheat was sold for two thousand five hundred Attic [drachmas]. As a result, an endless multitude of people died of hunger in the cities, and even greater numbers died of pestilential disease in the villages and fields. Others sold their most precious and valuable possessions to the richer people for the most meagre food. Others, having gradually sold off their estates, were reduced to utter destitution. Some, eating small scraps of grass and consuming deadly herbs indiscriminately, ruined their health. Several noblewomen in the cities also were reduced to extreme poverty and retreated to the countryside to beg. Some, drained of strength, staggered here and there like ghosts, swaying, tottering and collapsing, and fell down in the middle of the streets. They lay on their backs with palms outstretched, humbly begging that a little food be given them; and those at the point of death, gasping for breath, cried out that they were starving, barely able to utter even this cry. So in the middle of the marketplace and through the back alleys and harbours, dead and naked corpses lay unburied and abandoned for many days, offering a pitiful sight to onlookers. And since some people became food for dogs, some men for this reason killed dogs in particular, fearing that they might turn rabid and turn to devouring and mangling human beings, etc.

units.la: DE ALENDIS ET COERCEN-dis mendicis, appendix.
units.tr: On the feeding and restraining of beggars, an appendix.

units.la: Carolus M. in Constitutionibus imperat, ut pauperes in plateis aut quadriuijs iacentes, Ecclesiae alant. Ac in alio loco inquit: De mendicis, qui per plateas discurrunt, volumus, ut vnusquisq; fidelium nostrorum pauperem de beneficio, aut de propria familia enutriat, & non permittat alicubi ire mendicando: & vbi tales inuenti fuerint, nisi manibus laborent, nullus ei quicquam tribuere præsumat.
units.tr: Charlemagne, in his Constitutions, orders that the poor lying in the squares or at the crossroads be fed by the Church. In another place he says: Concerning beggars who run about through the streets, we want each of our faithful to feed a poor man from his benefice or from his own household, and not to allow him to go begging anywhere. And wherever such people are found, unless they work with their hands, let no one presume to give them anything.
